questions.prompt: A publisher signs a game patch, and Windows checks the signature on your machine. Which key does each side use?
questions.explanation: Only the private key can make a signature that the matching public key accepts, so it never leaves the publisher. The public key travels inside the certificate, where anyone can use it to check. If checking needed the private key, every user would hold the secret needed to sign malware.
options: The publisher signs with its private key; Windows checks with the public key in the certificate
The publisher signs with its public key; Windows checks with the private key in the certificate
Both sides use one shared secret key that was exchanged when the patch was first released
Windows uses no key at all, because the file's hash alone shows who made the file

questions.prompt: What does a SHA-256 hash do for trust?
options: It moves trust from where the hash came onto the bytes on your disk
It creates trust by proving which person originally wrote the file
It removes the need to trust any source of the file or of the hash
It proves the program is free of bugs and of any hidden behavior
questions.explanation: A hash says only that bytes match a recorded value. How far you can trust that depends on how the hash reached you.

questions.prompt: You download `mod.zip` and `mod.zip.sha256` from one page that an attacker can change. You hash the zip and it matches. What have you learned?
options: Nothing useful, because the attacker could write both files to agree
That the zip is safe, since a hash value cannot be faked by anyone
That the page's owner signed the zip with a key that only they hold
That the zip has no bugs, since the hash matched the value shown
questions.explanation: Verification succeeds, but the attacker wrote both the bytes and the hash. The match proves nothing about who made them.

questions.prompt: When is comparing a downloaded file with a hash worth doing?
options: The hash reached you by a route the attacker does not control
The hash sits on the same page as the download link itself
Both files show the same upload date in the download listing
The hash is a shorter string than the name of the download file
questions.explanation: A separate channel, a signed release, or a value you recorded yourself from a trusted copy keeps one attacker from changing both.

questions.prompt: An attacker controls the download page and replaces both the file and its hash. Why can't they also replace the signature?
options: They lack the publisher's private key, so a new signature would not verify
Signatures are stored on a server that the attacker cannot reach
A signature is just a longer hash, so the same hash rules protect it
Windows refuses to open any file whose download page was modified
questions.explanation: Only the private key can produce a signature that the publisher's public key accepts.

questions.prompt: An attacker signs a modified game file with their own key pair. Why does Windows not accept it?
options: It matches only the attacker's key, whose certificate is untrusted
The signature has too many digits for Windows to read it in full
The attacker's private key is shared with the game's own publisher
The file hash no longer matches the length stored in the signature
questions.explanation: A signature can verify against its own public key, but the policy asks whether the certificate chain is one Windows trusts.

questions.prompt: Given only 119, you try divisors in order 2, 3, 5, and so on. Which is the first that divides it?
questions.explanation: 119 ÷ 7 = 17, so 7 is the first to work, while checking a proposed answer takes one division. RSA uses this gap with enormous numbers.

questions.prompt: A publisher's private key is stolen. What can the thief do?
options: Sign anything until the certificate is revoked
Nothing, since a signature cannot be reused
Only sign files the publisher already released
Read all files the publisher has encrypted
questions.explanation: The signature says who approved the bytes, not that they are safe. A stolen key lets the thief approve anything until revocation.

questions.prompt: A Wesnoth build reports no embedded signature. What does the lesson say?
options: Unsigned is not malicious; look for published hashes
It is malware, since every genuine program is always signed
It is safe, since unsigned files are unable to run any code
It means the file was damaged while it was being downloaded
questions.explanation: Many open-source builds are legitimately unsigned. Treat the result as one fact and ask the next question.

questions.prompt: Windows reports a file is explicitly distrusted. What is the reasonable next question?
options: Why did Windows policy reject this publisher or signature?
Does the project publish a hash that I can compare against?
Was the file damaged in transit from the download server?
Is the save format of this game supported by the editor?
questions.explanation: Each result in the table leads to a different next question. An explicit distrust is a policy decision.

questions.prompt: `WinVerifyTrust` returns a `LONG`. Which status means the trust action succeeded?
options: Exactly zero, and no other value
Any nonnegative number at all, zero included
Any number that is greater than zero
Every value apart from `0xFFFFFFFF` itself
questions.explanation: Microsoft says only exact zero means success. Using HRESULT-style 'nonnegative is success' logic is the bug that the diff fixes.

questions.prompt: `meaning(status)` receives a status it has no message for. What does the lab do?
options: Treats it as a failure and prints the code in hexadecimal
Treats it as success, since it is not one of the known errors
Retries the check in a loop until the status returned is 0
Marks the file as unsigned and then prints nothing more at all
questions.explanation: Unknown statuses remain failures. The printed hexadecimal value lets you look it up.

questions.prompt: What does `WTD_UI_NONE` do in the trust data?
options: Prevents pop-up dialogs while the verification runs
Disables the signature check on the selected file
Skips the SHA-256 hash computation for the file
Hides the name of the file in the printed result
questions.explanation: The lab runs from a command line, so no dialog may appear.

questions.prompt: Why is `WinVerifyTrust` called twice in `verify_authenticode`?
options: The second call frees state that the first one created
The second call repeats the check once more to be sure
The first call hashes the file and the second verifies it
The second call undoes a change that was made to the file
questions.explanation: `VERIFY` may create provider state, and `CLOSE` frees it. The status that is reported comes from the first call.

questions.prompt: The lab uses `WTD_REVOKE_NONE` and cache-only retrieval. What is the tradeoff?
options: The result lacks a fresh revocation check, so it is not final
The check runs slower because it contacts the network each time
The check accepts files signed with the obsolete MD2 and MD4 digests
The check cannot be run on any DLL file that sits beside the game
questions.explanation: These choices make a reproducible offline classroom run. A release pipeline should use a stricter revocation policy.

questions.prompt: Why do `wide_path`, `file_info`, and `trust_data` stay alive until both calls finish?
options: `PCWSTR` only points at the data, so its owner must outlive both calls
Rust deletes every local variable before a call unless told otherwise
Windows needs these three values to be global variables to read them
The second call frees them automatically once the check is closed
questions.explanation: A pointer into a dropped vector would dangle. The safety comment names exactly such facts.

questions.prompt: A Windows DLL shows no embedded signature. What does the lesson caution?
options: Some are signed through catalogs, so do not call them simply unsigned
Every DLL without an embedded signature is malicious in practice
The lab already handles catalog signatures for every file it checks
Catalog signatures are the same thing as plain SHA-256 file hashes
questions.explanation: The lab checks only the embedded signature. A wider inventory needs explicit catalog handling.

questions.prompt: After you install a mod, the checker reports new hashes for several game files. Which are expected?
options: Only the files the mod replaced; any others need explaining
All of them, since installing a mod reinstalls the whole game
None of them, since a file's hash never changes after install
Only the main executable, since it is the file that loads the mod
questions.explanation: A SHA-256 value belongs to one exact file. A change in a file the mod did not touch is unexplained.

questions.prompt: A trusted Authenticode signature is shown on a game's EXE. What does it not prove?
options: That the software has no bugs, or that you meant this version
That the bytes match what the publisher originally signed
That a certificate chain which Windows trusts was involved
That the file was not changed at any point after signing it
questions.explanation: Signatures speak about who approved the bytes under a policy. They do not say the software is bug-free.

questions.prompt: `sha256` reads the file in a 64 KiB buffer. How many bytes is that?
questions.explanation: 64 × 1,024 = 65,536. Streaming keeps memory small, so the file does not have to fit in memory.

questions.prompt: A `GSAV` save has `05` in its name-length byte at offset 11. At which offset does its checksum start?
questions.explanation: The fixed fields fill offsets 0 to 11, which is 12 bytes. The name takes the next 5 bytes, offsets 12 to 16, so the checksum starts at 12 + 5 = 17 and the file ends at 17 + 4 = 21 bytes.

questions.prompt: Nia's save is valid, with stored checksum 842. You change only the level byte at offset 10 from `03` to `04`. What sum does the loader compute, and what happens?
questions.explanation: The level byte used to add 3 and now adds 4, so the total rises by one: 842 − 3 + 4 = 843. The stored checksum still says 842, so the file is refused until the checksum bytes are rewritten as `4B 03 00 00`, because 843 = 3 × 256 + 75 and 75 = 4 × 16 + 11 = 0x4B.
options: 843, so it refuses the save
842, so it accepts the save
846, so it refuses the save
4, because only the level byte is summed

questions.prompt: Why is a plain text editor a poor tool for changing a binary save?
options: Saving can quietly change bytes, such as converting line endings
It cannot open any file that is larger than a few kilobytes in size
It displays each byte in decimal, which hides the real stored value
It refuses to save any file that lacks a `.txt` extension on its name
questions.explanation: A hex editor in overwrite mode writes the exact bytes you typed. A text editor treats the file as characters, so it can alter bytes you never touched.

questions.prompt: In a hex dump, a byte sits on row `00000010` under column `05`. What is its offset?
options: `0x15`, which is 21
`0x105`, which is 261
`0x50`, which is 80
`0x05`, which is 5
questions.explanation: Add the row offset and the column number: 0x10 + 0x05 = 0x15, and 16 + 5 = 21. Joining the digits as `105` is a common slip, and the column alone ignores the row.

questions.prompt: Byte `0x0F` of Nia's save is `4A`, and the character column shows a `J`. What does that tell you?
options: Every byte is drawn as a character, so a number byte can look like a letter
The name field really ends with the letter `J` at that offset in the file
The editor has found a second magic number hidden somewhere in the save
Printable bytes are always part of the name, so the `J` belongs to the name
questions.explanation: 4A is 74, the ASCII code for `J`, but it is the first byte of the checksum. Nothing in the file marks which bytes were meant as text.

questions.prompt: Gold sits at file offset 6. Where will you find it in the game's memory once the save is loaded?
options: At an address unrelated to 6 that usually changes between runs
At address 6, since the loader keeps every file offset as its address
At the file offset added to the module's base address in memory
At the same offset, but inside the graphics card's own memory
questions.explanation: The game copies fields into its own structures at addresses of its choosing. An offset is a distance within a file, not a memory address.

questions.prompt: You change byte 6 of the save on disk while the game is running. What happens to the gold on screen?
options: Nothing until the next load; the game may overwrite the edit on exit
It updates at once, since the game rereads the file on every frame
It updates only once the checksum bytes at the end are rewritten too
It resets to 250 because the loader restores the first value it saved
questions.explanation: The running game uses the copy in its own memory. Editing a file changes it only for the next load, and a save on exit can erase the edit.

questions.prompt: What job does the magic number `GSAV` do at the start of the save?
options: It identifies the format so the loader can refuse other files early
It stores the character's name, so the loader can show it first
It holds the version number, so the loader knows which layout applies
It is the checksum itself, so the loader can find damaged files quickly
questions.explanation: A fixed pattern at the start tells the loader what it was given. A file without `GSAV` would have its bytes misread as gold and levels.

questions.prompt: A `GSAV` save has version 2, but the lab accepts only 1. What should an editor do?
options: Refuse it with an `UnsupportedVersion` error, since fields may have moved
Treat it as version 1 and edit the gold at offset 6 regardless
Lower the version byte to 1 so that the loader will accept the file
Skip the version check and only recompute the checksum afterwards
questions.explanation: A new version means the layout may have changed. Forcing the version byte to 1 would only hide the mismatch and risk corrupting the save.

questions.prompt: The gold bytes read `10 27 00 00`, lowest byte first. What is the gold?
questions.explanation: 0x10 is 16 and 0x27 is 39, so the value is 16 + 39 × 256 = 10,000. Joining the digits as `1027` ignores that each byte is worth 256 times the one before.

questions.prompt: The gold bytes `FA 00 00 00` are read with the most significant byte first. What value do you get, and what does it suggest?
options: 4,194,304,000, which is absurd, so the order is wrong
250, which is plausible, so the order is right
65,536, which is plausible, so the order is right
4,194,304,000, which is plausible for a late-game hero
questions.explanation: Read that way it is 250 × 16,777,216 = 4,194,304,000. When one order gives billions and the other a modest number, the modest one is probably right.

questions.prompt: A save's name-length byte is `08`. How many bytes long is the whole file?
questions.explanation: Twelve fixed bytes, plus 8 name bytes, plus 4 checksum bytes gives 12 + 8 + 4 = 24. Forgetting the checksum gives 20.

questions.prompt: In a 19-byte save, the name-length byte reads `C8`. What should a careful loader do?
options: Compare 12 + 200 + 4 = 216 with the real size and return an error
Read 200 bytes of name and stop quietly at the end of the file
Treat `C8` as a checksum byte and look for the length elsewhere
Assume the name is 3 bytes because the file is 19 bytes long
questions.explanation: `C8` is 200, so the file claims to be far longer than it is. The lab checks the claim against the real size instead of reading past the end.

questions.prompt: In an unfamiliar save, a byte just before some text equals the number of characters after it. What is that pattern?
options: The fingerprint of a length-prefixed string
The marker of a string ended by a `00` byte
The version number of the file format
The first byte of a checksum field
questions.explanation: Storing the length first lets a loader read exactly that many bytes. Strings that end with a `00` byte have no count in front of them.

questions.prompt: Gold goes from 250 to 1,250, and bytes `0x06`, `0x07`, and `0x0F` differ between two saves. Why did `0x0F` change?
options: It starts the checksum, which changes when any covered byte does
It is part of the gold, since the gold field runs from offset 6 to 15
It is the name-length byte, which grows along with the gold
It is a timestamp that the game rewrites on every single save
questions.explanation: A byte that changes whenever any other value changes is the mark of a checksum. `0x0F` is where the stored sum starts.

questions.prompt: Gold changes from 250 to 1,250, and bytes 8 and 9 stay `00`. Why can't you yet say the field is two bytes wide?
options: They could be the upper half of a 4-byte field that is still zero
Bytes 8 and 9 always belong to the name length in this format
A two-byte field cannot hold any value above 255 at all
A comparison cannot show bytes that stay the same in both saves
questions.explanation: A value bigger than 65,535 would reveal whether byte 8 changes. Until then, unchanged zeros prove nothing about the field's width.

questions.prompt: Gold is changed from 250 to 9,999 (`0F 27 00 00`) and nothing else. What sum does the loader compute, with the stored checksum still 842?
options: 646, so it refuses the save
842, so it accepts the save
54, since only the gold bytes are summed
10,591, so it refuses the save
questions.explanation: The new gold bytes add 15 + 39 = 54 instead of 250, so the total is 842 − 250 + 54 = 646. It no longer matches, so the loader rejects the file.

questions.prompt: In the loader's flow, which check comes first?
options: Whether the first four bytes are `GSAV`
Whether the sum matches the stored checksum
Whether the version byte is 1
Whether the gold is under 65,535
questions.explanation: The magic number is checked before anything else, since a file that is not a `GSAV` save has no meaningful fields. The checksum is the last gate.

questions.prompt: Why do real formats often use a CRC-32 or a hash rather than a plain sum of bytes?
options: A sum cannot notice two bytes being swapped, as the total is the same
A plain sum always takes four more bytes of space than a CRC-32 does
A CRC-32 can be edited without changing any of the bytes it covers
A plain sum is too slow to compute for files larger than 19 bytes
questions.explanation: Addition ignores order, so swapped bytes go unnoticed. A CRC-32 is designed to change when bytes are reordered.

questions.prompt: Why can't you recompute a MAC or a digital signature the way you recomputed this checksum?
options: It depends on a secret key you do not have
It is stored in a different byte order than the game
It needs the file to be compressed with gzip first
It covers only the gold bytes, which cannot be changed
questions.explanation: A plain sum needs nothing secret, so anyone can redo it. A keyed check or signature can be produced only by the holder of the key.

questions.prompt: Why should you use overwrite mode rather than insert mode when changing gold?
options: An inserted byte would shift every later field, including the checksum
Insert mode refuses to accept hexadecimal digits that are typed in
Overwrite mode updates the checksum for you when the file is saved
Insert mode makes the game read a new version number from the file
questions.explanation: Gold fills exactly four bytes, so you replace those four. Inserting shifts everything after them and the file ends up one byte too long.

questions.prompt: Renaming Nia to Grace changes the name from 3 to 5 bytes. Which set of steps does the save need?
options: Insert two bytes, set the length to `05`, recompute the checksum at offset 17
Overwrite two bytes after the name, keep the length, and keep the checksum
Insert two bytes and change only the version byte so that it reads 5
Set the length byte to `05` and keep the checksum at offset 15 as before
questions.explanation: A longer name is the one edit that must add bytes. Everything after the name moves, so the length and the checksum, now at 12 + 5 = 17, must both be right.

questions.prompt: A save starts with the bytes `1F 8B`. Why is changing the gold in a hex editor hopeless?
options: It is probably gzip-compressed, so the gold is not stored as plain bytes
The bytes are a version number, which locks the gold field in place
The pair `1F 8B` marks a checksum that covers the whole of the file
It is a ZIP archive, whose entries are stored one byte at a time
questions.explanation: `1F 8B` starts a gzip stream. The data has to be decompressed, edited, and compressed again, because changing one compressed byte upsets everything after it.

questions.prompt: A code pattern matches six executable locations in the exact supported build. What is the safest next step?
options: Refine the signature and verify the surrounding instructions until one meaning is proven
Patch all six locations, since at least one of them must be the instruction you wanted
Choose the first match, because the scanner returns addresses in sorted order
Turn every byte into a wildcard so the pattern is guaranteed to match something real
questions.explanation: Several matches mean the pattern is not a unique identity. Add stable surrounding bytes, reduce needless wildcards, and disassemble each candidate; a scanner should refuse ambiguity rather than make six writes.

questions.prompt: After a game update, why can the old module-base-plus-RVA calculation point at the wrong code even when the base is correct?
options: The instruction may have moved within the module, so the old RVA lands on different bytes
The loader refuses to add a base to an RVA once the executable has been rebuilt by its developer
The module base is always recalculated as zero after an update, so the sum is no longer valid
Updates convert every RVA into a file offset, which cannot be added to a live base address
questions.explanation: An RVA is only correct for the exact build it was measured on. A pattern searches the current module instead of trusting an old position.

questions.prompt: What does a byte pattern match give you by itself?
options: A candidate location that still needs checking in each supported build
Proof that the instruction is the gold-changing one in every version of the game
A guaranteed unique address, because the bytes of a pattern cannot appear twice in a module
A decoded instruction with its operands and meaning, ready to be patched in place
questions.explanation: The pattern shows where matching bytes sit; it does not prove what the instruction means. Semantic verification is a separate step.

questions.prompt: In `29 47 04 E8 3C 91 FF FF`, why are the four bytes after `E8` the ones to wildcard?
options: They hold a relative call distance that changes whenever the caller or callee moves
They hold the register number of the destination, which the compiler picks at random each build
They are padding bytes that the CPU skips, so they carry no meaning for the call at all
They store the version of the game, so they are different in every build that is released
questions.explanation: `E8` is a call whose four following bytes are a relative distance to the target. The distance shifts when code moves, even though the same function is called.

questions.prompt: What separates a justified wildcard from "a shrug" in a signature?
options: A written reason, such as "relative call displacement, changes when code moves"
A count showing that the wildcard appears in fewer than four positions of the signature
A test run proving that the pattern still matches after the wildcard bytes are removed
A rule that wildcards may only replace bytes whose value is zero in the design build
questions.explanation: The lesson says each wildcard needs a stated reason. Without one, you cannot tell whether you hid a changing byte or just an inconvenient one.

questions.prompt: What is the risk of putting wildcards over many positions in a signature?
options: The pattern becomes common and ambiguous, matching ordinary code in many places
The pattern becomes too long, so the matcher returns false near the end of every buffer
The pattern stops working on the build used to design it, because wildcards remove its anchors
The pattern gets copied to the target process, which can overwrite the instruction it was meant to find
questions.explanation: Too few wildcards make a signature fragile; too many make it match unrelated code. The skill is placing them where bytes truly vary.

questions.prompt: What does it mean when a pattern "overfits"?
options: It memorizes accidental details of one executable instead of describing the instruction you meant
It matches so many places that the scan runs out of memory before it reaches the module end
It grows longer than the module's executable section, so no window can ever fit inside it
It uses wildcards that were written down without a reason, so reviewers must reject the pattern
questions.explanation: An exact 30-byte sequence may work on one build and fail after an unrelated compiler layout change. Looseness that matches everywhere is the opposite mistake.

questions.prompt: A pattern matches exactly once in the build used to design it. What should you do before calling it version-tolerant?
options: Test it against another build you actually intend to support
Nothing, because a single match is enough proof that it will work in every other build
Add wildcards at random positions until the pattern also matches an unknown build
Lengthen the scan to every section of the module, so more locations are checked
questions.explanation: One match in the design build may simply mean the pattern is overfitted. A second supported build shows whether it finds the same kind of instruction.

questions.prompt: Why is it wrong to keep weakening a pattern until it matches an unknown build?
options: It can return success on the wrong code; the goal is the same instruction in every named build
It makes the pattern longer, which would exceed the limit the lesson sets for byte signatures
It changes the module's fingerprint, so the supported builds are then rejected by the scanner
It is allowed, as long as the final pattern matches at least one location in that build
questions.explanation: The pattern should find the same instruction in the builds you named, not any build at all. For a single supported build, an exact fingerprint plus signature is more honest.

questions.prompt: Why does the lesson use a `PatternByte` enum with `Exact(u8)` and `Any` rather than treating `0x00` as a wildcard?
options: A magic value would make a real zero byte impossible to match exactly
An enum is faster, because the compiler stores `Exact` bytes in registers during the scan
Zero is already reserved by Windows as a marker for pages that cannot be read safely
Rust cannot compare a `u8` value against zero inside an iterator without using an enum
questions.explanation: If zero meant "anything", you could never ask for an actual zero. The type states the choice explicitly instead of hiding it in a value.

questions.prompt: What does `matches_at` do when the pattern would run past the end of the buffer?
options: It returns `false`, because `get` gives no window for an incomplete range
It compares the bytes that exist and treats the missing ones as wildcards
It panics with an index error, which is how the caller learns the buffer was too small
It wraps around to the start of the buffer and compares the remaining pattern bytes there
questions.explanation: `bytes.get(range)` returns `None` for a range that does not fit, and the function maps that to "not a match". The older indexing loop could panic near the end.

questions.prompt: A buffer has 3 bytes and the pattern has 2. Which start offsets must `find_all` try?
options: 0 and 1
1 only
0 only
questions.explanation: The last legal start is `3 - 2 = 1`, which the inclusive range `0..=` includes. Using an exclusive end would miss it, and starting at 2 would run past the buffer.

questions.prompt: Why does `find_all` return early for an empty pattern or one longer than the input?
options: An empty pattern would match everywhere, and the subtraction could underflow
Both cases are legal and should match the first byte of the buffer before the loop begins
The early return is only there to speed up scans of buffers that are smaller than a page
Such patterns are slower to match, so the function avoids them to keep the scan time low
questions.explanation: Without the guard, the empty pattern appears to match between every byte and `bytes.len() - pattern.len()` underflows. Returning an empty list is the safe answer.

questions.prompt: Roughly how many comparisons does the simple scan do at most for a 1,000-byte buffer and a 4-byte pattern?
options: About 4,000
About 1,004
About 250
About 16,000
questions.explanation: The lesson says at most roughly `n × m` comparisons: 1,000 × 4 = 4,000. Faster algorithms matter only after measurement shows this loop is the bottleneck.

questions.prompt: In `parse_pattern`, what happens when one token is not valid hex, such as `ZZ`?
options: The parse stops and returns that error, so no half-parsed pattern escapes
The token becomes a wildcard, and the remaining tokens are parsed as usual
The token is skipped, and the pattern is returned with one byte fewer than the text
The program panics immediately, because `collect()` cannot hold a failed value
questions.explanation: `collect()` combines `Result` values into one `Result<Vec<_>>`, and the first error wins. A typo becomes an error before any memory is scanned.

questions.prompt: Why does the lesson say not to scan an entire process by default?
options: Find the intended module and executable section, copy it, and scan that local buffer
Whole-process scans are blocked by Windows, so only a single module can ever be read
A whole-process scan would change the pattern, because each module adds its own wildcards
Pattern scanning only works on stack memory, so heap regions must always be excluded
questions.explanation: A bounded executable region reduces false matches and keeps the scan within the code you mean. Scanning heaps or data could match by coincidence.

questions.prompt: What is the benefit of copying a region into a local `Vec<u8>` before matching?
options: The matching loop then uses only checked slices, with no remote reads failing mid-comparison
The copy hides the scan from the target process, so its pages are never marked as accessed
The copy lets the loop write the new bytes back into the game one window at a time
The copy changes the page protection to writable, so the pattern can use wildcards on it
questions.explanation: `ReadProcessMemory` can fail because a page changed. Once bytes are local, comparisons cannot hit remote pointers or partial Windows reads.

questions.prompt: The scan finds zero matches. According to the lesson, what does that most likely mean?
options: The build, scan range, or pattern assumption is wrong, such as the wrong executable or architecture
The pattern is perfect, since a unique instruction should not be found by the scanner at all
The module is currently unloaded, so the scanner must be run again until it finds one match
The instruction was moved into a data section, so the scan range must be widened to the whole process
questions.explanation: Zero matches means one of your assumptions failed, and the first questions are the exact supported build and architecture. Widening to unrelated sections would hide the problem.

questions.prompt: A pattern is ambiguous. What is the right way to fix it?
options: Extend the pattern into surrounding instructions until only the intended one matches
Lengthen the scan to another unrelated section until only one match is left in total
Take the first match and write down that the scanner chose it by address order
Replace the leading bytes with wildcards so that the matcher accepts a smaller set of windows
questions.explanation: The lesson says not to fix ambiguity by changing the search area. Add identity to the pattern, because several matches mean it does not contain enough.

questions.prompt: After the scanner reports exactly one match, which step still comes next?
options: Disassemble the neighboring bytes and confirm whole instructions and the build fingerprint
Patch the address right away, because a unique match proves the instruction's meaning
Copy the match offset into the process as the new module base for later lookups
Rescan the entire process once more, so the pattern can be shown to match nowhere else
questions.explanation: One match locates a candidate; semantic checks decide whether it is the right one. Unknown builds should be rejected.

questions.prompt: Why is `assert_eq!(pattern.len(), 2)` on a two-item array called decoration?
options: It only repeats what the code just wrote, so no incorrect implementation could make it fail
It tests the matcher too deeply, so it would fail whenever the scanning code is refactored
It compiles only in release builds, so it is skipped for every test run in debug mode
It checks the wildcard count rather than the bytes, which the lesson says is never allowed
questions.explanation: A useful test asks what wrong implementation would make it fail. The last-offset boundary test can catch an off-by-one; the length check cannot catch anything.

questions.prompt: Which bytes does the runnable Wesnoth lab actually search for?
options: The exact three-byte sequence `29 42 04`, measured from the pinned build
The eight-byte pattern `29 47 04 E8 ?? ?? ?? ??` with four wildcards
A single wildcard byte followed by the module's DOS signature
A relative call opcode `E8` with its distance filled in from the first build
questions.explanation: The lab uses measured bytes for `sub dword ptr [edx+4],eax`. The longer pattern in the lesson is illustrative and is not claimed to follow the real gold instruction.

questions.prompt: The scanner reports a match that points into a data section. Which question does the lesson suggest asking?
options: Did the scan include a non-executable section?
Is the module too large for a three-byte pattern to be read in one call?
Did the loader change the match into a forwarder string by mistake?
Is the pattern missing a leading `E8` opcode byte at its start?
questions.explanation: The symptom table links a match inside data to a scan range that included non-executable memory. The lab avoids this by keeping only readable executable regions.

questions.prompt: A first scan finds every address containing 100. You spend points and the visible value becomes 75. What should the next scan keep?
options: Only the old candidates that now contain 75
Every address that has ever contained 100
Every readable address that contains 75, ignoring the first scan
Only addresses that sit in executable pages
questions.explanation: The first scan creates a candidate set, and the second asks which members of that same set changed to the new value. Rescanning all memory for 75 would bring back unrelated copies.

questions.prompt: A learner's candidate list grows after a filter pass. What does the lesson say probably happened?
options: The program rescanned memory instead of re-reading only the existing candidates
The target allocated new memory, and a filter pass is meant to pick up those new addresses
The filter used `Changed`, which is allowed to add addresses that differ from before
The list grew because the scan used 1 MiB chunks, which double the candidates on purpose
questions.explanation: A filter re-reads only addresses already on the list, so it can remove candidates but never add them. Growth means a new search was run.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly separates `VirtualQueryEx` from `ReadProcessMemory`?
options: `VirtualQueryEx` describes a range's state and protection; `ReadProcessMemory` copies the bytes
`VirtualQueryEx` copies the bytes into the scanner; `ReadProcessMemory` only reports the protection
`VirtualQueryEx` writes a value into the range; `ReadProcessMemory` verifies that the write worked
`VirtualQueryEx` reads a single byte at the start; `ReadProcessMemory` reads the rest of the region
questions.explanation: Keeping "describe" and "read" as separate steps makes failures easier to explain. The query copies nothing from the target.

questions.prompt: The bytes `64 00 00 00` stand for 100 only under which interpretation?
options: As a little-endian `u32`, with the lowest byte stored first
As any four bytes, since four bytes always form a number on their own
As a pointer to the byte at address 100 in the target process
As an x86 instruction that ends with a zero opcode and no operands
questions.explanation: The same four bytes could be part of a pointer, an instruction, or unrelated data. That is why the first scan returns candidates, not an answer.

questions.prompt: The visible gold value is 1,000. Which four bytes does the scanner search for as a little-endian `u32`?
questions.explanation: 1,000 is `0x3E8`, so the lowest byte `E8` comes first, then `03`, then two zero bytes. The reversed order is big-endian, which this lab does not use.

questions.prompt: With 400 MiB of readable memory, about how many bytes does the first scan read?
options: About 419 million
About 400 thousand
About 160 thousand
About 72
questions.explanation: 400 × 1,048,576 = 419,430,400 bytes, because the first scan reads every readable byte once. Later passes read only the candidates.

questions.prompt: The first scan found 40,000 candidates of 4 bytes each. How many bytes does the second scan read?
questions.explanation: The second pass re-reads only the survivors: 40,000 × 4 = 160,000. It no longer depends on how large the game's memory is.

questions.prompt: The first scan is O(n) in the size of memory. What happens if the game uses twice as much memory?
options: The scan reads about twice as many bytes
The scan reads about four times as many bytes
The scan reads the same number of bytes
The scan reads about half as many bytes
questions.explanation: O(n) means the cost grows in step with the input. O(n²) is the case where doubling the input makes the work four times worse.

questions.prompt: Comparing every one of 40,000 candidates with every other candidate costs how many comparisons?
questions.explanation: 40,000 × 40,000 = 1,600,000,000, which is O(n²) and 40,000 times the work of reading the list once. Doubling the candidates would make it four times worse.

questions.prompt: Why is finding one candidate's previous value in a hash table keyed by address called O(1) on average?
options: Hashing the address picks a bucket directly instead of reading the whole candidate list
The table keeps candidates sorted, so a lookup always finds the value in the first position
The table copies every candidate into memory next to the target, so no search is needed
The table's lookups are guaranteed to take identical time no matter how many collisions occur
questions.explanation: The lesson says collisions and an overloaded table can slow individual lookups, so this is not a promise of equal timing. It is a statement about average growth.

questions.prompt: Which regions should the scanner keep when looking for a visible value such as gold?
options: Committed regions with readable protection, skipping guard and no-access pages
Reserved regions that have never been committed, because gold is stored in unused address space
Only regions marked executable, because every game value is stored next to its code
Free regions, since the game has not yet claimed them and their bytes cannot change
questions.explanation: State tells whether a range is committed, reserved, or free, and protection tells what can be done to it. Reading a guard or no-access page would fail or have side effects.

questions.prompt: Why does the region walk check that `next > current` after `checked_add`?
options: A zero-sized region would otherwise cause an infinite loop
Windows reports region bases in descending order, so the walk must confirm which way it moves
The check proves that the region is committed before the scan reads any of its bytes
The check rounds the region up to a whole page, so reads begin on a page boundary
questions.explanation: The walk advances by region size, so a reported size of zero would never move forward. `checked_add` separately turns overflow into an error instead of wrapping to zero.

questions.prompt: Why is `MemoryRegion` a plain struct of integers and Booleans instead of a reference to the region's bytes?
options: A normal local reference cannot borrow memory owned by another process
The struct must stay small, since Windows allows at most 250,000 regions in one process
References to bytes are forbidden in Rust whenever the data came from a system call
The Booleans already hold the bytes of the region in a compressed form for later reads
questions.explanation: The struct is a local description. `base` and `size` are numbers because the target's memory lives in another address space and is copied only on request.

questions.prompt: Why does a general scan use `windows(4)` rather than stepping through the chunk four bytes at a time?
options: A value may start at any byte, so every byte offset has to be checked
A step of four skips the final chunk bytes, which are always larger values than the others
`windows(4)` uses less memory than a step, because it never copies the chunk into a buffer
Aligned scans cannot find little-endian values, so only overlapping windows can read them
questions.explanation: The lesson says an aligned-only scan can step by four, but a general scan checks every offset. Overlapping windows allow unaligned values.

questions.prompt: A chunk was copied from target address `0x5000`. A match is found at local offset 12. Which target address does the scanner report?
questions.explanation: The scan reports `base + offset`, and 12 is `0xC`, so the result is `0x500C`. The local offset alone is not a target address.

questions.prompt: Why do adjacent 1 MiB chunks overlap by three bytes?
options: A four-byte value can begin in the last three bytes of a chunk and would otherwise be split
The overlap gives the scanner a safety margin, so that Windows never returns a short read
Three bytes is the size of the header that every chunk carries from `ReadProcessMemory`
The overlap lets the scanner compare each chunk with the one before, to detect changed pages
questions.explanation: Without it, a value straddling the boundary would never exist as a complete four-byte window in either buffer.

questions.prompt: Why does `Candidate` store `previous` next to `address`?
options: "Changed" compares two reads of the same address, so the earlier read must be kept
The previous field is the address of the next candidate, which makes the list faster to walk
The previous value is used to rebuild the region list when the game frees its memory
The scanner writes `previous` back to the game when a refused write needs to be undone
questions.explanation: Filters such as increased, decreased, changed, and unchanged all need the last value of that exact address. Update `previous` for survivors.

questions.prompt: With `Filter::Increased`, what does `keep(&filter, 40, 55)` return?
options: `true`, because 55 is greater than 40
`false`, because the value changed by more than ten
`false`, because `Increased` only accepts values equal to the previous one
`true`, because any difference from 40 satisfies the filter
questions.explanation: `Increased` is `current > previous`, and 55 > 40. A candidate that merely differs would satisfy `Changed`, not `Increased`.

questions.prompt: Which candidate survives `Filter::Unchanged`?
options: One whose previous value was 9 and whose current value is 9
One whose previous value was 9 and whose current value is 12
One whose previous value was 9 and whose current value is 3
One whose previous value was 9 and that can no longer be read
questions.explanation: `Unchanged` keeps candidates where `current == previous`. The unreadable candidate is treated as removed, not as unchanged.

questions.prompt: What is the main benefit of the `Filter` enum over passing strings such as `"changed"`?
options: A misspelling cannot compile, and an exhaustive `match` forces every case to be handled
The enum stores each filter in fewer bytes, so the candidate list shrinks faster
The enum lets the scanner accept any text, because unknown names fall into a default case
The enum removes the need to re-read candidates, since the filter knows the new values already
questions.explanation: With strings, a typo silently behaves like an unknown filter. With an enum, adding a new filter makes the compiler point out every `match` that needs updating.

questions.prompt: During a filter pass, a candidate address can no longer be read. How should the scanner treat it?
options: As removed from the list, without crashing the scan
As a successful match, since an unreadable value cannot have changed
As proof the whole scan is invalid, so every candidate must be discarded
As a reason to pause the target process until the memory becomes readable again
questions.explanation: The game can free or re-protect memory at any time. A robust tool drops that candidate, reports skipped work, and continues.

questions.prompt: What does "the scanner's snapshot is always slightly behind the running process" mean?
options: The game keeps running between queries, reads, and later checks, so memory may change meanwhile
The scanner reads memory in the order it was allocated, so older pages are always seen first
Windows delays each `ReadProcessMemory` result by one frame so that the game can finish writing
The snapshot is a saved file on disk, which the game overwrites only when it exits
questions.explanation: Between the region query and the read, the game can free an allocation or change its protection. This is a normal race, not necessarily a bug.

questions.prompt: Why does the lab cap candidates at 250,000 and refuse to continue past that?
options: A common value such as zero can match millions of places and exhaust memory
Windows allows a process to hold only 250,000 addresses in a `Vec` at one time
The limit stops the scanner from finding the same address twice during one pass
The cap is the number of pages in a 1 MiB chunk, so it matches the read size
questions.explanation: The limit is a correctness rule: it bounds local memory and later re-read time. The lab's error tells the learner to choose a less common value.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes the purpose of chunk, region, candidate, output, and time limits?
options: They keep a memory-safe program from becoming unusable by exhausting memory, time, or the terminal
They remove the need for bounds checks, since a limited program can never read out of range
They make the scanner invisible to the game, because it then performs only small reads
They let the scanner write more quickly, because the limits switch the process into a faster mode
questions.explanation: The lesson says that without limits, perfectly memory-safe code can still make an unusable program. Safety from panics and usability are separate concerns.

questions.prompt: Why does the guarded write re-read the value just before writing four bytes?
options: The game kept running after the scan, so the address could hold a newer value now
Writing without a read first is not permitted by the Windows memory manager
The read lets the program save a copy of the region for the next full scan
The read proves that the address belongs to the executable, so it is safe to modify
questions.explanation: This closes a time-of-check/time-of-use gap. If the value no longer equals `candidate.previous`, the write stops instead of overwriting newer state.

questions.prompt: One address survives filtering, but the guarded write is refused. What does the lesson say that means?
options: The value changed after filtering, so scan again; the refusal is safety working
The tool is broken, since a surviving candidate is proof that the write must succeed
The address belongs to another process, so the learner should restart the target
The chosen value type was wrong, so the whole scan has to be redone with a new type
questions.explanation: The refusal cases are successful safety behavior: they stop a write to an address whose last read is out of date.

questions.prompt: Why can exact byte equality be misleading when scanning floating-point values?
options: `NaN` does not equal itself, `-0.0` equals `0.0`, and the displayed text may be rounded
Floats are stored big-endian, so the byte order of every float differs from integers
Floats cannot be stored at four-byte addresses, so every scan must use eight-byte windows
Visible decimals are always exact, so only the sign bit can ever cause a mismatch
questions.explanation: `-0.0` and `0.0` compare equal despite different bit patterns, and visible text may round the stored value. A `ValueKind` should say whether it compares bits, values, or a tolerance.

questions.prompt: The first pass finds zero candidates. Which phase should you inspect first, according to the troubleshooting table?
options: Value type, endianness, range permissions, or the target build
The guarded write, since it runs before the first candidate is stored
The output limit, since the terminal prints at most 25 results
The overlap size, since three bytes is too few for four-byte values
questions.explanation: Zero first-pass candidates point at how the value was searched for. Things like the guarded write only happen after a single survivor exists.

questions.prompt: Why does the lab open the process with extra write access (`true`)?
options: Only because this lab may offer a final guarded write
Because scanning memory cannot start without write access to the target
Because the first pass has to mark each region before reading it
Because the write right is needed to read the 1 MiB chunks without errors
questions.explanation: The scanner itself only reads. The write right is requested because one surviving candidate can unlock an optional replacement.

questions.prompt: After an `int3` breakpoint fires, why restore the original byte, rewind `EIP`, set the trap flag, and continue for one instruction?
options: To let the real instruction run once before putting `0xCC` back
To make the process permanently single-threaded while the breakpoint is installed
To turn the game's x86 instructions into readable source code on the debugger's side
To skip the instruction that was replaced, so the program resumes at the next one
questions.explanation: The CPU pauses after consuming the one-byte `0xCC`, so `EIP` points just past it. Rewinding and restoring lets the displaced instruction execute, and the trap flag pauses right afterward so the debugger can reinsert the breakpoint.

questions.prompt: Which sequence matches the debugger's event loop?
options: Wait for an event, decode it, inspect or update state, continue it, then wait again
Continue the event, decode it, wait for the next one, then inspect the state afterward
Decode the event, wait for it to arrive, update state, then stop the loop until detach
Inspect the state, wait for any event, continue it once, then decode what was received
questions.explanation: The loop is `WaitForDebugEvent`, decode, inspect or update, `ContinueDebugEvent`, and back to waiting. Continuing before decoding would resume the target too early.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a kind of event that Windows reports to a debugger?
options: A DLL being loaded into the target
A change in the player's gold value
A write to a file by the debugger
A mouse click inside the debugger's window
questions.explanation: Windows reports process creation, DLL loading, exceptions, and process exit. A breakpoint is one exception that the tool deliberately causes and handles.

questions.prompt: Why convert raw Windows event structs into an owned `DebugEvent` enum right at the FFI boundary?
options: The rest of the code then works with safe typed data, and any handles can be closed or transferred
The enum is required by Windows, since `WaitForDebugEvent` returns only Rust values
The enum keeps the target running longer, because owned data does not need a continue call
The enum lets the debugger skip exceptions, since only enum variants can raise them
questions.explanation: Converting early keeps unsafe layouts at the edge. The lesson also says to close or transfer ownership of handles so a long session does not leak them.

questions.prompt: Why does `SoftwareBreakpoint` store `original_byte` along with `address`?
options: The displaced instruction byte must be put back for the real instruction to run
The original byte is the value that tells the debugger how many threads the process has
The byte holds the thread ID that was suspended when the breakpoint was reached
The original byte is used as the key for the map that holds all of the breakpoints
questions.explanation: A software breakpoint overwrites one instruction byte with `0xCC`, so the debugger has to remember what was there. The map is keyed by address, not by that byte.

questions.prompt: Why is the breakpoint table a `HashMap` keyed by address?
options: Several breakpoints can coexist without a single global current-breakpoint slot
A map lets Windows look up breakpoints itself when an exception reaches the target
A map stores each breakpoint in its own page, so one cannot overwrite another
Hash keys make `0xCC` appear at each address, so the CPU can find the breakpoints
questions.explanation: Keying records by address means each breakpoint carries its own state. The debugger looks up the exception address to see whether it owns it.

questions.prompt: Which order does the lesson give for setting a software breakpoint?
options: Read the original byte, store it, write `0xCC`, flush the instruction cache, mark it armed
Write `0xCC`, read the original byte, mark it armed, store it, then flush the cache
Mark it armed, write `0xCC`, flush the instruction cache, then read the original byte
Flush the instruction cache, mark it armed, store the byte, then write `0xCC` over it
questions.explanation: The original byte must be read and stored before it is overwritten; otherwise it is lost. Marking armed comes after the write and the cache flush.

questions.prompt: What is the trap flag used for in the breakpoint cycle?
options: It makes the CPU raise a single-step exception after one instruction so `0xCC` can be reinserted
It stops every other thread in the process from running while the original byte is restored
It marks the exception as belonging to Windows, so the debugger knows to pass it onward
It tells the instruction cache to flush, so the restored byte is the one that executes
questions.explanation: After the original instruction runs once, the single-step exception gives the debugger a safe moment to put `0xCC` back and clear the trap flag.

questions.prompt: In `BreakpointPhase`, what does the `Armed` state mean?
options: The target currently contains `0xCC` at the debugger-owned address
The original byte is temporarily restored for one thread to step over
No debugger-owned byte is installed at this address at the moment
The breakpoint was hit and is waiting for a `ContinueDebugEvent` call
questions.explanation: `SteppingOriginal` is the state where the original byte is restored for one thread, and `Disabled` means nothing is installed. `Armed` means `0xCC` is in place.

questions.prompt: Why check an exception's address against your breakpoint map before treating it as yours?
options: Windows and the target may use breakpoints internally, and those must be passed onward
Every exception that carries a code of breakpoint is created by the debugger's own writes
An address outside the map means the process has exited, so the loop should stop
Addresses in the map are the only ones that Windows will report as first-chance exceptions
questions.explanation: The lesson lists the exception code, address, map membership, first-chance status, and current phase and thread. Unhandled exceptions are passed on with the correct continue status.

questions.prompt: What does the term instrumentation bias describe?
options: The tool used to measure a program changes what the program does
A debugger's tendency to show only the first instruction of each function it meets
The extra memory used by a debugger when it stores a copy of the whole target
The gap between the compiled instructions and the source code they came from
questions.explanation: Pausing a thread, writing `0xCC`, or single stepping all affect the target. A difference seen only while attached comes from the measurement, not the game's normal logic.

questions.prompt: A behavior appears both with the debugger attached and when running without it. What does that suggest?
options: It is probably part of the target rather than an artifact of the pause
It was caused by the breakpoint byte, since attached runs always change the code
It proves the target can observe the debugger and is acting on what it sees
It is a timing difference, since only elapsed time can change while attached
questions.explanation: The table says a behavior that happens both ways is probably part of the target. Behavior that appears only attached points at scheduling or at the target noticing the debugger.

questions.prompt: Why does `ContinueGuard::drop` continue with `DBG_EXCEPTION_NOT_HANDLED` if the event was never continued?
options: It releases the pending event without swallowing a target exception the debugger did not own
It tells Windows that the debugger handled the event so the exception is cleared for good
It restores the original byte at every breakpoint before the target is allowed to run again
It detaches the debugger from the target, so the guard can drop all of its handles safely
questions.explanation: The guard exists so an early parsing error cannot leave an event uncontinued. Using the not-handled status keeps unrelated exceptions flowing to the target.

questions.prompt: What does the lesson recommend as the first milestone for a new debugger?
options: Launch a tiny practice target, print process and thread events, and continue every event
Attach to the game directly and set several breakpoints before printing any events
Build a graphical interface with symbols first, then add the event loop under it
Single-step the game from its first instruction so that every event is already known
questions.explanation: Do not start with stepping, symbols, and a GUI. Get the continue-every-event loop and a clean exit working, then add one breakpoint.

questions.prompt: At the Wesnoth income breakpoint `add dword ptr [eax+4], edx`, which value is the income delta?
options: `EDX`
`EAX`
`EAX + 0x4`
`EIP`
questions.explanation: The side record is `EAX`, the gold address is `EAX + 4`, and `EDX` is added to it, so `EDX` is the income. The tool reads gold before the `add` runs.

questions.prompt: The debugger stops at the income instruction and `EAX` holds `0x01200000`. At which address is the gold value read?
questions.explanation: The instruction's memory operand is `[eax+4]`, so gold sits at `EAX + 4`. The address `0x009B4D00` is the instruction itself, not the data.

questions.prompt: Which action belongs in a debugger's cleanup when it detaches or exits?
options: Restore every armed breakpoint, flush the cache, continue pending events, and close handles
Leave the breakpoint bytes installed, so the game can reuse them on the next run
Keep the pending event unresolved, so the target stays safely paused after detach
Close the handles first, then restore the breakpoint bytes through those same handles
questions.explanation: A debugger that pauses correctly but cannot cleanly detach is not finished. Leaving `0xCC` in the target would crash it the next time that instruction ran.

questions.prompt: A PE section reports an instruction RVA of `0x1200`, and Windows loads the module at `0x7FF600000000`. What is the live virtual address?
questions.explanation: An RVA is a distance from the module's live base. Add the two: `0x7FF600000000 + 0x1200 = 0x7FF600001200`. A file offset answers where bytes sit on disk; it is not automatically the address the CPU executes.
options: 0x7FF600001200, the live base plus the RVA
0x1200, since an RVA is already the final live address
The file offset of the section, since that is where bytes sit
0x7FF600000000, the module base without adding the RVA

questions.prompt: What is a Portable Executable, or PE?
options: The Windows `.exe` format; headers say where code and data live
A file holding only raw CPU instructions with no separate sections
A format that stores the full memory contents of a running process
A header block that exists only inside the debugger while it runs
questions.explanation: An EXE is not one solid blob of instructions. Its headers describe where code, data, imports, resources, and relocation information are.

questions.prompt: What do a file offset and an RVA each measure?
options: Offset: a spot in the file; RVA: a distance from the loaded base
Offset: a spot in the loaded image; RVA: a spot in the file
Offset: a live address; RVA: a distance from the preferred base
Offset: a distance from the module base; RVA: a spot in the file
questions.explanation: The same section has two places, numbered differently. A section row converts between them; the numbers are related but not interchangeable.

questions.prompt: Which reason does the lesson give for the file and image layouts differing?
options: Separate alignments, zero-filled data, and loader fixes after mapping
The file is compressed, then unpacked to a larger size at load time
Windows shuffles the order of sections so the code is harder to read
The file keeps instructions in a different byte order than memory
questions.explanation: Sections have separate file and virtual alignments, zero-initialised data may need no file bytes, and relocations and imports are applied after mapping.

questions.prompt: Which order does a parser follow through the headers?
options: DOS header, PE signature, COFF header, optional header, section table
Section table, optional header, COFF header, PE signature, DOS header
COFF header, DOS header, section table, PE signature, optional header
PE signature, section table, DOS header, optional header, COFF header
questions.explanation: Each structure confirms the image or says where the next one begins. A section row cannot be trusted before the headers that locate it have passed their checks.

questions.prompt: What does the DOS field at `0x3c` (`e_lfanew`) contain?
options: A file offset pointing at the `PE\0\0` signature
An RVA pointing at the first byte of the code section
The live address of the module once it is loaded in memory
The number of section rows that follow the optional header
questions.explanation: The comment in the code says it is a file offset, not an RVA or a live address. It is how a parser leaves the old DOS header and finds the PE signature.

questions.prompt: Why must a parser never jump to a later header using a guessed offset?
options: A wrong header should stop the parse before its numbers are trusted
Later headers are encrypted until the earlier ones have been read
The guessed offset would be an RVA, which Rust would then reject
Guessing an offset makes the file larger when it is saved to disk
questions.explanation: Each header tells where the next begins or how large it is. Following that chain is what keeps invalid numbers from being trusted.

questions.prompt: Why is the "optional" header not optional for an executable?
options: The name comes from object files, which can omit it; images need it
Executables need it only when they have more than 96 sections
It becomes required only when the program runs as administrator
It is truly optional, though every Windows game happens to include it
questions.explanation: The image base and entry-point RVA live there. Object files can omit it, which is where the old name comes from.

questions.prompt: What does `u32::from_le_bytes` state about PE numbers?
options: They are stored in little-endian byte order
They are stored in four bytes, whatever the field
They are signed values, so negative numbers can appear
They are written as text digits that have to be parsed
questions.explanation: The helper reads the bytes as a little-endian integer. `checked_add` and `get` handle overflow and out-of-file reads.

questions.prompt: Which facts does the COFF header give a parser?
options: The target CPU, the section count, and the next header's size
The image base address and the entry-point RVA of the program
The name and the permission flags of every section in the file
The file offset where the old DOS header begins in the image
questions.explanation: The COFF header follows the `PE\0\0` signature. The image base and entry point are in the optional header, and section details are in the section table.

questions.prompt: Why does the parser reject a section count above 96?
options: A wild count means a wrong offset or a damaged file
Windows refuses to load any image that has over 96 sections
Each section row would stop fitting in its fixed 40 bytes
The `u16` type cannot hold a number that is above 96 at all
questions.explanation: The cap is deliberately boring. It is a sanity check on the data, not a rule of the loader.

questions.prompt: The optional-header magic reads `0x20B`. What does this mean for the image base?
options: It is PE32+, with an eight-byte image base at +24
It is PE32, with a four-byte image base at +28
It is PE32+, with a four-byte image base at +24
It is PE32, with an eight-byte image base at +28
questions.explanation: `0x10B` is PE32 with a four-byte base at +28; `0x20B` is PE32+ with an eight-byte base at +24. The fields have different sizes, so the offset changes.

questions.prompt: The section table starts at byte `T`, and each row is 40 bytes. Where does the row for the fourth section (index 3) start?
questions.explanation: Row `index` starts at `T + index × 40`, so index 3 gives 3 × 40 = 120. The fourth row has index 3 because counting starts at 0.

questions.prompt: Why does the parser look for a zero byte in the eight-byte name and use `unwrap_or(8)`?
options: Names fill a fixed field and need not end in NUL
Names end in a zero byte, so the check is only a safeguard
Names can be any length, so the field has no limit
Section names are stored as RVAs, so they need decoding
questions.explanation: A name of exactly eight characters has no terminator. The fallback uses all eight bytes.

questions.prompt: What does the loader use to set a section's page protection?
options: The characteristic flags; names are only conventions
The section name, such as `.text` or `.data`, read by the loader
The position of the section within the section table
The size of the section's data as stored on the disk
questions.explanation: `.text` is normally readable and executable, but the flags are what is enforced. A strangely named section can still be executable.

questions.prompt: Which pairing matches the normal permissions of the named sections?
options: `.text` is readable and executable; `.data` readable and writable
`.text` is readable and writable; `.data` is executable code
`.rdata` is readable and writable; `.text` is read-only data
`.data` is read-only; `.rdata` is executable and holds the code
questions.explanation: `.rdata` is normally read-only data. Code is in `.text`, and writable variables are in `.data`.

questions.prompt: For the 32-bit course games, which optional-header magic should the inspector report?
questions.explanation: The memory-patching chapters use 32-bit builds, so they are PE32. The parser supports both forms so that it can say what it found.

questions.prompt: Your encoder's output can be decoded by your decoder. Why is one real captured fixture still valuable?
questions.explanation: An encoder and decoder written from the same mistaken idea can agree perfectly with each other. A known real frame anchors the test to the actual protocol and exposes shared mistakes in lengths, byte order, compression, or field layout.
options: Both halves might share one wrong assumption and still agree
Captured bytes make bounds checks and size limits unnecessary
A fixture switches TCP into a mode that keeps message boundaries
Real data guarantees every later game version stays compatible

questions.prompt: The 4-byte header of a Wesnoth frame ends in `4E`. How many bytes is the complete TCP payload of that frame?
options: 82 bytes
78 bytes
86 bytes
74 bytes
questions.explanation: 0x4E is 78, and the length does not count the 4 header bytes themselves, so the whole frame is 4 + 78 = 82.

questions.prompt: Which wire bytes announce a 78-byte gzip body in the lesson's big-endian format?
questions.explanation: 78 is hexadecimal 0x4E, written as a 32-bit number with the most significant byte first. Little-endian order would put `4E` first.

questions.prompt: A complete frame is 50 bytes long on the wire, header included. Which header does it carry?
questions.explanation: The length excludes the 4 header bytes: 50 - 4 = 46, which is 0x2E. 0x32 is 50, the mistake of counting the header.

questions.prompt: The header `FF FF FF FF` is followed by only four payload bytes. What should the parser do first?
options: Reject the claim because it exceeds the configured maximum
Allocate the claimed size and wait for the rest of the data
Treat the four bytes as a complete frame of length four
Decompress the four bytes to see whether they are valid
questions.explanation: The header is a claim, not permission. Checking it against the limit comes before allocating or waiting for about four gigabytes.

questions.prompt: A header claims 4 payload bytes (well under the limit), but only 2 have arrived so far. What does this tell the parser?
options: Nothing is wrong yet; TCP may deliver the rest later
The frame is forged and the connection should be closed
The header is invalid and its length must be read again
The two bytes are the whole payload and TCP lost the rest
questions.explanation: Having fewer bytes so far does not prove a frame is false. The reader keeps buffering, within its limits and timeouts.

questions.prompt: Framing found a complete frame, but gzip decompression of its payload fails. Which layer does the lesson tell you to inspect?
options: The compression wrapper and its payload
The TCP byte stream between the two sockets
The game-level schema of the chat fields
The Simple WML tokenizer and its tags
questions.explanation: Each layer has its own failure. A decompression error points at the gzip data, not at TCP or the later WML and game-meaning layers.

questions.prompt: The WML parses cleanly but the game ignores the message. Where should you look next?
options: At the expected message fields and the connection state
At the length prefix, checking its byte order again
At the gzip header and its magic bytes `1F 8B`
At the capture interface that recorded the bytes
questions.explanation: Valid WML only means the text structure is fine. Whether the game acts on it depends on the schema fields and where the session is.

questions.prompt: What happens to `Cursor::position` when `take` fails because too few bytes remain?
options: It stays where it was, so no field is left half-read
It moves to the end of the buffer to stop further reads
It is reset to zero so parsing can restart
It advances by however many bytes were available
questions.explanation: `take` computes and checks the whole range before it changes `position`, so an error leaves the parser exactly where it started.

questions.prompt: Why does `take` use `checked_add` when computing `self.position + count`?
options: `count` comes from the input and could overflow the addition
It converts the count from big-endian into native order
It lets the returned slice borrow from the input buffer
It rounds the end position up to a multiple of four
questions.explanation: A hostile length could be huge. `checked_add` turns an overflow into an error instead of a wrapped, wrong position.

questions.prompt: Why does the lesson prefer returning `ParseError` over `unwrap()` on network input?
options: `unwrap()` blurs bad input together with a programmer bug
`unwrap()` is slower because it copies the whole buffer
`unwrap()` swaps the byte order of the length field
`unwrap()` cannot be called on slices in Rust code
questions.explanation: Short or malformed network input is normal. It should be a `Result` the caller can handle, not a panic.

questions.prompt: What does the lifetime `'a` on `Cursor<'a>` express?
options: Slices from `take` borrow from the original input, not copies
The cursor owns its own copy of every payload it returns
The parser must finish within `'a` milliseconds
Slices stay valid even after the input buffer is freed
questions.explanation: The cursor holds only a position number. Everything it returns points into the borrowed frame, so it cannot outlive it.

questions.prompt: Why does `decode_wesnoth_frame` cap both `compressed_len` and the decompressed output?
options: A small compressed input can expand into a very large output
The two limits must add up to exactly `MAX_FRAME` bytes
Gzip stores its compressed size as a little-endian number
TCP delivers the payload in two separate halves of data
questions.explanation: Capping only the compressed size would not stop a tiny, highly compressible input from filling memory after decompression.

questions.prompt: Why does the decoder read up to `MAX_FRAME + 1` bytes of decompressed output?
options: Reaching the extra byte shows the output is over the limit
The extra byte holds the gzip footer's checksum value
It leaves room for the 4-byte length header in memory
One more byte is needed to terminate the UTF-8 text
questions.explanation: Reading one byte past the limit separates "exactly at the limit" from "too large" without an unbounded allocation.

questions.prompt: A peer advertises a legal one-megabyte frame, then sends one byte every few seconds. Which protection addresses this?
options: A read timeout or cancellation plus a cap on buffered input
A larger `MAX_FRAME` so the slow frame finishes sooner
The trailing-byte check run after the frame is complete
Converting the length with `u32::try_from` on arrival
questions.explanation: Parsing bounds protect completed inputs. The transport must also bound the time and memory spent waiting for a frame.

questions.prompt: Why does the decoder return `TrailingBytes` when the cursor stops before the end of the input?
options: It parses one frame, and extra bytes could hide ignored data
Gzip data ends on a four-byte boundary, so extras are an error
The length header is repeated at the end of every frame
Extra bytes mean the length was written in the wrong order
questions.explanation: A valid prefix with something appended is suspicious. A stream reader should split exact frame slices first.

questions.prompt: A game update renames a required WML field. Why is this riskier than adding an optional field?
options: It can break old and new readers on each other's messages
Optional fields are not allowed in tagged text formats
Renaming a field changes the length prefix of the message
A tolerant format ignores renames but rejects new fields
questions.explanation: A tolerant tree format may skip an unknown optional field, but a missing required field can break both directions.

questions.prompt: Why does `simple_field` reject `"` and newline characters in this lab?
options: They would change the structure of the quoted WML field
They are not legal anywhere inside valid UTF-8 text
They make the gzip output bigger than `MAX_FRAME` allows
They cannot be stored in a big-endian length prefix field
questions.explanation: A quote could end the field early and a newline could start a new line, letting a value rewrite the message layout.

questions.prompt: Why does `encode_wesnoth_frame` use `u32::try_from(compressed.len())` instead of `as u32`?
options: `as u32` could silently drop the high bits of a huge length
`as u32` reverses the byte order of the stored length
`try_from` compresses the data a second time for safety
`as u32` is not accepted on a `Vec` length in Rust
questions.explanation: A truncated length would produce a header that disagrees with the payload. `try_from` turns that case into an error.

questions.prompt: The lesson says a plain zlib stream is not interchangeable with gzip here. Why?
options: Both use DEFLATE but wrap it in different headers and sums
Zlib compresses text while gzip is meant for binary data
Zlib output is too large to fit within the 4-byte header
Gzip data is encrypted while zlib data is left readable
questions.explanation: The wrapper is part of the wire format. A correct gzip frame should begin with `1F 8B` after the length.

questions.prompt: `decode_wesnoth_frame` receives a header `00 20 00 00` (2,097,152) with `MAX_FRAME` of 1,048,576. What happens?
options: It returns `TooLarge` before slicing or decompressing
It returns `Truncated` after reading the payload bytes
It decompresses first and then returns `InvalidGzip`
It returns `TrailingBytes` once one frame is parsed
questions.explanation: The advertised length is checked against the cap right after it is read. Even if the bytes were present, the frame is refused.

questions.prompt: The socket closes in the middle of a read. Which failure category from the lesson is this?
options: A transport failure
A framing failure
A content failure
A schema failure
questions.explanation: Closed or timed-out sockets are transport problems. Framing is about impossible lengths, content about gzip, UTF-8, or WML.

questions.prompt: `decode_wesnoth_frame` gets the 6 bytes `00 00 00 05 61 62`. Which error comes back?
options: `Truncated`
`TooLarge`
`TrailingBytes`
`InvalidGzip`
questions.explanation: The header claims 5 payload bytes but only 2 remain, so `take` fails before any decompression is attempted.

questions.prompt: Why can one call to `read` not be assumed to return one complete application message?
questions.explanation: TCP preserves ordered bytes, not message-shaped chunks. One read may return part of a frame or several frames together. Your protocol must define a length, delimiter, or fixed size, and the reader must loop until that rule is satisfied.
options: TCP is a byte stream and does not keep the sender's write boundaries
TCP converts each message into UDP datagrams of random size
Windows trims the first byte from each read result it returns
Ports force each message on one connection to be the same size

questions.prompt: In the lesson's model, what is the client's "move north" message?
options: An intent: a request that the server may accept or reject
The final truth that the server must copy into its own state
A broadcast that the other clients must apply unchecked
A rule update that replaces the server's movement checks
questions.explanation: The server applies the shared rules, so the client's message is only a request until the reply says what was accepted.

questions.prompt: A client sends "move north" from `(10, 15)`, but a wall blocks the move. The server replies with `(10, 15)`. What should the client do?
options: Correct its display to the position the server reported
Keep drawing `(10, 14)` because the client pressed the key first
Resend the same request until the server finally agrees
Close the connection because the two states disagree
questions.explanation: The reply reports what the server actually accepted. The client may have predicted `(10, 14)`, but its own prediction is not authoritative.

questions.prompt: A sender writes two messages back to back. Which result can one `read` call return?
