options: The whole first message plus the start of the second one
The second message first, then the first message
The payload of the first message, with its header removed by TCP
Exactly one message, because TCP delivers each write as a unit
questions.explanation: TCP keeps bytes in order but ignores write boundaries, so a read can end anywhere. It never reorders bytes or strips headers.

questions.prompt: Two framed messages total 13 bytes on the wire. Read #1 returns 8 bytes. How many bytes are still to come?
options: 5 bytes
4 bytes
6 bytes
13 bytes
questions.explanation: 13 - 8 = 5. In the lesson those 5 bytes finish the second length field and the second payload.

questions.prompt: In the lesson's example, read #1 ends after the first two bytes of the second message's 4-byte length field. What must the receiver do with those two bytes?
options: Keep them in a buffer until read #2 supplies the other two
Throw them away and wait for the next full message
Treat them as a complete 2-byte length and parse a payload
Pass them straight to game logic as a short message
questions.explanation: A frame cannot be parsed until its header is complete, so the receiver holds the leftover bytes and appends what arrives next.

questions.prompt: Why does `read_frame` call `read_exact` for the 4-byte header instead of a single `read`?
options: It keeps reading until all four bytes have arrived
It verifies that the sender used big-endian byte order
It makes TCP deliver the header inside a single packet
It skips header bytes whose value happens to be zero
questions.explanation: A plain `read` may return fewer bytes than requested. The helper must wait for the full header before trusting the length.

questions.prompt: Why does `read_frame` compare the length with `max_size` before creating `vec![0_u8; length]`?
options: The length comes from an untrusted peer and could demand huge memory
The length is smaller than the 4-byte header itself is, by design
Rust vectors cannot hold more than four bytes of payload data
The check converts the big-endian length into little-endian form
questions.explanation: A corrupt or hostile length field could ask for gigabytes. Bounding it first keeps the allocation under the caller's control.

questions.prompt: `read_frame` reads the header `00 00 00 02` followed by `41 42`. What does a successful call return?
options: A vector holding only `41 42`
A vector holding `00 00 00 02 41 42`
The number `2` as a `u32`
A vector holding `41 42 00 00`
questions.explanation: The header gives the payload length and is consumed. The function returns one complete payload without it.

questions.prompt: What does `u32::from_be_bytes([0, 0, 1, 2])` produce?
questions.explanation: Big endian puts the most valuable byte first: 1 x 256 + 2 x 1 = 258. Reading the same bytes in the wrong order gives 33,619,968.

questions.prompt: Why does the reader use `u32::from_be_bytes` instead of a pointer cast to `u32`?
options: The protocol fixes the wire order, which may differ from the CPU's
A pointer cast cannot read more than two bytes from a socket
Rust refuses to compile pointer casts on little-endian x86
Big-endian numbers are smaller than the CPU's native numbers
questions.explanation: A cast would use the host's byte order, which is little endian on x86. Network code must follow the protocol, not the CPU.

questions.prompt: TCP delivered every byte of your request to the server's socket. What does that prove about the request?
options: Only that the bytes reached the receiving socket in order
That the server parsed a complete message from them
That the server accepted the request and updated its state
That a meaningful reply has already been sent
questions.explanation: TCP reliability stops at the ordered byte stream. Acknowledgments, request IDs, and retries belong to the application protocol.

questions.prompt: A login reply arrives before any login request. Which of the protocol's four questions does this problem belong to?
options: Which messages are allowed right now
Where one message ends and the next begins
What each part of a message means
How the bytes are encoded in memory
questions.explanation: Message order is part of the protocol. The bytes may be well formed and still illegal at this point in the conversation.

questions.prompt: Bytes just arrived from the TCP stream carrying a gzip-compressed WML chat message. What does the receiver do first?
options: Split off one frame using the big-endian length
Parse the WML tags to find the sender's name
Gunzip the whole buffer, header bytes included
Build the typed `Message` value and hand it over
questions.explanation: The receiver undoes the layers in reverse order: framing first, then decompression, then serialization, then meaning.

questions.prompt: The TCP connection works and gunzip succeeds, but the parser reports unbalanced tags. Which layer failed?
options: Serialization: the WML text is not well formed
Transport: TCP lost part of the stream
Framing: the length prefix used the wrong byte order
Compression: the gzip magic bytes were missing
questions.explanation: Each layer has its own failure. A valid connection and valid gzip say nothing about the tagged text inside.

questions.prompt: What is WML in this chapter?
options: Wesnoth's tagged text format, written with `[tag]` blocks
The 4-byte length prefix that is placed before each frame
The compression scheme that produces the gzip payload bytes
The Rust enum that models the decoded message kinds
questions.explanation: WML is the serialization layer: structured data written as bracketed tags. Compression and framing wrap it, not the other way round.

questions.prompt: Why might a fast game send frequent position updates over UDP?
options: A newer update makes an old one useless, so freshness wins
UDP guarantees each datagram arrives exactly once and in order
UDP merges datagrams into one long stream for the receiver
UDP encrypts positions so a lost one cannot be read later
questions.explanation: UDP keeps datagram boundaries but promises no delivery or order. That is acceptable when later data replaces earlier data.

questions.prompt: A match event with `event_id` 91 is retried after an acknowledgment was lost. What must the receiver do?
options: Recognize the repeated `event_id` and skip a second score
Add the score again, since TCP delivered a second copy
Drop the later events that come from the same sender
Reset the match so that both sides start in sync again
questions.explanation: Retries are an application concern. Event identity lets the receiver treat a repeat as the same event.

questions.prompt: A server replies "queued" when a request enters a work queue. What does that reply establish?
options: Received only; it may not be validated, applied, or saved yet
It passed validation and was already applied to the match
It was written to the database and can no longer be lost
It will be handled before any request queued after it
questions.explanation: Asynchronous work means the sender continues early. The protocol must say which stage each reply confirms.

questions.prompt: Recomputing a leaderboard from a collected set of finished-match results is an example of what?
options: Batch processing
Stream processing
Framing
Byte-order conversion
questions.explanation: A batch waits for a group of data and processes it together. Stream processing handles events one by one as they arrive.

questions.prompt: Why should a service bound its queue as well as its message size?
options: An unbounded queue eats memory and makes results staler
A bounded queue lets TCP keep message boundaries intact
A bigger queue speeds up the slowest job in the chain
Fixed-size queues are the sole way to parse length frames
questions.explanation: If input arrives faster than it is processed, the backlog grows. The lesson says what to drop is a decision about message meaning.

questions.prompt: `ConnectNamedPipe` reports `ERROR_PIPE_CONNECTED` immediately after the server creates its pipe. What does that result mean here?
questions.explanation: A fast client can connect after `CreateNamedPipeW` but before the server calls `ConnectNamedPipe`. Windows reports that race as `ERROR_PIPE_CONNECTED`. The server should treat this specific result as a successful connection, not tear down a healthy client.
options: A client already connected in the small window before the call
The pipe name is invalid, so the server must create it again
The client must be disconnected before the server carries on
Message mode has changed to byte mode on this pipe handle

questions.prompt: In a named pipe exchange, who creates the pipe name?
options: The server creates it and waits; the client opens that name
The client creates it and the server later opens it
Both create it at the same instant
The operating system creates it once a message is written
questions.explanation: A server creates a known pipe name and waits. After the client opens the name, both sides read and write with ordinary calls.

questions.prompt: What does a named pipe give the lesson's one-request, one-reply exchange that a shared mapping did not?
options: A connection whose read and write order is explicit
Pointers into the other program's own memory
A larger buffer than the mapping's 4096 bytes
Automatic encryption of each message it carries
questions.explanation: Shared memory needed an extra timing agreement for a concurrent writer. A pipe's request and reply follow one another.

questions.prompt: In byte mode, what can a single read return?
options: Part of one write, or data from several writes
One complete write, exactly, on every single read
The length header of a write, and nothing beyond it
Nothing at all until the pipe has been closed
questions.explanation: Byte mode is a stream like TCP. Message mode is the one that preserves write boundaries.

questions.prompt: The lab uses message mode and also a 4-byte length header. Why both?
options: Message mode keeps boundaries; the header lets the receiver validate
The header is needed since message mode strips the first four bytes
Message mode cannot carry UTF-8 text unless a header precedes it
The header is the setting that switches the pipe into message mode
questions.explanation: The receiver can reject a damaged or unexpected frame instead of trusting every byte Windows delivered.

questions.prompt: The lab frames the text `hi!`, which is 3 UTF-8 bytes. How many bytes does the frame have?
options: 7 bytes
3 bytes
4 bytes
11 bytes
questions.explanation: A 4-byte little-endian length plus 3 text bytes makes 7.

questions.prompt: A message is `café`, where `é` takes 2 UTF-8 bytes. What length does `frame` write in the header?
questions.explanation: `str::len` counts UTF-8 bytes: c, a, f, and 2 for é makes 5. The visible character count of 4 would be wrong.

questions.prompt: A received frame declares a text length of 2000 bytes. Which check rejects it?
options: The check that the declared length is at most 1024
The check that the header holds at least four bytes
The check that the text bytes are valid UTF-8 text
The check that the client is on this same machine
questions.explanation: `MAX_TEXT_BYTES` is 1024. The check for the header being too large comes before the size comparison.

questions.prompt: `ReadFile` reports only 3 bytes read. What does `read_frame` do?
options: Rejects it as having no length header
Reads the text as 3 bytes long
Waits for one more byte before continuing
Decodes it as UTF-8 text
questions.explanation: A header needs 4 bytes. The first check, `bytes_read >= 4`, fails.

questions.prompt: The header declares 10 bytes of text, but `ReadFile` returned 12 bytes in total. What happens?
options: The frame is rejected because 12 is not 10 + 4
The frame is accepted and the extra bytes are ignored
The frame is accepted as 12 bytes of text
The text is decoded and the length is repaired
questions.explanation: The received frame size must equal 4 plus the declared length. 12 does not equal 14.

questions.prompt: Why does `read_frame` check the header exists before looking at the declared length?
options: Later checks depend on facts the earlier ones prove
The declared length is stored after the text bytes
UTF-8 has to be checked before the length is
Windows verifies the header for the program already
questions.explanation: The checks run in dependency order: header present, length within limit, size matching, then UTF-8.

questions.prompt: Why is "local" not the same as "trustworthy" for a pipe?
options: Another program in the account might guess the pipe name
Local pipes are not able to carry UTF-8 text at all
The pipe name is announced to every remote computer
Local clients are the same program as the server
questions.explanation: The receiver treats IPC data as untrusted input and validates everything before making a `String`.

questions.prompt: What does `PIPE_REJECT_REMOTE_CLIENTS` do in the lab?
options: Windows refuses clients that connect from another computer
It encrypts the data that remote clients send over
It lets remote clients read from the pipe but not write
It forces the pipe to use byte mode, not message mode
questions.explanation: Named pipes can support remote clients. The flag keeps this lab's channel on the local machine.

questions.prompt: What does the lesson say about `ImpersonateNamedPipeClient` and token duplication?
options: The lab does not use them; they solve other identity issues
They are required before the server can send its reply
They let the server read the client's private memory
They are used to validate the length header bytes
questions.explanation: The channel only exchanges framed messages. It does not change privileges or start anything as another identity.

questions.prompt: Why does `write_frame` check that `bytes_written` equals the frame length?
options: A short write sends a frame whose header disagrees with it
The header must be rewritten after every write call
Windows writes twice as many bytes as the call requested
A short write changes the pipe over into byte mode
questions.explanation: A successful synchronous call still reports how much it wrote. Accepting less would break the protocol.

questions.prompt: In the `ConnectNamedPipe` match, how are results handled?
options: `Ok` and `ERROR_PIPE_CONNECTED` continue; others are returned
Every error is treated as if the connection had succeeded
`Ok` alone continues, and `ERROR_PIPE_CONNECTED` is returned
`ERROR_PIPE_CONNECTED` closes the pipe and starts over
questions.explanation: The documented race counts as success, but unexpected errors still propagate instead of being hidden.

questions.prompt: The lesson warns against passing a received command string to PowerShell. What should the tool do instead?
options: Define a small message enum and reject unknown variants
Pass the string on after trimming the extra spaces
Check it is under 1024 bytes, then run the command
Run the command when the client is a local one
questions.explanation: Data should select one defined action, not become code. A length limit alone does not make a string safe to execute.

questions.prompt: How does the client put its end of the pipe into message read mode?
options: Call `SetNamedPipeHandleState` with `PIPE_READMODE_MESSAGE`
Call `CreateNamedPipeW` with `PIPE_ACCESS_DUPLEX` set
Call `ConnectNamedPipe` after its first read completes
It cannot, since the server sets the mode for both ends
questions.explanation: The server selects the type when creating the pipe, while the client sets its own read mode after opening it.

questions.prompt: The client runs before any server exists. What happens?
options: `CreateFileW` fails, with advice to start the server first
The client makes the pipe itself and waits for a server
The client writes into a pipe that fills up and stalls
The client falls back to shared memory automatically
questions.explanation: `OPEN_EXISTING` needs a pipe with that name. The lab adds context telling you to start the server in another window.

questions.prompt: Which extra measure does the lesson suggest for a larger tool built on this design?
options: Rate-limit messages and keep queues bounded
Accept longer messages for faster work
Skip validation for local clients
Share one global buffer between all clients
questions.explanation: It also suggests versions, an enum of allowed messages, authentication of sensitive clients, and an explicit security descriptor.

questions.prompt: A 32-bit game holds a `*const f32` and a `*const u8`. How many bytes does each pointer itself take up?
questions.explanation: These plain raw pointers in a 32-bit process each hold a 32-bit address, so both are 4 bytes. The pointee types decide what gets read at the destination: 4 bytes as a float, or 1 byte.
options: 4 and 4, because a pointer's own size is set by the process
4 and 1, because each pointer matches what it points to
8 and 8, because pointers are always 8 bytes
It depends on the value stored at the destination

questions.prompt: Which kind of storage does this book mean by "memory" when it talks about a game's health value?
options: RAM, which holds the running game's state until power-off
The storage drive, which keeps saves and art between sessions
CPU registers, which hold every value the game ever used
The CPU cache, which keeps a permanent copy of each value
questions.explanation: RAM holds the running game's code, objects, and current state, and it is wiped at power-off. The drive keeps files, and registers and caches only hold what the CPU is working on right now.

questions.prompt: Why does saving a game have to write a file to the drive?
options: RAM loses its contents at power-off, while a drive keeps them
RAM can only hold numbers, so saved text must go on a drive
The CPU empties RAM whenever the game window loses focus
A drive is faster to read than RAM, so saves belong there
questions.explanation: Health and other live state sit in RAM, which does not survive a power-off. A drive is slower than RAM, so the last option has the speed relationship backwards.

questions.prompt: A byte has its bits set as 0110 0100 (place values 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1). What decimal value does it hold?
questions.explanation: Add the place values of the positions holding a 1: 64 + 32 + 4 = 100. Mixing up which positions are set gives the other totals.

questions.prompt: What is the largest value one byte can hold, and why?
options: 255, because all eight place values added together make 255
256, because a byte has 256 patterns and the last one is 256
128, because the leftmost bit is the biggest single place value
99, because a byte can show only two decimal digits
questions.explanation: With every bit set a byte holds 128 + 64 + 32 + 16 + 8 + 4 + 2 + 1 = 255. There are 256 patterns, but they start counting at 0.

questions.prompt: Why does exactly one hex digit describe half of a byte?
options: Four bits hold 0 to 15, the same range as one hex digit
Four bits hold 0 to 9, the same range as one decimal digit
Eight bits hold 0 to 15, the same range as one hex digit
Hex digits ignore bit positions, so any split of a byte works
questions.explanation: A half byte has place values 8, 4, 2, and 1, which reach 15 when all are on, and one hex digit covers 0 to 15. That is why two hex digits are always one byte.

questions.prompt: What does "little endian" mean for a multi-byte number on x86 Windows?
options: The least-significant byte sits in the lowest-numbered box
The most-significant byte sits in the lowest-numbered box
The bytes are stored in a random order picked at each launch
Each byte's own bits are written in reverse inside its box
questions.explanation: On x86 the byte worth the least comes first in memory. Big endian is the opposite order, and neither reorders the bits inside a byte.

questions.prompt: Four boxes hold `E8 03 00 00` as a little-endian `u32`. What number is that?
options: 235, because the bytes are added together
232, because only the first box counts
3,892,510,720, because the bytes are read in written order
questions.explanation: The first box counts ones and the second counts 256s, so 232 + 768 = 1,000, which is `0x3E8`. Reading the bytes as written, most significant first, gives the huge wrong number.

questions.prompt: You work out that a `u32` of 300 is `0x012C`. Which bytes should a hex dump show for it on x86?
options: `2C 01 00 00`, with the low byte first
`00 00 01 2C`, exactly as it is written
`01 2C 00 00`, written then padded on the right
`2C 01`, since zero bytes are never stored
questions.explanation: 300 is `0x012C`, so the low byte `2C` comes first, then `01`, then two zero bytes to fill all four boxes. A `u32` always occupies four boxes.

questions.prompt: In the four-box example at `0x1000`, which item is the interpretation rather than the location or the byte pattern?
options: The number 100, read as a little-endian `u32`
The address `0x1000`, which names the first box
The bytes `64 00 00 00`, stored starting at that box
The four boxes, each holding one byte of the value
questions.explanation: Only the reading step turns the pattern into 100. The address says where, and the bytes say what is stored there.

questions.prompt: The lesson says a type answers which two questions?
options: How many bytes to read, and what the bits inside them mean
Where the bytes start, and how long the object stays alive
Which process owns the bytes, and who may write to them
How fast the bytes load, and which register will hold them
questions.explanation: A type is the instruction for reading bytes: a size and a meaning. Location and lifetime are separate ideas.

questions.prompt: What does the type name `i32` tell you?
options: A signed whole number using 32 bits, which may be negative
An unsigned whole number using 32 bits, never negative
A number with a fractional part using 32 bits
A whole number stored in 32 bytes with a sign flag
questions.explanation: `i` means signed integer and the number is the size in bits. `u` is unsigned and `f` is floating point.

questions.prompt: Why is an `i32` range split around zero while a `u32` range starts at 0?
options: Both have 4,294,967,296 patterns; the `i32` spends half on negatives
The `i32` has half as many patterns, because it uses only 16 bits
Negative numbers are kept in a second four-byte box beside it
The `i32` has twice as many patterns, so it covers more numbers
questions.explanation: Both types use 32 bits, so they have the same number of patterns. The `i32` uses half of them for negative numbers, which moves the whole range around zero.

questions.prompt: The bytes `00 00 20 41` are read as a `u32` and then as an `f32`. What changed in memory between the two readings?
options: Nothing; only the type used for reading changed
The scanner rewrote the bytes into floating-point form
The CPU flipped the byte order of the four boxes
Each byte was converted from hex to decimal in RAM
questions.explanation: Both readings are correct and the bytes never change. The `u32` reading gives 1,092,616,192 and the `f32` reading gives 10.0.

questions.prompt: Why can a scan for the whole number 10 not find the float 10.0?
options: They are different byte patterns: `0A 00 00 00` versus `00 00 20 41`
The scanner skips any address that holds a value above 9
Floats live in CPU registers and are never written to RAM
Whole numbers are stored big endian while floats are little endian
questions.explanation: A scanner searches for one specific byte pattern, so it must know the type first. 10 and 10.0 are stored as different patterns.

questions.prompt: An `f32` is asked to hold 10.1. What does it actually store?
options: The nearest value its 32 bits can express, 10.100000381…
Exactly 10.1, because floats keep their decimal digits
10.0999999, always rounded down to the next lower value
10, because the fractional part is dropped on storing
questions.explanation: Most fractions cannot be stored exactly, so the `f32` keeps the closest representable number. That is why scanners accept a small range for floats.

questions.prompt: A position is three `f32` values in a row, with x at +0x00. At which offset does z begin?
options: +0x08, because each `f32` takes four bytes
+0x02, because z is the third value
+0x04, because z follows y directly
+0x0C, because each value takes twelve bytes
questions.explanation: x is at +0x00, y at +0x04, and z at +0x08, because each value is four bytes long and offsets step by 4, not by 1.

questions.prompt: What makes an ordinary number a pointer?
options: The code treats the number as the address of something else
Its size: pointers always fill exactly four bytes
A marker bit that is set inside the stored bytes
Its location: pointers are only ever stored on the stack
questions.explanation: Nothing in the bytes marks a pointer. It is a pointer only because the code that reads it uses it as an address.

questions.prompt: The little-endian bytes `00 50 00 00` could be the number 20,480. What other reading does the lesson give them?
options: A pointer to the address `0x5000`
A float equal to 5.0
Four separate `u8` values that add up to 80
The letter P followed by three padding bytes
questions.explanation: The same bytes are `0x5000` as a `u32`, and if the code uses that number as an address it is a pointer. The code that reads them decides.

questions.prompt: A pointer stored at `0x2000` holds the value `0x5000`. Which statement is correct?
options: Reading `0x2000` gives `0x5000`; a second read there reaches the player
Reading `0x2000` gives the player object, and `0x5000` is a spare copy
Reading `0x5000` gives the address `0x2000` back, so the pointer repeats
The player starts at `0x2000` and `0x5000` is the size of its fields
questions.explanation: The first read returns the pointer's own value. Following it, called dereferencing, is a second read at that address.

questions.prompt: In the library-card comparison, a librarian shelves a different book where the old one was, and your card still says shelf `0x5000`. What does this model?
options: A stale pointer that looks fine but leads to another object
A corrupted pointer whose stored bytes are visibly damaged
A type mismatch that makes the read stop one byte too early
An offset that was rebuilt after the game restarted
questions.explanation: Nothing about the card looks damaged, yet it sends you to the wrong book. A non-zero pointer can still be completely wrong.

questions.prompt: Why would a game keep a pointer to an object instead of using one fixed address?
options: The object can be rebuilt elsewhere and the pointer updated
A pointer lets the object use less RAM than a direct field would
Windows forbids reading any object except through a pointer
A pointer keeps the object at one address even after a restart
questions.explanation: When the game updates the pointer, code that reads it again follows the new address. A pointer does not make an address permanent.

questions.prompt: A `*const f32` and a `*const u8` both hold `0x5000`. What differs when each is followed?
options: How many bytes are read there and how they are interpreted
Which address the pointer holds, since the types shift it
How many bytes the pointer itself takes up in memory
Which process the address is looked up in
questions.explanation: The pointee type describes the data at the destination. The pointer's own size comes from the process architecture.

questions.prompt: A player object starts at `0x5000` and its health is at offset `0x30`. Where is health read?
options: `0x5030`, the base plus the offset
`0x0030`, because an offset is itself an address
`0x4FD0`, found by subtracting the offset from the base
`0x5300`, because the offset is shifted one digit left
questions.explanation: An offset is a distance, not a place. The base says where the object starts and the sum says where to read.

questions.prompt: Why can a field offset keep working after a restart when an object's address may not?
options: It is a distance inside the layout, while the base may move
Offsets are saved on the drive, while addresses exist only in RAM
Windows rewrites each offset to match the new base on launch
The game re-checks every offset before it finishes loading
questions.explanation: Health can stay 48 bytes into the same layout for that build while the object's base moves. Recheck the offset if the game or layout changes.

questions.prompt: How does a stack frame differ from a heap object in how long it lasts?
options: A stack frame lasts through one call; a heap object may outlive many calls
A heap object lasts for exactly one call; a stack frame lasts the whole run
Both last until the game restarts, and then both are freed together
Stack bytes are never reused, but heap bytes are reused instantly
questions.explanation: Later calls can reuse a finished frame's bytes. A heap object lives until the game removes it, and its address may then be reused.

questions.prompt: A debugger and your own tool both show `0x5000`. Why might they not name the same bytes?
options: Virtual addresses belong to one process, each with its own space
One tool is 32-bit and the other silently converts to decimal
Windows hides the lower half of every address from other tools
Addresses are randomized again each time a tool displays them
questions.explanation: That is why an external tool opens a process handle and asks Windows to read an address in that game's space.

questions.prompt: Why is a memory scan described as a snapshot gathered over a short stretch of time?
options: The game keeps updating bytes while the scanner copies them
The scanner copies only half of the bytes to save time
Windows freezes the game, so every copied value is out of date
A scan records only values that changed since the last scan
questions.explanation: A scan copies selected memory while the game runs, so fields may describe slightly different moments. It is not a frozen picture of the whole game.

questions.prompt: You read an enemy pointer, the game removes that enemy and reuses its address for another, and then you read health. What can happen?
options: Both reads succeed, but the answer describes the wrong enemy
The second read always fails because the address was freed
Windows returns the first enemy's health from a cache
The pointer automatically updates to follow the new enemy
questions.explanation: Both reads can succeed and still mislead you. Recheck a promising candidate and its object identity before trusting it.

questions.prompt: A tool only maps regions and reads bytes. Which handle design best follows least privilege?
options: Request query and read rights, without write or operation rights
Request every process right now, in case a later feature needs them
Request write and remote-thread rights as a safety net, then leave them unused
Open no handle and infer the memory map from the PE section table
questions.explanation: Permissions should match the operation the tool performs now. Query-and-read rights are enough for a read-only mapper, make intent clear, and are less likely to fail under ordinary Windows security rules.

questions.prompt: How do a page and a region differ?
options: A page is a fixed unit, commonly 4 KiB; a region is a run of pages with matching rules
A page is a run of regions with matching state; a region is a fixed 4 KiB unit
A page belongs to the EXE file on disk; a region exists after the process starts
A page holds code and a region holds data, and the two do not overlap in memory
questions.explanation: A 200 KiB read-only region is many pages sharing the same rules, not one enormous hardware page.

questions.prompt: With 4 KiB pages, what is the offset inside its page of address `0x0040_1F10`?
questions.explanation: A 4 KiB page is `0x1000` bytes, so the low three hex digits are the offset and the rest, `0x401`, is the virtual page number.

questions.prompt: For `0x1234_5ABC` with 4 KiB pages, what does translation change?
options: The page-number part, `0x12345`; the offset `0xABC` stays the same
The offset part, `0xABC`; the page number `0x12345` stays the same
Both parts, so no digits of the address survive translation
Neither part, because translation checks permissions on the address
questions.explanation: The offset selects one byte inside the page, so translation from virtual page to physical frame leaves it untouched.

questions.prompt: Two games both use virtual address `0x0040_0000`. What does this show?
options: An address is a spot in one process's map, so one number can differ between processes
Both games are reading the same physical RAM cell, so they can overwrite each other
The address was assigned by ToolHelp, so the games share one module list
ASLR is turned off for the games, so every address is identical across processes
questions.explanation: A virtual address is part of a process's map. It does not directly name a RAM chip cell, and one process can have nothing mapped at that number.

questions.prompt: Why does `ReadProcessMemory` take a process handle?
options: So Windows knows which process's map should interpret the address
So the CPU can copy bytes using the handle's number as an offset
So the handle's value can serve as the physical address for the read
So the read can skip the page-protection check for that process
questions.explanation: The same address number can be mapped in one process and absent in another. The handle chooses the map.

questions.prompt: A page is `MEM_COMMIT`. Does that mean it is currently sitting in physical RAM?
options: No; Windows may restore it from storage on access, a page fault and not a bug
Yes; committed means a physical frame is held for the page at each moment
Yes; a page fault means the scanner or the game has a bug that must be fixed
No; committed pages are stored inside the PE file and are copied in on each read
questions.explanation: A page fault is handled by the operating system as normal behavior. Commit says storage is ready, not that the page is resident.

questions.prompt: What does `MEM_RESERVE` mean?
options: The address range is set aside, but no physical or page-file storage is committed
The range is reserved for the kernel and user-mode code cannot see it
The range holds a mapped PE image that has been relocated into place
The range is committed and protected as read-limited until a write request
questions.explanation: `MEM_FREE` has nothing reserved, `MEM_RESERVE` holds the addresses without storage, and `MEM_COMMIT` is usable according to its protection.

questions.prompt: Which pairing of type and meaning is correct?
options: `MEM_IMAGE` is a mapped EXE or DLL; `MEM_PRIVATE` is private memory like heap blocks
`MEM_IMAGE` is private heap memory; `MEM_PRIVATE` is a mapped EXE or DLL file
`MEM_IMAGE` is a mapped file for sharing; `MEM_PRIVATE` is the stack of one thread
`MEM_IMAGE` is unused address space; `MEM_PRIVATE` is a reserved range
questions.explanation: Type says where committed pages came from. `MEM_MAPPED` is a mapped file or shared section.

questions.prompt: What should a scanner do with a `PAGE_GUARD` region?
options: Skip it, because the first access raises an exception and clears the guard flag
Read it twice, because the first read clears the guard flag
Treat the exception as ordinary data and continue scanning the next byte
Change its protection to read-write so the scanner can read it
questions.explanation: Windows uses guard pages for mechanisms such as growing thread stacks. Touching one changes its state, so a scanner should leave it alone.

questions.prompt: How should a reader treat an `RWX` region in a module?
options: As a question to investigate, since some runtimes generate code legitimately
As proof of tampering, since code is not writable in normal software
As harmless, since a page that is executable cannot also be modified
As a place to test a write, since the page is already allowed to change
questions.explanation: The lesson asks who created it, whether it is inside the expected image, whether a clean run shows it, and whether its lifetime fits a known feature. The lab reports RWX regions but never writes to them.

questions.prompt: What does 'write xor execute' suggest about normal memory?
options: It should be writable or executable, not both at once
It should be writable and executable so the loader can patch it
It should be readable or writable, but not both at once
It should be executable after every guard flag has been cleared
questions.explanation: Normal compiled code is readable and executable, and data is writable but not executable. Keeping the roles separate is the point.

questions.prompt: `VirtualQueryEx(current = 0x401800)` returns `BaseAddress = 0x401000` and `RegionSize = 0x3000`. What is `next`?
options: `0x404000`, from the base plus the size
`0x404800`, from the queried address plus the size
`0x402000`, from the base plus one page
`0x401800`, since the walk starts from where it asked
questions.explanation: The walk advances from the returned base to the first address after the whole run. Starting from `current` would skip into the middle of the next region.

questions.prompt: In the walk, `VirtualQueryEx` returns `0`. What should the loop do?
options: Break, because the walk is done and no stale information is used
Retry with the same address until Windows returns a nonzero value
Use the last `MEMORY_BASIC_INFORMATION` again and move on
Add one page to `current` and continue until the end of memory
questions.explanation: A zero return means nothing was described. Consuming the leftover structure would give a phantom region.

questions.prompt: What do the checked addition and `ensure!(next > current)` protect against?
options: A wrapped address, and an endless loop if the reported range does not move forward
A region with write rights, and a handle that has been closed by another thread
A guard page read, and a module that has been unloaded between two queries
A page with the wrong type, and a mismatched architecture in the target
questions.explanation: Checked addition stops an invalid region wrapping to a low address, and the progress check prevents a loop that never ends.

questions.prompt: What is true of every page in the run described by one `RegionSize` from `BaseAddress`?
options: They share one state, one type, and one protection
They belong to one module and have the same RVA
They were committed at the same instant by one thread
They hold the same bytes, so a scan of the first page covers the rest
questions.explanation: A new run begins wherever any of the three changes. `AllocationBase` can be shared by several runs that differ in protection.

questions.prompt: In `Process::open_by_name(&process_name, false)`, what does `false` mean?
options: It requests query and read rights, without `PROCESS_VM_OPERATION` or write rights
It asks Windows to open the process without checking the DACL for this call
It tells the wrapper to keep the handle open after the tool exits
It selects the 32-bit view of the process even when the target is 64-bit
questions.explanation: The lab answers 'what permissions exist?' and does not need permission to change them. The handle should match the question.

questions.prompt: Which name is a position relative to the image base, such as `0x3CCD91`?
options: An RVA
A file offset
A physical address
A live virtual address
questions.explanation: A file offset is a position in the file on disk. A live virtual address is image base plus RVA in one run, and a physical address is hardware memory after page translation.

questions.prompt: The scanner visits only committed, readable, non-guarded regions, yet one `ReadProcessMemory` still fails. Why is that possible?
options: The process kept running, so page state can change between query and read
The query result is cached, so it describes the machine as it was at boot time
Committed pages cannot be read until the handle also has write rights
The scanner skipped the guard pages, which makes later reads in that run fail
questions.explanation: This is another time-of-check/time-of-use race. A robust scanner treats a failed region read as a normal event, reports it, and continues when safe.

questions.prompt: A returned region has base `0x1000` and size `0x5000`, while the module ends at `0x4000`. How big is the size the lab shows?
options: `0x3000`, because the region end is clipped to the module end
`0x5000`, because the full returned size is printed
`0x4000`, because the module end is used as a size
`0x1000`, because the lab shows the base address as the size
questions.explanation: The lab computes the clipped end with `.min(module_end)` and prints `region_end - region.base`: `0x4000 - 0x1000 = 0x3000`.

questions.prompt: Which parallel scanner design gives workers the most stable input?
options: Copy bounded readable code regions once, then scan immutable local buffers
Let every worker repeatedly query and read arbitrary remote pages as it goes
Give every byte its own operating-system thread and merge the results at the end
Patch matches as soon as any worker finds one, so the next worker sees new bytes
questions.explanation: Remote memory changes and Windows reads can fail. Copying once keeps that unstable boundary in one stage, and workers then compare over immutable slices.

questions.prompt: In the lesson's design, which stage touches the running Wesnoth process?
options: Only the capture phase that copies each region
Every worker, so each of them holds its own process handle
The merge stage, which re-reads the pages that were matched
The sort stage, which confirms each address in the live game
questions.explanation: The workers scan ordinary `Vec<u8>` buffers owned by the scanner. That keeps the unstable operating-system boundary in one place.

questions.prompt: Which benefit comes from scanning copied snapshots instead of live memory?
options: A page cannot disappear halfway through a worker's comparison
The scan reads fewer bytes in total, because copies are compressed in memory
The workers can write matches directly back into the live game safely
The scan no longer needs a pattern, since a snapshot knows its own contents
questions.explanation: Copied bytes can also be saved and replayed in tests. The copy does not reduce what is read, and the lab never writes to the game.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes safety and progress promises?
options: Safety says what bad result must never happen; progress says what must eventually finish
Safety says every thread finishes in time; progress says no thread reads a byte twice
Safety is about speed on large inputs; progress is about memory used by each worker
Safety only applies to code using `unsafe`; progress applies to code that uses atomics
questions.explanation: The lesson gives rules such as "the result cap is never exceeded" for safety and "the main thread joins every worker" for progress.

questions.prompt: Why is "it uses atomics" not a complete concurrency argument?
options: You must name which safety fact each atomic protects and what lets each loop finish
Atomics are slower than locks, so they make a scanner unsafe on large inputs
Atomics cannot be shared between threads, so they must be cloned for each worker
Atomic operations are only valid on integers that are smaller than a pointer
questions.explanation: The lesson wants a reason for each atomic: for example, the index hands out regions once and the counter bounds the results.

questions.prompt: Why does the real tool cap all copied executable bytes at 128 MiB?
options: Memory safety stops corruption but not an unbounded allocation exhausting the machine
Windows refuses to read more than 128 MiB from any one process at one time in total
The pattern is only valid inside the first 128 MiB of a module's code, so more is wasted
Rust cannot index a `Vec<u8>` larger than 128 MiB when building for 32-bit Windows
questions.explanation: Safe code can still be logically unbounded. A limit on the total snapshot makes memory use predictable.

questions.prompt: What happens when a page changes between `VirtualQueryEx` and `ReadProcessMemory`?
options: That one region is skipped with a diagnostic, and no partial buffer reaches a worker
The worker receives the partial buffer, and the sort stage later removes bad addresses
The whole scan restarts from the first region until no page changes at all
The process is paused by the scanner until the page can be read completely
questions.explanation: A partial copy could produce wrong matches. Skipping one region and reporting it keeps the other snapshots trustworthy.

questions.prompt: What does `next_region.fetch_add(1, ...)` give each worker?
options: The next unclaimed region number, so no region is handed out twice
A copy of a region, which the worker may modify without affecting the others
A lock on the entire snapshot list, which the worker must release afterward
The number of matches found so far, which the worker adds to its own list
questions.explanation: The atomic increment returns the old value and moves the counter on in one step. When the index passes the slice, the worker finishes.

questions.prompt: Why is dynamic scheduling, where workers fetch the next index when free, better than fixed quarters?
options: A worker that gets small regions can keep helping while another scans a large one
It guarantees that every worker scans exactly the same number of bytes in total
It removes the need for an atomic counter, because each worker owns its own range
It makes the order of results fixed, so the final sort is no longer needed
questions.explanation: Fixed shares can leave one worker idle while another is stuck with big regions. Sorting is still needed, since completion order varies.

questions.prompt: If one large snapshot were split into fixed chunks for a 3-byte pattern, by how many bytes must adjacent chunks overlap?
options: 2 bytes (`pattern.len() - 1`)
3 bytes (`pattern.len()`)
1 byte (the first matching byte)
0 bytes, since windows already cross chunks
questions.explanation: An overlap of `pattern.len() - 1` lets a match across the boundary appear whole in one chunk. The merge must then remove duplicates from the overlap.

questions.prompt: Why does the tool use at most `available_parallelism()` workers and never more workers than snapshots?
options: Thread creation costs memory and time, and surplus workers would have nothing to scan
Windows allows only one thread per snapshot, so extra threads are killed at their start
Each worker needs a whole region to itself, so threads must equal the number of cores
Extra workers would each read the same region again, which would double every address
questions.explanation: A thread per region would be costly when a module has many runs. A worker with no region to claim would simply finish at once.

questions.prompt: Why is a per-thread result limit of 4,096 not enough with eight workers?
options: The workers together could still produce 32,768 items
Eight workers would each skip 4,096 items, so no result would ever be recorded
The limit would be applied eight times, so only 512 items could ever be kept
Each worker would reset the limit when it claimed another region from the queue
questions.explanation: 8 × 4,096 = 32,768. A bound across every worker needs one shared counter, not one limit per thread.

questions.prompt: With a global cap of three, worker 1 has two matches and worker 2 finds two more. How many can be published?
options: Three in total, because only one of worker 2's matches gets the last slot
Four in total, because each worker checks the counter at the same time
Two in total, because the second worker is cancelled after its first match
Five in total, because the cap applies only to matches that came from worker 1
questions.explanation: Each match must reserve a slot through the shared counter. Reading "2 of 3 used" and then appending would publish four.

questions.prompt: What does `fetch_update` do in `reserve_match`?
options: It checks that the counter is below the cap and increments it as one atomic step
It reads the counter first and then adds one in a separate step after the check
It resets the counter to zero when the cap is reached, so scanning can continue
It copies the counter into each worker, so every worker has its own private count
questions.explanation: Doing the check and the increment together is what keeps two workers from taking the same last slot. Separate steps would allow a gap.

questions.prompt: What is the job of `Release` when storing the cancellation flag and `Acquire` when loading it?
options: Release publishes the cancellation, and Acquire lets other workers observe it
Release frees the worker's snapshot memory, and Acquire allocates the next snapshot
Release locks the match list for one thread, and Acquire unlocks it for the others
Release stops the process under test, and Acquire resumes it after the workers end
questions.explanation: The ordering communicates two small state transitions. The snapshot bytes themselves need no such protection because they never change.

questions.prompt: Why do the snapshot bytes need no mutex or atomic?
options: They are immutable, so many workers can read them without conflict
They are stored in a different process, so the workers cannot touch them
They are read one at a time by the main thread, so the workers only get copies
They are marked executable, and Windows serializes every read of executable pages
questions.explanation: Shared reads of data that never changes are safe. The shared mutable pieces are only the index, the counter, and the flag.

questions.prompt: Why does the scanner call `dedup()` after sorting if clipped regions should not overlap?
options: Downstream correctness should not depend on the hope that no overlap ever occurs
Sorting turns each address into two copies, and `dedup` removes the extra copy
Without it, the compiler would treat the match list as unsorted and refuse to compile
Deduplication is what makes an ambiguous pattern unique, so it must always run
questions.explanation: The lesson calls it defensive. It also matters if chunking is added later, because overlapping chunks would report some addresses twice.

questions.prompt: Capture takes 80% of a run and scanning takes 20%. What is the best overall speedup from parallelizing the scan perfectly?
options: Roughly 1.25x
Roughly 5x
Roughly 10x
Roughly 0.8x
questions.explanation: The 80% that stays serial remains, so the best case is 1 ÷ 0.8 = 1.25. More workers shrink only the 20% part.

questions.prompt: The parallel scanner reports zero matches on the supported Wesnoth build. What does that mean?
options: The build, capture, or signature assumption is wrong, and parallelism does not change that
The workers finished too quickly, so the scan should be repeated with more threads
The cap was reached, which the scanner reports as a zero count to stay safe
The sort step removed every address, since a unique match is not allowed to stay
questions.explanation: A supported build should give one address. Zero or many mean the same things as in the single-threaded scanner.

questions.prompt: What should happen if one scanner worker panics?
options: The main thread's join reports it as an error instead of waiting forever
The other workers continue silently, and the missing region is left out of the results
The panic is hidden by the sort step, so the final list still looks complete
The process under test is stopped, since a worker panic corrupts its memory
questions.explanation: One progress promise is that a worker panic becomes an error rather than an endless wait. The main thread joins every worker before publishing.

questions.prompt: A guard faces (1, 0). The unit direction to the player is (0.6, 0.8). With VIEW_CONE_COS = 0.5, can the guard see the player, ignoring walls and distance?
questions.explanation: For unit vectors the dot product is the cosine of the angle between them. 0.6 is at least cos 60° = 0.5, so the player is less than 60° from the facing (about 53°) and inside the cone.
options: Yes: 0.6 × 1 + 0.8 × 0 = 0.6, which is at least 0.5
No: 0.8 is larger than 0.6, so the target lies mostly to the side
Yes: any direction with a positive y part falls inside the cone
No: 0.6 + 0.8 = 1.4 is above 1, so the dot product is invalid

questions.prompt: A guard stands at `(0, 0)` and the player at `(4, 3)`. What is `offset`, and what does it mean?
options: `(4, 3)`, the arrow from the guard to the player
`(4, 3)`, the arrow from the player to the guard
`(5, 0)`, the distance placed on the x axis
`(7, 0)`, the two parts added together
questions.explanation: Offset is the target's position minus the guard's: (4 − 0, 3 − 0). It is a vector, an arrow, not a single number.

questions.prompt: The guard's `VIEW_DISTANCE` is 10. A player is at offset `(4, 3)`, another at `(15, 0)`. Which pass the distance check?
options: Only the first, at distance 5 (the second is 15 away)
Only the second, since 15 is the larger number
Both, since each is within 20 units on some axis
Neither, since each is more than 10 along one axis
questions.explanation: Pythagoras gives √(16 + 9) = 5 for `(4, 3)`, within 10, and √225 = 15 for `(15, 0)`, which fails.

questions.prompt: For two unit vectors, what does the dot product equal?
options: The cosine of the angle between them
The angle between them in degrees
The distance between their tips
The product of their lengths added together
questions.explanation: For unit vectors, `a.x × b.x + a.y × b.y` is the cosine of the angle. For a guard facing east it is simply the other vector's x part.

questions.prompt: Why does `VIEW_CONE_COS = 0.5` stand for 60°?
options: A triangle with three sides of 1 has 60° angles, so 1 − 1² ÷ 2 = 0.5
Half of the 120° cone is 60°, so the constant is simply that fraction
Any cosine equals half its angle in degrees, divided by 60
The cone is split into two halves, and each half is worth 0.5
questions.explanation: Two unit vectors 60° apart have tips 1 apart, so the formula gives 1 − 1² ÷ 2 = 0.5. The constant is a cosine, not a fraction of the cone.

questions.prompt: What does `direction.dot(self.facing) < VIEW_CONE_COS` reject?
options: Directions more than 60° from the facing, on either side
Directions less than 60° from the facing, on either side
Directions on the guard's left side of the facing only
Directions that lie farther than 10 units from the guard
questions.explanation: Cosine falls steadily as the angle grows, so a dot product below 0.5 means an angle above 60°. The cone is 60 + 60 = 120° wide.

questions.prompt: A player stands at `(0, 5)` and the guard at `(0, 0)` faces east `(1, 0)`. Does the guard see them?
options: No: direction `(0, 1)` gives dot product 0, a 90° turn to the side
Yes: they are 5 units away, well inside the distance of 10
Yes: the dot product is 1, so they are directly ahead of the guard
No: the dot product is negative, so they are behind the guard
questions.explanation: 0 × 1 + 1 × 0 = 0, which is below 0.5. Distance passes, but the cone check fails.

questions.prompt: Why does the code compare the dot product with a constant instead of computing the angle?
options: Getting an angle needs a slower inverse cosine
An angle cannot be stored in an `f32` value
The dot product is already measured in degrees
An angle would change the guard's own facing
questions.explanation: Comparing with a cosine worked out once gives the same answer using two multiplications and one addition.

questions.prompt: On tick 8 the guard is at `(4, 0)`, the player at `(8, 0)`, and the wall spans x 5.5 to 6.5, y −1 to 1. Why does the sample `(5.6, 0)` stop the walk?
options: It lies inside both bounds of the wall, so the walk returns `false`
It is the first sample more than 1 unit away from the guard
It sits exactly on the line y = 0, which counts as being the wall
It is the sample closest to the player's position at `(8, 0)`
questions.explanation: A point is inside a box when each coordinate lies between the corners: 5.5 ≤ 5.6 ≤ 6.5 and −1 ≤ 0 ≤ 1. The walk stops there and never tests the rest.

questions.prompt: A line runs from `(0, 0)` to `(4, 3)`, and a wall covers x 2 to 3, y −1 to 1. Does the wall block sight?
options: No: the line's y is 1.5 to 2.25 over x 2 to 3, above the wall's top
Yes: the line crosses x = 2 inside the wall's range of x values
Yes: the wall sits between the two end points along the x axis
No: a line with slope 3 ÷ 4 can never meet an axis-aligned box
questions.explanation: The line has y = 0.75 × x, so over the wall's x range it passes over the box. Sharing an x range is not enough, so no sample lands inside.

questions.prompt: `SIGHT_STEP` is 0.1. How many samples does a check across the full view distance of 10 need?
options: 10, one for each unit
1, since a ray is a single test
questions.explanation: Each sample is tested against every wall, so line of sight costs more with distance. Engines use exact ray casts instead of stepping.

questions.prompt: What does utility AI do each time it chooses?
options: Scores every option for the situation and runs the highest
Walks through a priority list and runs the first that succeeds
Moves between named states along fixed arrows
Picks randomly among options that score above 0
questions.explanation: A state machine asks which mode it is in. Utility scoring asks which option is best right now. Priority lists belong to behaviour trees.

questions.prompt: A fighter at health 0.3 has an enemy in view, no cover, and one potion. Which option scores highest?
options: Take cover, at 0.72, ahead of heal at 0.70 and attack at 0.58
Heal, at 0.70, which beats both attack and take cover
Attack, at 0.58, since it scores best when an enemy is in view
Attack, at 0.58, since it is the first option in the match
questions.explanation: Take cover scores 0.9 − 0.6 × 0.3 = 0.72, ahead of healing at 1.0 − 0.3 = 0.70 and attacking at 0.4 + 0.18 = 0.58.

questions.prompt: Take cover scores `0.9 − 0.6h` and Heal scores `1.0 − h`. At what health do they tie?
options: 0.5, since the two scores meet at half health
questions.explanation: Setting 0.9 − 0.6h = 1.0 − h gives 0.4h = 0.1, so h = 0.25. Below that health, healing beats cover.

questions.prompt: Hurt (health 0.3), in cover, and out of potions, which option does the fighter choose?
options: Attack, since cover and heal both score 0
Take cover, since it was chosen last time
Heal, since low health always means heal
Nothing, since no option scores above 0.58
questions.explanation: Once in cover, taking cover scores 0, and healing with no potions scores 0. Attack, at 0.58, is all that is left.

questions.prompt: With nobody in view and full health, every option scores 0. What does `choose` return?
options: `None`, so another system such as patrol keeps control
`Attack`, since it is the first option in the list
`Heal`, since health is full and healing is safe
An error, since no score is above zero to pick from
questions.explanation: `choose` keeps only scores above 0, then picks the highest. With none left, nothing on the list is worth doing.

questions.prompt: Near a switch point, a tiny health change can flip the choice every tick. How do games damp this?
options: Add a small bonus to whatever the NPC is already doing
Round health to the nearest whole number before scoring
Run the scoring only once every second instead of each tick
Remove the option that scored lowest on the last tick
questions.explanation: A rival option must then beat the current action clearly before the NPC switches, so the choice stops flickering.

questions.prompt: In a behaviour tree, what is the difference between a selector and a sequence?
options: A selector stops at the first success; a sequence at the first failure
A selector runs every child; a sequence runs only its last child
A selector holds a score; a sequence holds the current state
A selector runs children right to left; a sequence left to right
questions.explanation: The guard's tree is one selector of sequences, tried in priority order. At 20 health the first sequence reaches flee and the rest are never inspected.

questions.prompt: Where do values such as `seen_for` and `last_known` live in a behaviour tree design?
options: In a shared store kept beside the tree, called a blackboard
Inside each leaf node, where they are reset on every tick
In the selector at the root, which keeps one value per child
They are recalculated from scratch on every tick of the game
questions.explanation: The tree keeps no memory between ticks by itself, so engines store these values in a blackboard.

questions.prompt: How did the guard's four arrows into Flee appear in the behaviour tree?
options: As one child placed first, since priorities restart at the top
As four separate sequences, one for each of the other four states
As a blackboard value that every node in the tree must read first
They disappear, since a behaviour tree has no way of making a guard flee
questions.explanation: Because priorities are re-checked from the root each tick, the single first child covers every state.

questions.prompt: In the toy C++ `Guard` struct, where is the one-byte `state` field, and where does `seen_for` start?
options: State at `0x14`, `seen_for` at `0x18`, with 3 padding bytes between
State at `0x10`, `seen_for` at `0x11`, with no padding between them
State at `0x14`, `seen_for` at `0x15`, with no padding between them
State at `0x18`, `seen_for` at `0x1C`, with 4 padding bytes between
questions.explanation: Four floats fill 0x00 to 0x0F and health fills 0x10 to 0x13, so the state is at 0x14; a 4-byte field must start at a multiple of 4, so bytes 0x15 to 0x17 are padding.

questions.prompt: The `Guard` structure ends at `0x24` bytes. What is that in decimal, and why is it not 33?
options: 36, since three padding bytes follow the one-byte state
36, since every field is padded out to a width of 8 bytes
33, since padding bytes are not counted in a structure's size
32, since the last field is left out of the structure's size
questions.explanation: Eight 4-byte fields (32 bytes) plus one state byte and three padding bytes give 36, which is 2 × 16 + 4. Alignment makes the compiler insert padding.

questions.prompt: In a toy C++ program, you write 9 into the state byte. What can happen, and why?
options: It depends on the `switch`: a range check gives a default branch, a bare jump table may crash
It goes to Patrol, since every out-of-range value is treated as state 0 by the compiler
It crashes at once, since one byte cannot hold a value that lies past the last real state
It becomes Chase, since 9 wraps around to 1 when it is stored inside a single byte
questions.explanation: Compilers often turn a switch into a jump table. With a range check, 9 takes the default branch; without one, the code reads past the table and usually crashes. In Rust, safe code cannot store 9 in a `GuardState`.

questions.prompt: The tool captured a valid gold address, but the second snapshot has a different side pointer. What should the advanced pipeline do?
questions.explanation: A remote address has meaning only while the object path and target profile still support it. A changed side pointer invalidates the earlier destination, so the correct transaction outcome is no write.
options: Stop without writing because the object identity changed
Write to the old address because it was valid earlier
Search all writable memory for the old gold number
Ignore the pointer and compare only the PID

questions.prompt: What is the lesson's central idea about the six pipeline phases?
options: Data crosses a gate before the tool acts on it, since a raw address read once may be stale
More code is safer, since each added phase makes the game run slower and so steadier
A raw address is permanent, so the phases exist mainly to improve the layout of the output
The phases run in parallel threads, which hides the delay between reading and writing
questions.explanation: The point is not extra code. A single long function trusts earlier facts after the game may have changed, while gates check them again.

questions.prompt: Why does `Snapshot` keep `player`, `side`, `gold_address`, and `gold`, not just the gold number?
options: Comparing all four catches a changed pointer link, not only a changed gold value
Four fields make the struct large enough to be read as one 16-byte record
Each field is a different player's gold, so the tool shows all four sides
Rust requires a struct with `Eq` to have at least four fields to compile
questions.explanation: Equality then asks whether the whole chain and its value stayed the same, which is stronger than comparing the final address only.

questions.prompt: In the `Snapshot`, what can a changed `side` value mean?
options: The faction or match state moved on, so the earlier chain no longer applies
The gold number was rounded, so the other fields must be recalculated again
The tool opened the process with the wrong rights, so some reads have failed
The player count dropped below the cap, so the whole table is now smaller
questions.explanation: `player` changing means the root reaches another object, and `side` changing can mean the faction or match moved on. Either invalidates a proposed action.

questions.prompt: How does `stable_snapshot` decide a result is acceptable?
options: It captures twice and returns the first if the two match; otherwise it retries
It captures once and returns the result, since a single read is always consistent
It captures twice and returns the larger gold value, so the newest data always wins
It captures five times and returns the first one, since five is the safe number
questions.explanation: Equal consecutive captures suggest a quiet moment. The loop retries up to five times with a message and then fails with an error.

questions.prompt: Why does the lesson say two equal reads are not a mathematical proof?
options: A changed state could have existed between the reads without showing in either
Equal values can occur only when the game is paused, so the check never really works
The two reads run at the very same moment and so always return identical values
A snapshot cannot be compared with another snapshot using `==` in Rust at all
questions.explanation: It is an optimistic consistency check that assumes a short read sees a quiet moment, then verifies the assumption. It does not lock the running game.

questions.prompt: Which choices does the lesson name as stronger than two reads when a larger structure must be perfectly atomic?
options: A debugger pause, a game-provided snapshot API, or a version counter
A longer sleep between reads, a larger retry cap, or a bigger buffer
Reading the player root twice, the side twice, and the address twice
Opening the process with full write rights, a lock file, or a copy of memory on disk
questions.explanation: These tools give a real guarantee that the structure did not change mid-read. Two equal reads are a practical gate for a tiny offline lab.

questions.prompt: Why does `stable_snapshot` stop after a retry cap and not loop until it sees stability?
options: An endless loop can make a broken tool look frozen
A cap of five makes the game finish its turn before the next read
Without a cap, the first capture would be written to the game
The compiler removes a loop that has no maximum number of attempts
questions.explanation: If the pointer path keeps changing, waiting forever helps nobody. Stopping with an error is more useful than appearing frozen.

questions.prompt: When the tool runs with no arguments, what rights does it request, and why?
options: Query and read only, so a tool that only looks has a handle that cannot write
Query, read, operation, and write, since the handle must be the same for every run
Write only, since reads are allowed for every process by default
No rights at all, since the operating system chooses them after the handle opens
questions.explanation: The command decides what access it needs before opening the process. The `--set` mode adds the operation and write rights.

questions.prompt: In `Process::open_by_name("wesnoth.exe", replacement.is_some())`, what does the second argument do?
options: It asks for write access only when a replacement value was given
It tells the tool which gold amount to write into the process
It tells the tool to retry the open up to five times until it works
It asks for a 32-bit handle, so a 64-bit target is refused
questions.explanation: The decision about write rights happens before the process is opened. `is_some()` is true only when the user passed `--set`.

questions.prompt: Which sequence matches the lesson's write path?
options: Re-capture and require equality, write four little-endian bytes, read back and compare
Write the new value, re-capture the snapshot, then print success if no error was raised
Capture once, write four big-endian bytes, then read the process handle's status code
Re-capture once, write eight bytes to cover the pointer, then restart the whole match
questions.explanation: Each gate enforces one arrow in the diagram. The precondition comes before the write, and the postcondition is checked after it.

questions.prompt: Just before writing, the fresh snapshot differs from the one the caller approved. What does the tool do?
options: It writes nothing and stops, since the earlier snapshot is out of date
It writes to the new address from the fresh snapshot instead
It writes to the old address anyway, since the caller already approved it
It writes zero to both addresses to be safe and reports success
questions.explanation: The approval applied to specific evidence. If that evidence changed, the right response is to capture again, not to write.

questions.prompt: What does the read-back after the write protect against?
options: Reporting success when the requested value never actually reached memory
The game changing the visible gold after the match has already been ended
The tool writing more than four bytes into the gold field of the side object
A second user running the same tool against the same process at the same time
questions.explanation: A write call returning without error does not prove the postcondition. The tool reads the value and requires it to equal the replacement.

questions.prompt: Why does the lesson say the write path is not a database transaction?
options: Windows cannot roll the game back, so it only checks a precondition and a postcondition
A transaction needs a network connection, which this offline lab does not have available
A database holds numbers, but a game keeps its gold in a text form instead
A transaction is always read-only, while this tool is written to change values
questions.explanation: If the write succeeds but is wrong, nothing is automatically undone. The guarded action checks before and after instead.

questions.prompt: The player root reads as null. What is the correct response in the failure table?
options: Start a supported local match and do not invent an address
Write to address zero and wait for the game to create the root
Search every writable region for the old gold number
Use the last known address from the previous run instead
questions.explanation: A null root means no supported local match is ready. Guessing an address would break the idea that actions need evidence.

questions.prompt: The target is not a 32-bit process. What does this profile do?
options: It refuses the run, since the profile does not describe that target
It adapts the offsets automatically, since pointer sizes can be inferred
It runs in read-only mode and ignores the architecture afterwards
It continues, since pointer width belongs to the tool and not the game
questions.explanation: The pointer path and 32-bit pointer reads belong to the 32-bit Wesnoth 1.14.9 course build. Another architecture means the offsets do not apply.

questions.prompt: The tool is run with `--set 5000000`. What happens, given the lab limit?
options: It refuses before touching the game, since it exceeds the 1,000,000 lab limit
It writes 5,000,000 once the usual snapshot checks have passed in the pipeline
It writes 1,000,000 instead, since the tool silently clamps the value to the limit
It opens the process with write rights first, then reports the error much later
questions.explanation: The argument is validated up front with `ensure!(value <= MAX_GOLD)`. Rejected input never reaches a handle with write rights.

questions.prompt: After the match ends, the tool is run again with `--set`. What should it do?
options: Report a null or unstable object and refuse to write to address zero
Write the value to the last gold address that was valid in the previous match
Write the value to a new address chosen by scanning for the number
Succeed quietly, since the gold field remains valid after a match ends
questions.explanation: A trustworthy tool has more stop paths than force paths. The null or unstable object is a stop, not an instruction to guess.

questions.prompt: The lesson suggests unit-testing decision logic with fake snapshots. What does that make possible?
options: Testing comparisons and decisions without opening any process
Testing the real Wesnoth gold address without the game running
Skipping the read-back check, since fake data cannot be wrong
Writing to a second process, so two games share one snapshot
questions.explanation: Keep remote input and output at the edge. The middle of the program compares ordinary typed values, which tests can build by hand.

questions.prompt: Which upgrade would make the snapshot say more about which game build it came from?
options: Adding a target-profile name and an executable hash to the snapshot
Adding a longer sleep between the two captures in the stable check
Adding a second write to the gold field after the read-back
Adding the replacement value to the snapshot's equality check
questions.explanation: Recording the profile and the hash ties the evidence to an exact build. A timestamp and module base would also help, but a sleep or a second write add no identity.

questions.prompt: Player records are `0x270` bytes apart and gold is at offset `0x04`. What offset from the table base reaches the third player's gold? Use hexadecimal.
questions.explanation: The third player has zero-based index 2. First find the record: `2 × 0x270 = 0x4E0`. Then add the gold field: `0x4E0 + 0x04 = 0x4E4`. Keeping stride math separate from field math makes the layout easier to verify.

questions.prompt: Why is `PlayerSnapshot` described as a copy and not a live reference into Wesnoth?
options: The remote process may change right after the read, so the struct holds values from one moment
Rust cannot hold a reference to another process, so a copy is the only choice that compiles
The game freezes while the tool reads, so the copy stays valid for the whole match
A reference would hide the gold field, and a copy always shows every field in the record
questions.explanation: A snapshot is a photograph, not a live window. It may be stale a moment later, which keeps timestamps and failed reads honest.

questions.prompt: Which pipeline does the lesson use to keep an observer from becoming the game's state owner?
options: Remote bytes, then a validated copied snapshot, then display or analysis
Display or analysis, then a live pointer, then remote bytes
Remote bytes, then display directly, then a validated copy at the end
A validated snapshot, then remote bytes, then a lock held on the game
questions.explanation: The tool owns only what it copies. Each layer has one job: read, validate, and present.

questions.prompt: Gold and income change at the end of a turn. What does the lesson say about a sampling rate of thousands of reads per second?
options: It adds overhead without making such slow values more truthful
It guarantees that no change in gold is ever missed, at no real cost
It is required, since a read below that rate always returns stale data
It makes failures easier to follow, since each read is logged separately
questions.explanation: Reading once per second answers strategy-level questions. The lesson suggests once or twice a second for a learning tool.

questions.prompt: In an inline record table the address is `base + index × record_size`. How does a pointer table differ?
options: The same math locates a pointer slot; reading the slot gives the record address
The same math gives the record address directly, so no extra read is needed
The index is added to the record size only, and the base address is ignored
The slot holds the player's gold itself, so the index alone is enough
questions.explanation: The two layouts need different read steps. A pointer table's records may be separately allocated elsewhere.

questions.prompt: An inline table starts at `0x1000` with 32-byte records. Where does player index 2 begin?
options: `0x1040`, because two strides of `0x20` come after the base
`0x1020`, because one stride of `0x20` comes after the base
`0x1060`, because three strides of `0x20` come after the base
`0x1200`, because 2 × 0x100 is added to the base
questions.explanation: Index 2 skips two records: `0x1000 + 2 × 0x20 = 0x1040`. Zero-based indexing means index 0 starts at the base itself.

questions.prompt: A nearby `imul eax, edx, record_size` instruction multiplies the player index by what?
options: A constant that states the record size, which still needs confirming on two players
A pointer that names the next record, which is followed until a null one appears
The player count, which is why a table can never have more than one player
The gold offset, which is why gold always sits at the start of a record
questions.explanation: The compiler had to know the stride to generate that code, so the constant can be read off. The lesson still says to confirm it with two real players.

questions.prompt: Two known players' record addresses differ by exactly one record size. What have you learned?
options: The stride between players, but not yet a full record layout
The offset of every field in a record, including gold and income
The number of players in the match, which you can now cap in code
The base address of the pointer root, which is also the first record
questions.explanation: A difference between two records gives the stride only. Fields inside the record still need their own confirmation.

questions.prompt: Why does the lesson say not to cast an unknown memory range to a giant struct?
options: Unconfirmed fields would be treated as facts; read confirmed fields by offset instead
Rust forbids any struct larger than 64 bytes from being read from another process
A cast makes the remote process change the layout to fit the struct
A giant struct always misaligns gold, since gold must be read as a `u8`
questions.explanation: Only fields you verified should appear in the snapshot. Guessing a whole layout hides which assumptions are untested.

questions.prompt: `PlayerLayout` stores `gold: 4`. What does the lesson say about that number?
options: Gold is four bytes from each record's base here, and tests must confirm it
Gold is four bytes long, which settles the matter for every build of the game
Gold belongs to the fourth player, so a value of 4 selects the right record
It is proven true once stored, since a struct field cannot hold a wrong number
questions.explanation: Storing a number does not make it true. Range checks and behavior tests decide whether it still holds for this exact build.

questions.prompt: `read_players` calls `ensure!(count <= 16, ...)`. What problem does the cap prevent?
options: A corrupted count turning one bad read into thousands of reads
A player slot claiming more than 16 bytes of its own record
A match containing more than 16 gold values to show on the display
A debugger staying attached while the record table is being read
