options: The CPU writes it to the shared pool, and the GPU reads the same bytes
The CPU copies it across a PCI Express bus into the GPU's own video RAM
The security processor copies it between two separate memory pools
The hypervisor encrypts it in the game partition and decrypts it for the GPU
questions.explanation: On a gaming PC the textures and buffers are copied across the PCI Express bus. A console's CPU and GPU share one pool, so no copy is needed.

questions.prompt: The PlayStation 5's memory bus is 256 bits wide and each wire carries 14 billion bits per second. How many bytes per second is that?
options: 448 GB: 256 x 14 = 3,584 billion bits, divided by 8 bits per byte
3,584 GB: 256 x 14 = 3,584 billion, counting each bit as a byte
1,792 GB: 256 x 14 = 3,584 billion bits, divided by 2 for the two directions
1.75 GB: 14 billion bits divided by 8 bits per byte, for a single wire
questions.explanation: Multiplying the width by the rate gives total bits per second. Dividing by 8 turns bits into bytes, which gives 448 GB every second shared by the CPU and GPU.

questions.prompt: At 60 frames per second, roughly how much time does the console have for all of one frame's work?
options: About 16.7 ms, from 1,000 ms divided by 60
About 60 ms, since each frame uses the full number of frames
About 33.3 ms, from 1,000 ms divided by 30
About 6.0 ms, from 1,000 ms divided by 60 and then by 3
questions.explanation: A second has 1,000 ms, so 60 frames each get 1,000 / 60, which is about 16.7 ms. A background task that takes 2 ms at the wrong moment makes a visible stutter.

questions.prompt: Why can console developers spend a frame's time budget almost to the last millisecond?
options: Every console of one model has the same chip, memory and clocks, so one measurement holds for all
The console's hypervisor stretches a frame when a game runs late, so a late frame never shows up
Console games skip all operating system calls, so nothing else uses time in a frame
Unified memory removes the frame limit, because the GPU can simply wait for the CPU
questions.explanation: A PC game must run on thousands of part combinations, while a console game targets exactly one. Developers can even compile shaders ahead of time for the single GPU.

questions.prompt: The PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X use the same x86-64 instruction set as many PCs. Why is moving a console game to PC still porting work?
options: The game's code calls the console's own operating system and graphics interfaces
The console CPU cores store numbers in the opposite byte order from a PC
The console encrypts its machine code with an instruction set that PCs do not run
The console GPU cannot be addressed by a PC's graphics driver at all
questions.explanation: The instruction set is shared, but machine code calls into the console's OS and graphics interfaces, such as a console version of Direct3D 12 on Xbox.

questions.prompt: A malformed save file crashes a game on a console with a hypervisor and two partitions. Why does the damage stay inside the game partition?
options: System partition memory, which holds account tokens, is not mapped into the game
The security processor restarts the whole console, so any damage is erased on reboot
The game partition is read-only, so a crash cannot change any of the saved data on disk
The hypervisor rewrites each save file with a checksum before the game can open it again
questions.explanation: A partition is a virtual machine that sees only the cores, memory and devices the hypervisor gives it. The game partition can still make narrow, checked requests of system services.

questions.prompt: Which description fits the console's security processor?
options: A small separate processor that starts before the main cores and holds keys they never see
A main CPU core reserved for the hypervisor, which runs keys on behalf of the game partition
A chip on the network adapter that scans all incoming data for modified software
A fuse bank that counts the security version and refuses old boot images itself
questions.explanation: Most console chips contain such a processor. It performs the checks and, later, decrypts game content without handing the keys to the game or the system software.

questions.prompt: Why does the chain of trust need no check on the boot ROM itself?
options: It is written into the chip at manufacture and nobody can change it, so it is where trust starts
It is signed by the bootloader, which lets the chain check itself in a loop
It is rechecked by the hypervisor every time a game starts, so it never needs a first check
It is stored in flash, where the owner can replace it with a signed update
questions.explanation: Every later stage is trusted only because an earlier stage checked it. The chain ends at the one piece of code that cannot be altered.

questions.prompt: An RSA-2048 public key would need 2,048 fuses. How do chips avoid this?
options: They fuse a 256-bit SHA-256 hash of the key, and the key itself travels in flash with the bootloader
They fuse only the first 256 bits of the key, and the rest is guessed from the signature
They fuse a 256-bit SHA-256 hash of the signature, and the key is read from the security processor
They fuse the key once at the maker and use a different 256-bit key for every boot stage
questions.explanation: A 256-bit hash costs 256 fuses. The boot ROM hashes the key that came with the image and compares it with the fused value, so the full key can safely live in flash.

questions.prompt: What does the boot ROM do first with the public key that came with the boot image?
options: It hashes the key and compares the result with the hash held in fuses
It uses the key to check the image's signature straight away
It compares the key with the previous image's key stored in flash
It sends the key to the online service for approval
questions.explanation: A mismatch means someone supplied their own key. Only once the key is trusted does the ROM check the signature, then the security version, and then jump to the code.

questions.prompt: Three of eight anti-rollback fuses are blown. An update that fixes a security hole raises the version to 4. What is true afterwards?
options: Fuse 3 is blown, and version-3 images are refused from then on
Fuse 2 is unblown, and the old image is kept for recovery purposes
Four fuses are blown, but version-3 images are still accepted for older games
Fuse 7 is blown, so the console now counts down from eight
questions.explanation: The minimum accepted security version equals the number of blown fuses, and it only ever rises because a fuse cannot be unblown.

questions.prompt: Why do makers raise the security version only for updates that fix a security flaw?
options: A bank of eight fuses can only count to 8, and each increase spends a fuse forever
Raising the version slows the console's boot by one check for each increase
Raising the version needs a new signature key from the maker for each update
A higher version makes the hypervisor refuse every game released before the update
questions.explanation: A fuse cannot be unblown, so the counter is a limited resource. Spending it on every update would use it up.

questions.prompt: A console game package is both signed and encrypted. What does each protection do?
options: The signature proves it came unchanged from the platform holder; the encryption hides its contents
The signature hides the contents; the encryption proves who made the package
The signature stops the game from being downloaded; the encryption stops it being installed
The signature protects the keys; the encryption protects the security version
questions.explanation: The two protections do different jobs. Encryption keeps code from being read or copied to run elsewhere, and its keys stay inside the security processor.

questions.prompt: Why do consoles generally not let ordinary games mark memory as both writable and executable?
options: Code a game writes for itself at run time was never signed, but all code must be
Writable memory is kept on a different chip from executable memory on a console
A game that runs its own code would slow the hypervisor's scheduling of the partitions
Executable memory is kept encrypted, so a game could not write bytes into it
questions.explanation: Everything a console runs must carry the platform holder's signature, so memory that is both writable and executable is a place where unsigned code could appear. An emulator's fastest technique needs exactly that combination.

questions.prompt: The owner of a Windows PC and the owner of a retail console each try to run an unsigned program. What happens?
options: Windows warns, then runs it as the owner decides; the console refuses to run it
Both refuse, because every operating system rejects code that has no signature
Both run it after a warning, because the owner is the administrator on each
Windows refuses, and the console runs it only when it is offline
questions.explanation: On a PC an Authenticode signature is optional for ordinary programs. On a console the platform holder decides which code may run, through signatures.

questions.prompt: How does a console's security goal differ from a PC's, according to the lesson?
options: It also defends the platform holder and publishers against the owner, who cannot switch it off
It defends only against network attackers, because the owner has no access to the hardware
It defends the owner more strongly, with keys the owner can export when needed
It defends the hypervisor from games, but leaves the system partition open to the owner
questions.explanation: A PC's security defends its owner against other people, and the owner is the administrator who can switch protections off. A console is built so that the owner cannot, down to fused debug ports.

questions.prompt: In remote attestation, what does the security processor sign?
options: The service's nonce plus the boot measurements, using a key unique to that console
A hash of the whole game library, using the platform holder's one shared key
The owner's account name together with the console's printed serial number
A list of the games last played, using a key stored in the boot image file
questions.explanation: The measurements are hashes recorded by each boot stage of the next stage before it ran. The service checks the signature and compares them with the values genuine software produces.

questions.prompt: Why does an online service ban a console that fails attestation, instead of just ignoring the report?
options: A modified console can cheat, run pirated games, or send odd messages, so nothing it says is trusted
The console's report damages the service's servers, so a ban is technically necessary to stop it
Console makers publish their attestation protocols, so any console that fails is seen as hostile
A failed report proves the owner copied games, which is the offence the ban would punish
questions.explanation: The ban is the service's decision under its terms of service, not a technical malfunction. It protects other players and the store.

questions.prompt: Even with remote attestation, why do well-designed online games still check every action on the server?
options: No client check is perfect, so trusting a console's claim is as weak as trusting a PC's
Attestation works only for the store and cloud saves, never for matchmaking itself
The server cannot read the measurements, so it has to rely on checking actions instead
Consoles send actions too slowly for the client to check them without any server help
questions.explanation: Attestation is one layer, not the whole defence. The server's own checks do not rely on the console telling the truth.

questions.prompt: According to the lesson, how is running pirated games treated, whatever way the console was modified?
options: As copyright infringement however the console was modified
As legal when the console was modified under a country's circumvention exemption
As a terms-of-service matter only, with no copyright issue involved
As acceptable when the games were bought digitally, since a licence check passed
questions.explanation: Anti-circumvention laws and their exemptions vary by country and device. The lesson also stresses that it is not legal advice and that none of its labs modify a console.

questions.prompt: At step 11 of the trace, `JNZ 0x02` does not jump. Why not?
questions.explanation: `JNZ` jumps only while Z is 0, and Z records whether the last result was zero. The instruction just before it, `DEX`, computed X = 1 − 1 = 0, so Z became 1. `ADD` sets Z too, but `DEX` ran after it, and neither `STA` nor `JNZ` changes Z.
options: DEX at step 10 made X zero, so Z became 1
A holds 20 at that point, which is not zero
0x02 is not a valid jump target in this memory
JNZ can jump only once for each run of a program

questions.prompt: Which of the toy CPU's instructions leave the zero flag Z alone?
options: `STA` and `JNZ`
`LDA` and `DEX`
`ADD` and `STA`
`LDX` and `JNZ`
questions.explanation: `LDX`, `LDA`, `ADD` and `DEX` all set Z to 1 when their result is zero. `STA` and `JNZ` do not change it, and `HLT` just stops.

questions.prompt: Why does `LDA a` cost 3 cycles in the toy CPU?
options: It fetches 2 instruction bytes and reads 1 data byte, with one cycle per memory access
It fetches 1 instruction byte and reads 2 data bytes, with one cycle per memory access
It fetches 2 instruction bytes and writes 1 data byte, with one cycle per memory access
It fetches 2 instruction bytes, plus an extra cycle for loading the new value into A
questions.explanation: `STA a` also costs 3, but it writes the data byte instead of reading one. `LDX #n` and `ADD #n` cost 2 because they fetch 2 bytes and touch no other memory.

questions.prompt: `JNZ a` costs 2 cycles when it does not jump and 3 when it does. What is the extra cycle for?
options: Loading the new address into PC when the jump is taken
Reading the zero flag from the CPU's registers before the test
Fetching the opcode a second time after the jump has been taken
Writing the old value of PC to memory so the jump can be undone
questions.explanation: The common cost is two instruction-byte fetches. The extra cycle is spent only on a jump, to load the target into PC.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between `ADD #5` and an instruction with an operand written without `#`, such as `LDA 0x80`?
options: `#5` is the number 5 itself; the other operand is an address whose stored byte is used
`#5` is an address in RAM, while the other operand is a plain number to be added
`#5` is read from the display register, while the other operand is read from the RAM
`#5` costs an extra memory read, while the other operand needs none at all
questions.explanation: An address operand needs another memory read, which is why `LDA` costs 3 cycles and `ADD #n` costs 2.

questions.prompt: X holds 0 and `DEX` runs. What do X and Z hold afterwards?
options: X = 255 and Z = 0, since X wraps below 0 and the result is not zero
X = 0 and Z = 1, since X cannot go below 0
X = 255 and Z = 1, since the wrap means the result counts as zero
X = 1 and Z = 0, since the CPU takes the absolute value
questions.explanation: The registers are 8 bits wide, so subtracting 1 from 0 wraps around to 255. Z is 1 only when the result is 0.

questions.prompt: A holds 250 and `ADD #6` runs. What do A and Z hold afterwards?
options: A = 0 and Z = 1, since 256 wraps past 255 back to 0
A = 256 and Z = 0, since the sum is kept in full
A = 0 and Z = 0, since the wrapped result is not tested
A = 255 and Z = 1, since the sum stops at the top
questions.explanation: Eight bits hold 0 to 255, so 250 + 6 = 256 wraps back to 0, and the zero flag is set because the result is zero.

questions.prompt: The last instruction, `HLT`, is at `0x0D`. Why does the program take 14 bytes?
options: The last byte is at address 13, and addresses 0 to 13 make 14 bytes
`0x0D` is 14 in decimal, so the program has 14 bytes
The program has 7 instructions, and each one takes 2 bytes
Each of the 8 lines is 2 bytes long, minus 2 for the one-byte instructions
questions.explanation: Each address is the previous one plus that instruction's length, so `STA 0xF0` sits at `0x0B` and `HLT` at `0x0D`. `0x0D` is 13, and counting from 0 gives 14 bytes.

questions.prompt: In the trace, how many total cycles have been used after step 4, `STA 0x80`?
options: 10, from `LDX` 2, `LDA` 3, `ADD` 2 and `STA` 3
9, from `LDX` 2, `LDA` 3, `ADD` 2 and `STA` 2
8, from `LDX` 1, `LDA` 2, `ADD` 2 and `STA` 3
13, from `LDX` 2, `LDA` 3, `ADD` 2 and `STA` 3 plus the jump
questions.explanation: Each instruction costs its fetches plus its data accesses: 2 + 3 + 2 + 3 = 10. The `STA` writes the new 15 to gold at that point.

questions.prompt: The first pass of the loop costs 12 cycles and the second costs 11. Why is the second pass 1 cycle cheaper?
options: The second `JNZ` does not jump, so it costs 2 cycles instead of 3
The second `LDA` finds its value in A already, so it needs no memory read
The second `DEX` costs no cycle, because X is already zero
The second `ADD` is skipped, because gold already holds 15
questions.explanation: The first pass is 3 + 2 + 3 + 1 + 3 = 12, and the second is 3 + 2 + 3 + 1 + 2 = 11. The whole run is 2 + 12 + 11 + 4 = 29 cycles.

questions.prompt: After `HLT` at `0x0D`, PC is `0x0E`. Why?
options: Fetching the opcode moves PC on by one, so it sits one past the `HLT`
The `HLT` instruction adds 1 to PC so the next run can start there
PC always ends one past the last address the program uses, whatever its length
The `STA 0xF0` before it left PC pointing past the display register
questions.explanation: `fetch` reads the byte at PC and adds 1 to PC, so each fetch consumes one byte of the instruction.

questions.prompt: In the lab's `write` function, what happens to a store at `0xF1`, the buttons register?
options: Nothing; the buttons are read-only, so the `_ => {}` arm discards it
The value is stored in the buttons register, where later reads see it
The value goes into RAM at `0xF1`, because `0xF1` follows the display
The function stops with an error, because storing to a device is not allowed
questions.explanation: `write` has arms for RAM and the display, and its last arm covers the read-only buttons and the unused `0xF2` to `0xFF`. `read`, by contrast, returns the buttons register.

questions.prompt: Why does the lab report an unknown opcode as an `IllegalOpcode` error instead of guessing?
options: An emulator that guessed would hide bugs in the guest program and in itself
A real CPU always stops with a power-off when it meets an unknown opcode
Guessing would take more cycles than the budget of a frame allows
Rust cannot compile a `match` that continues after an unknown value
questions.explanation: `Opcode::decode` returns `None` for anything that is not an instruction, and the `?` turns that into an error naming the address. Real CPUs might raise an exception or do something undocumented.

questions.prompt: What does the lab's `fetch` do each time it is called?
options: It reads the byte at PC and adds 1 to PC
It reads the byte at PC and leaves PC where it is
It adds 1 to PC and then reads the byte at the new PC
It reads the byte at PC and adds the instruction's length to PC
questions.explanation: Each call consumes one byte of the instruction, so an opcode fetch and an operand fetch together move PC by 2. That is how PC lands on the next instruction.

questions.prompt: The NES's 2 KiB of RAM is mirrored through the range up to `0x2000`. How many copies of the 2,048 bytes does that range hold?
options: 4, since 8,192 bytes divided by 2,048 is 4
2, since 8,192 bytes divided by 4,096 is 2
8, since 8,192 bytes divided by 1,024 is 8
16, since `0x2000` is 16 times `0x0200`
questions.explanation: The address decoder ignores the top address bits for RAM, so the same bytes answer again at `0x0800`, `0x1000` and `0x1800`. `0x2000` is 2 x 4,096 = 8,192.

questions.prompt: In the toy lab, why can a frame never overshoot its 18-cycle budget by more than 2?
options: The last instruction starts at 17 used or less and costs at most 3, so 20 is the limit
Every instruction costs at most 2 cycles, so the overshoot is at most 2 cycles too
The budget is checked in the middle of an instruction, so none can run past the budget
The emulator pays back every overshoot immediately, within that same frame itself
questions.explanation: The check `used < budget` runs before each instruction, never during one. At the start the last instruction has at most 17 cycles used, and `JNZ` taken, `LDA` and `STA` cost 3, so 17 + 3 = 20 = 18 + 2.

questions.prompt: The 18-cycle frame stops after step 8, `ADD #5`. What do gold in RAM and register A hold?
options: Gold still holds 15, and the new total 20 lives only in register A, not yet in RAM
Gold holds 20, and A still holds the old 15 that was loaded at the start of the pass
Gold and A both hold 20, because the `STA` at `0x06` has already finished its store
Gold holds 10, its value at power-on, and A holds 20 after the addition on this pass
questions.explanation: The `STA` that would copy A to gold is at `0x06` and has not run. That is why a snapshot of RAM alone would lose the 20.

questions.prompt: How many bytes is the lab's save state, and where do they come from?
options: 255: 13 bytes of registers and bookkeeping, 240 of RAM, and 2 of I/O registers
256: one byte for each address in the machine, from `0x00` to `0xFF`
242: 240 of RAM and 2 of I/O registers, with the registers kept elsewhere
253: 13 bytes of registers and bookkeeping and 240 of RAM, without the I/O registers
questions.explanation: PC, A, X, Z and the halted flag take 1 byte each, and the 64-bit cycle count takes 64 / 8 = 8 bytes, making 13. Then 13 + 240 + 2 = 255.

questions.prompt: Why does loading a save state refuse a Z or halted byte that holds a value such as 7?
options: No real run of the machine could have produced it, so the data must be damaged
A value above 1 would overflow the register, so the emulator has to protect itself
A Z byte must always equal the halted byte, so any other value is a mismatch
The emulator can store a flag only as 0 or 1 in a file, since the others are reserved
questions.explanation: Reading a state back is parsing input from outside the program. The lab also refuses anything that is not exactly 255 bytes long.

questions.prompt: Frame 1 ends after step 8 and the cheat writes 99 to gold. What does step 9 do to that 99?
options: It stores A's 20 over it, because A already held the new total
It leaves the 99 alone, because the cheat wrote it later than the game did
It adds 5 to the 99, because `ADD #5` runs against gold
It stops the program, because gold changed behind the game's back
questions.explanation: The game had already loaded gold into A and added 5 before the cheat wrote to RAM. A cheat can lose a race against a value held in a register.

questions.prompt: Frame 2 has a budget of 17 cycles. Why does it finish the whole program?
options: Steps 9 to 13 cost 3 + 1 + 2 + 3 + 1 = 10 cycles, well inside the budget
Steps 9 to 13 cost 3 + 2 + 3 + 1 + 3 = 12 cycles, which is just inside the budget
Frame 2 gets an unlimited budget, because the program has already halted
The cheat adds cycles to the budget, because it writes to RAM at the end
questions.explanation: Steps 9 to 13 are `STA 0x80`, `DEX`, `JNZ` falling through, `STA 0xF0` and `HLT`. The display shows 20 at step 12, and the cheat writes 99 to RAM again at the frame's end.

questions.prompt: What does `used.saturating_sub(budget)` do when a frame ends early because the CPU halted?
options: It gives 0, since it stops at 0 instead of wrapping around
It gives a huge number, since it wraps around below 0
It stops the program, since a negative result is an error
It returns the budget, since the frame did not use it
questions.explanation: The value returned is the overshoot, which the caller takes off the next frame's budget. A frame that ends early has no overshoot to report.

questions.prompt: A watchpoint records `self.cpu.pc` inside `write` whenever gold at `0x80` is written, and the `STA 0x80` is at `0x06`. Which PC value does it record?
options: `0x08`, since fetching the `STA`'s two bytes already moved PC on
`0x06`, since PC still holds the address of the `STA` while it runs
`0x80`, since PC is set to the address that is being written to
`0x04`, since PC shows the instruction just before the `STA` in memory
questions.explanation: `step` fetches the opcode and then the operand before it calls `write`, so PC has advanced by 2 to `0x08`. The recorded values are therefore not `0x06`.

questions.prompt: A 32-bit game running on 64-bit Windows shows `cs` = `0023` in x64dbg. At which privilege level is its code running?
questions.explanation: Only the lowest two bits of `cs` hold the privilege level. `0x23` is 2 × 16 + 3 = 35, or `0010 0011` in binary, and its lowest two bits are `11` = 3. The upper bits pick a different code segment (a 32-bit one), but the level is still ring 3, user mode.
options: Ring 3, because `0x23` is `0010 0011` and its lowest two bits are `11`
Ring 0, because `0x23` is smaller than the 64-bit value `0x33`
Ring 2, because the hex value `0x23` begins with the digit 2
None; the value of `cs` only picks a segment and says nothing of privilege

questions.prompt: A tool opened a game with `PROCESS_QUERY_INFORMATION` (`0x0400`) and `PROCESS_QUERY_LIMITED_INFORMATION` (`0x1000`), so its handle's rights are `0x1400`. It calls `ReadProcessMemory`, which needs `PROCESS_VM_READ` (`0x0010`). What happens?
questions.explanation: `0x0400` is 4 × 256 = 1,024 = 2¹⁰ (bit 10) and `0x1000` is 2¹² (bit 12), so `0x1400` has bits 12 and 10 set. The read needs bit 4, which is 0, so the AND is 0 and the kernel returns an error status. Nothing faults: the system call returns normally with `STATUS_ACCESS_DENIED`, and `kernelbase.dll` reports error 5. Running as administrator affects what `OpenProcess` may grant; it cannot add rights to a handle that already exists.
options: The kernel refuses with `STATUS_ACCESS_DENIED`, because `0x1400` AND `0x0010` is 0
The kernel copies the bytes, because a handle that can query a process can also read it
The processor raises a general-protection fault inside the tool when it makes the call
The read succeeds if the tool runs as administrator, since that adds missing rights

questions.prompt: Why are there exactly four privilege rings on x86?
options: The level is stored in two bits, and two bits give 2 × 2 = 4 patterns: `00`, `01`, `10`, `11`
The level is stored in one byte, but the processor defines only the first four of its 256 values
The page-table flag byte has four permission bits, and each one stands for one ring
Windows ships four kinds of driver, and each kind needs its own ring to run in
questions.explanation: The current privilege level is the lowest two bits of `cs`. Two bits can hold four patterns, which is exactly the four rings. Windows uses only 0 and 3.

questions.prompt: The kernel's own code segment value is `0x10`. At which ring does code with that `cs` run?
options: Ring 0, because `0x10` is `0001 0000` and its lowest two bits are `00`
Ring 1, because the digit 1 in `0x10` is the ring number
Ring 3, because every value of `cs` that is a multiple of 16 is user mode
Ring 2, because `0x10` is 16 and 16 divided by 8 gives 2
questions.explanation: Only the lowest two bits of `cs` give the level. In `0001 0000` they are `00`, so ring 0. The first digit of the hex value is part of the segment choice, not the ring.

questions.prompt: A program tries to load the kernel's `cs` value `0x10` into `cs` to promote itself to ring 0. What does the processor do?
options: Refuses, since raising privilege is allowed only through kernel-prepared entry points such as `syscall`
Accepts it, but only for the one instruction after the load, which is too short to do anything useful
Accepts it if the program is running as an administrator, because that user may change processor settings
Accepts it, then checks every later instruction against the page table's user/supervisor bit before running
questions.explanation: The processor refuses any segment change that would raise privilege, except through a few kernel-prepared entry points, and `syscall` is the most important of them. Administrator rights live in the access token, not in the processor ring.

questions.prompt: A user page's entry has the lowest byte `0x67` and a kernel page's has `0x63`. How do these two example entries differ?
options: Only in bit 2, the user/supervisor bit, since `0x67` − `0x63` = 4 = 2²
Only in bit 1, the write bit, since the difference of 4 means the page is read-only
In bits 6 and 5 together, the dirty and accessed bits, since 64 + 32 is more than 4
In bit 0, the present bit, so the kernel page is simply not mapped
questions.explanation: The difference is 4, a single bit: bit 2. The kernel page is still present, writable, and accessed, but ring 3 is refused. Leaf byte is only a teaching example, since a real walk also checks higher-level entries.

questions.prompt: In the user-page byte `0x67`, bits 6, 5, 2, 1, and 0 are set. What do the two bits the processor sets by itself mean?
options: Bit 5, accessed, is set on first use of the page; bit 6, dirty, is set on first write to it
Bit 5, dirty, is set on first use of the page; bit 6, accessed, is set on first write to it
Bit 5, user, is set when ring 3 touches the page; bit 6, write, is set when ring 0 does
Bit 5, present, is set when the page is loaded; bit 6, cache, is set when it is used
questions.explanation: The processor sets bit 5, accessed, the first time the page is used, and bit 6, dirty, the first time it is written. The user, write, and present bits (2, 1, 0) are set by the kernel when it builds the mapping.

questions.prompt: The `ntdll.dll` syscall stub begins with `mov r10, rcx`. Why?
options: `syscall` overwrites `rcx` with the return address, so the first argument is saved in `r10` for the kernel to find
The Windows x64 calling convention passes the first argument in `r10`, so the stub must copy it there from `rcx` first
The kernel's entry code clears `rcx` for security, so the stub moves it to `r10` before the call
`r10` holds the service number, so the stub copies it from `rcx` where the caller left it
questions.explanation: The x64 convention puts the first argument in `rcx`, but `syscall` saves the next instruction's address there. Moving the argument to `r10` first lets the kernel find it. The service number goes in `eax`.

questions.prompt: System service numbers change between Windows builds. What does that mean for a tool that hard-codes one?
options: It may call a different kernel routine on another build, so the book never copies a number
It works on any build, because the number is looked up by name in the kernel's table at run time
It still works on the same build, but Windows blocks it from reading memory without the right
It fails only on 32-bit programs, since WoW64 renumbers services but 64-bit programs keep theirs
questions.explanation: The numbers index the kernel's internal routine table and are not a stable interface. A hard-coded number can point at a different routine, or none, on another build.

questions.prompt: Why does the kernel's entry code switch to a kernel stack that belongs to the thread, instead of using the program's stack?
options: The program's stack pointer could point anywhere, and everything from user mode must be assumed hostile
The program's stack is stored on disk, so the kernel cannot reach it quickly enough to save registers
The kernel needs a much larger stack than the program has, and user stacks cannot be grown
The program's stack is in the user half of memory, which the processor locks while ring 0 code runs
questions.explanation: Everything user mode supplies, including the stack pointer, could be hostile. A kernel stack under its own control makes sure the saved registers have a safe place.

questions.prompt: A read request starts at a high user address and has a length large enough to run past the largest 64-bit number and wrap to a small address. What does the kernel do?
options: Rejects it during its own range check, because the range would wrap or reach into the kernel's half
Accepts it, because every address in the range is a valid user address once the wrap-around is applied
Accepts it if the handle has `PROCESS_VM_READ`, since rights are checked before any range
Accepts the first part, then stops at the top of user space and returns `STATUS_PARTIAL_COPY`
questions.explanation: A range that reaches the kernel's half, or wraps around, is rejected by the kernel's own check. The user/supervisor bit cannot do this job, since the copy runs in ring 0.

questions.prompt: A handle holds rights `0x1010` and the read operation needs `PROCESS_VM_READ`, `0x0010`. What is `0x1010` AND `0x0010`, and what does the kernel do?
options: `0x0010`, the whole requirement, so the read is allowed
`0x1000`, the leftover query right, so the read is refused
`0x1020`, the sum of both values, so the read is allowed
`0x0000`, since the two values share no bits, so the read is refused
questions.explanation: AND keeps only bits set in both values. Bit 4 (`0x0010`) is set in both, so the whole requirement survives and the read is allowed.

questions.prompt: The same handle, `0x1010`, is used for a write, which needs `PROCESS_VM_WRITE` (`0x0020`). Why is it denied?
options: `0x0020` is bit 5, which is 0 in `0x1010`, so the AND is 0
`0x0020` is bit 12, which is 0 in `0x1010`, so the AND is 0
`0x1010` includes the query right, which the kernel treats as a ban on writes
The handle's read right at bit 4 automatically cancels the write right at bit 5
questions.explanation: `0x0020` = 2 × 16 = 32 = 2⁵, so bit 5. In `0x1010` only bits 12 and 4 are set, so the AND is 0. The rights were fixed when the handle was created.

questions.prompt: `ReadProcessMemory` asked for 4 bytes but a page became unavailable during the copy. What should the caller do?
options: Check the returned byte count, because a partial read can come back as a failure
Trust that 4 bytes arrived, since a read either succeeds fully or crashes the tool
Retry the same call with a bigger buffer, since the buffer was too small
Check the `cs` register, since a partial copy means the call ran in the wrong ring
questions.explanation: If a page becomes unavailable mid-copy, the API may report a failed or partial read, so the caller must inspect the byte count instead of assuming all 4 arrived.

questions.prompt: `STATUS_PARTIAL_COPY` is `0x8000_000D`. What does the top hex digit 8 tell you about it?
options: The top two bits are `10`, a warning: some of the bytes did arrive
The top two bits are `11`, an error: no byte was copied at all
The top two bits are `01`, information, so the call fully succeeded
The top two bits are `00`, success, since 8 is a high value in the table
questions.explanation: An NTSTATUS's top two bits give severity: `00` success, `01` information, `10` warning, `11` error. `8` is `1000`, so `10`, a warning. `STATUS_ACCESS_DENIED`, `0xC000_0022`, starts with `1100`, an error.

questions.prompt: After the kernel runs `sysret`, where does execution resume?
options: At the address saved in `rcx`, the `ret` right after `syscall` in the stub, now at ring 3
At the first instruction of `kernelbase.dll`, which then restarts the whole call from the top
At the kernel's entry point again, which checks whether the user program is finished
At the address in `r10`, where the stub saved the program's first argument
questions.explanation: `syscall` stored the return address in `rcx`; `sysret` drops to ring 3 and resumes there, at the stub's `ret`. `r10` holds the first argument.

questions.prompt: A 32-bit game runs on 64-bit Windows. How does `cs` differ from a 64-bit program's, and why does its call take an extra hop?
options: It reads `0023` instead of `0033`, and WoW64 translates the call into the native 64-bit path
It reads `0010` instead of `0033`, and WoW64 raises the game to ring 0 for each system call it makes
It reads `0033` too, and WoW64 only widens every number in the call to 64 bits before entry
It reads `0023`, but the call reaches the kernel directly with no translation step at all
questions.explanation: The two modes use different code segments, 0x23 and 0x33, both with level 3. WoW64 translates the 32-bit call into the native service path, which may need converted pointer-sized arguments and structures.

questions.prompt: The input samples are false, true, true, true. How many times does this lesson's controller toggle the lamp?
questions.explanation: The controller remembers whether the previous sample was pressed. Only the first true follows a false; the other true samples describe the same held press. This assumes already debounced logical input, not a bouncing physical contact.
options: Once, when `false` first becomes `true`
Three times, once for every `true` sample in the list
Four times, because every sample counts as an event
Zero times, because the controller ignores a button that stays held

questions.prompt: Which description fits the lesson's idea of firmware?
options: Software that operates a device, usually kept in nonvolatile memory such as flash
Software that can never be replaced after the factory, written only in assembly language
Any program shipped inside a physical product, whichever processor and OS it runs on
The code in a PC's driver that exchanges reports with a plugged-in controller
questions.explanation: Firmware is a role, not a file type or a language. The flash it lives in can be erased and programmed again, and the driver on the PC is a different piece of software.

questions.prompt: Which statement about flash memory matches the lesson?
options: It keeps its contents without power and can be erased and programmed again
It loses its contents when power is removed, so firmware must be reloaded at each boot
It can be written only once, at the factory, which is why firmware cannot be updated
It is the chip's working RAM, where the call stack and writable state live
questions.explanation: Flash is nonvolatile and reprogrammable. Working state and the call stack sit in SRAM, which does not retain contents without power.

questions.prompt: In the lesson's USB controller table, which software samples the buttons and prepares the reports?
options: The controller firmware, running on the controller's own processor
The device driver, running on the PC's processor as part of its OS
The game application, running on the PC's processor after it starts
The PC's firmware, running on the processor before the OS loads
questions.explanation: Firmware, driver, and game cooperate across a device boundary but run in different places. The driver exchanges reports with the controller; the game turns a press into a game action.

questions.prompt: An application runs on an embedded Linux system inside a camera. Is it bare-metal firmware in this lesson's sense?
options: No; bare-metal means no OS at all, and sitting inside a device does not change that
Yes; anything that runs from flash inside a device counts, whichever OS it runs on
Yes; Linux on a microcontroller is the standard way to build any bare-metal firmware
No; bare-metal firmware must be written in assembly and can never be written in Rust
questions.explanation: Bare-metal programming uses no OS, though firmware can also use an RTOS or embedded Linux. Neither of those is the arrangement this lesson builds.

questions.prompt: The modelled board has 256 KiB of flash. How many bytes is that?
options: 262,144 bytes, which is 256 x 1,024
256,000 bytes, which is 256 x 1,000
65,536 bytes, which is 64 x 1,024
131,072 bytes, which is 128 x 1,024
questions.explanation: A KiB is 1,024 bytes, so 256 KiB = 256 x 1,024 = 262,144. The 64 KiB figure belongs to the board's SRAM, not its flash.

questions.prompt: The vector table's first entry is `0x20010000`, just above the 64 KiB of RAM. Why is the stack pointer started there?
options: The stack grows toward lower addresses, so it begins at the top of RAM
The stack grows toward higher addresses, so it begins just past the end of RAM
The address `0x20010000` is where the flash region ends, so the stack is kept beside the code
The peripheral registers begin there, so the stack can reach them quickly
questions.explanation: RAM runs from `0x20000000` to `0x2000FFFF`. Pushing onto a downward-growing stack moves it back inside that range, starting from one past the last byte.

questions.prompt: SRAM starts at `0x20000000` and is 64 KiB long, which is `0x10000` bytes. What is the last address inside it?
options: `0x2000FFFF`
`0x2000FFFE`
questions.explanation: The last byte is the start plus the length minus one: `0x20000000` + `0x10000` - 1 = `0x2000FFFF`. `0x20010000` is the first address after the region.

questions.prompt: What do the addresses in the lesson's region table, such as flash at `0x00000000`, refer to?
options: The emulated device's own address space, not addresses inside the PC process running QEMU
Offsets inside the PC process that runs QEMU, which a debugger on the PC can attach to
Locations on the PC's physical RAM, which QEMU reserves for the guest at boot
Positions inside the ELF file on disk, before any loader copies it anywhere
questions.explanation: These are the model's addresses. Loading an image into the modelled flash does not reproduce the electrical procedure for programming a physical flash chip.

questions.prompt: After the lamp controller is powered off and on again, what has survived?
options: Its instructions in flash; the lamp state is rebuilt by the program at each boot
Its instructions and also the last lamp setting, because both are held in flash
Its last lamp setting only, because the instructions are reloaded from the PC each time
Nothing, because flash is wiped whenever the board loses power
questions.explanation: Instructions survive in flash. The lamp state is working state that the program starts again, so remembering it needs an explicit storage design.

questions.prompt: Why would writing the lamp state to flash on every main-loop pass be a poor way to remember it?
options: Flash has erase and program constraints and finite endurance that RAM does not
Flash loses its contents quickly, so the stored state would vanish before the next boot
Flash can be read only by the debugger, so the firmware could never see the saved value
Flash writes overwrite the vector table, which would stop the board starting
questions.explanation: Flash is nonvolatile but wears with repeated erase and program cycles, so a loop that writes every pass would burn through its endurance.

questions.prompt: What do the first two entries of the Cortex-M vector table contain?
options: The initial stack pointer, then the reset-handler address
The reset-handler address, then the initial stack pointer
The address of `main`, then the address of the first interrupt handler
The first instruction of the application, then its checksum
questions.explanation: The table holds values and addresses, not instructions. The core loads the stack pointer from the first entry and jumps to the address in the second after reset.

questions.prompt: A writable static counter must start at 7. How does it get its starting value?
options: It lives in `.data`; reset startup copies the 7 from flash into RAM before the application runs
It lives in `.bss`; reset startup fills it with 7 because the linker reserves RAM for it
It lives in `.rodata`; the application reads the 7 from flash each time it needs the counter
It lives in `.text`; the linker patches the 7 into the instructions during the build
questions.explanation: `.data` has an initial value stored in the image and a working place in RAM, so startup copies one to the other. `.bss` is the section that starts as zeros.

questions.prompt: A writable static counter starts at zero. What does the image need for it?
options: A reserved RAM range that startup fills with zeros, so no zero bytes are stored
A run of zero bytes stored in flash, which startup copies into RAM on every boot
A copy of the counter in `.rodata`, which startup reads and writes back to RAM
Nothing at all, because the hardware always clears SRAM when the chip is reset
questions.explanation: `.bss` reserves a range and startup writes the zeros, so the image stays smaller. The runtime and linker agree on where the range begins and ends.

questions.prompt: Where do the local variables of a function live, according to the lesson?
options: In registers or on the stack, as the compiler chooses while the program runs
In `.data`, with their initial values copied from flash by reset startup
In `.bss`, so that they start as zero at reset
In `.rodata`, so that their values cannot change while the program runs
questions.explanation: Locals are separate from the static sections. The compiler may keep one in a register or place it on the stack.

questions.prompt: Why is a source file containing only `fn main()` not a complete firmware image?
options: The image also needs a vector table, startup code, and a memory layout from the runtime and linker
The image also needs a guest OS to schedule that function, which the emulator then supplies
The image also needs a bootloader, which every design must include ahead of the reset vector
The image also needs a driver on the PC, which installs the function into the flash
questions.explanation: Reset starts from the vector table, not from a function named main. `cortex-m-rt` prepares static data and then calls the application's entry function.

questions.prompt: Which description matches a bootloader, as the lesson uses the word?
options: Software whose job is to select, check, or load the application that runs next
Startup software that is stored in read-only memory and can never be changed
The runtime code that copies `.data` from flash into RAM after reset
The part of the vector table that holds the initial stack pointer
questions.explanation: A boot ROM is the startup software stored in read-only memory. A bootloader may support updates and recovery, and its work stays distinct from the Rust runtime's initialization.

questions.prompt: What does the lesson call the logical change from `false` to `true`, and how does the controller spot it?
options: A rising edge, found by remembering the previous sample
A debounce, found by counting several stable samples in a row
A reset, found by comparing the stack pointer with the vector table
A toggle, found by reading the lamp's output pin
questions.explanation: A press counts as new only when the current sample is pressed and the remembered one was not. That is why the controller stores `was_pressed`.

questions.prompt: In the lesson's trace, sample 4 is `false` right after two `true` samples. What is the lamp state after it?
options: On, because releasing the button is not a new press
Off, because releasing the button switches the lamp off again
Off, because `was_pressed` is cleared and so resets the lamp
On, because a release toggles the lamp a second time
questions.explanation: Only a false-to-true change toggles. Sample 2 turned the lamp on and sample 3 was still held, so the release at sample 4 leaves it on.

questions.prompt: The six samples are `false, true, true, false, true, false`. How many times does the lamp toggle?
options: Twice, at samples 2 and 5, ending with the lamp off
Three times, once for each `true` sample in the list
Four times, once for each change from true to false or back
Once, because the lamp can only change a single time in each run
questions.explanation: A toggle needs a `true` preceded by a `false`. Sample 3 is the same press still held, so only samples 2 and 5 toggle, ending with the lamp off.

questions.prompt: In `sample`, the line `self.was_pressed = pressed;` runs on every call, whether or not the lamp toggled. Why?
options: The next call needs the latest sample, or a held button would look like a new press
It makes the lamp state follow the button, so the lamp is on only while it is held
It resets the toggle so the lamp can change again on the very next sample
The borrow checker requires every field in `&mut self` to be assigned on each call
questions.explanation: Rising-edge detection compares the current sample with the last one. Skipping the update would leave stale information behind.

questions.prompt: Does rising-edge detection also cure switch bounce?
options: No; the controller expects a stable logical press, so firmware must debounce the raw input first
Yes; only the first contact of a bounce counts as a rising edge, so the rest are ignored
Yes; a bounce is just a held button, which the edge rule already handles
No; bounce is cured by writing the lamp state to flash after each sample
questions.explanation: Bounce briefly makes and breaks contact several times, which would look like several presses to an edge detector. A debounce policy, often several stable samples over time, comes first.

questions.prompt: Under `#![no_std]`, which of these still works without extra allocation support?
options: `Option` and `Result`, since they come from `core`
`Vec`, because it comes from the `core` library as well
File reading, because `core` includes a file system layer too
`println!`, because `core` includes terminal output as well
questions.explanation: `no_std` keeps `core` but leaves out the OS-oriented standard library. Collections like `Vec` need allocation support, and files, threads, and terminal printing do not appear automatically.

questions.prompt: Why is the firmware entry function declared with `-> !`?
options: It never returns, since there is no desktop caller waiting for a return value
It returns an error code to the reset handler, which the debugger can then display
It is a marker that lets `fn main` skip the vector table and run straight away
It tells the linker that the function belongs in RAM instead of flash
questions.explanation: On a microcontroller nothing is waiting for `main` to finish. The `#[entry]` attribute marks the function that startup calls, and the lab ends in a loop.

questions.prompt: What does semihosting do in this lab?
options: The target asks the emulator to do a host-side job, such as printing text on QEMU's terminal
It makes the emulated board drive a real UART pin that the PC reads over a serial cable
It lets Windows provide `println!` to the guest as it would for any ordinary process
It lets the firmware read the PC's real memory directly from inside the emulator program
questions.explanation: Semihosting is a request channel to a debugger or emulator. It is neither an emulated UART nor an OS service, and it suits a short trace but not timing measurements.

questions.prompt: The built ELF file is much larger than 256 KiB. Does that mean the firmware cannot fit in the board's flash?
options: No; the file includes debug metadata that never loads into flash, so size is not usage
Yes; the loader copies the whole ELF file into flash, so its full size must fit
Yes; ELF files always count their sections twice, so the true size is even larger
No; ELF files are compressed, so the loader can unpack them into a larger flash
questions.explanation: ELF carries sections, addresses, and other information a loader or debugger can use. Only the loaded sections occupy the microcontroller's flash.

questions.prompt: A button is wired active-low. Which electrical event matches the logical `false` to `true` press?
options: A high-to-low change on the input pin
A low-to-high change on the input pin
The pin staying low for the whole sample
The pin being disconnected, so it floats between levels
questions.explanation: Active-low means a low level represents a press. A pull resistor keeps the unpressed input at a defined level, so it does not float.

questions.prompt: On a real board the lamp reacts to the release of the button instead of the press. What does the lesson advise?
options: Compare intended and observed transitions, then check pin polarity and setup, not the rule
Edit `sample` so it toggles on the `true` to `false` change, matching what the board shows
Add a flash write on every sample, so each change is recorded before the lamp reacts
Remove the library tests, since they disagree with what the real board does
questions.explanation: Changing the control rule to compensate for a wiring mistake hides the cause. The tests check the rule, not the electrical wiring, so the boundary to inspect is polarity, debounce timing, timer rate, or register setup.

questions.prompt: What is a watchdog on a real microcontroller?
options: A timer that resets a stalled device unless firmware services it
A tool that finds every bug in the firmware without needing to run it
A peripheral that copies the stack into flash when the program panics
A debugger feature that stops the processor at each GPIO write it sees
questions.explanation: A watchdog needs a careful configuration and recovery policy on real hardware. It is not a cure for an unexplained bug.

questions.prompt: A recompiler has translated a guest loop into host code and stored it. The guest program then writes a new byte into the middle of that loop, over the operand of an `ADD` instruction. What must the emulator do before the loop runs again?
questions.explanation: The stored host code still adds the old number, which no longer matches the guest's memory. Code is data, and a guest may legally rewrite its own instructions, so the recompiler has to watch for writes to translated addresses and discard those translations. Otherwise the emulated program runs code that no longer exists.
options: Discard the stored translation that covers the changed address and translate it again
Nothing, because the stored translation is still correct for the guest's memory now
Run the old translation one more time, and only then translate the block again
Stop the guest, because guest code is never allowed to change its own bytes at all

questions.prompt: PC holds `0x04`, the bytes at `0x04` and `0x05` are `03 05` (`ADD #5`), and A holds 10. What do A and PC hold after one pass of the loop?
options: A = 15 and PC = `0x06`
A = 15 and PC = `0x05`
A = 10 and PC = `0x06`
A = 5 and PC = `0x04`
questions.explanation: Fetching the opcode moves PC to `0x05`, and fetching the operand moves it to `0x06`, the first byte of the next instruction. Executing sets A = 10 + 5 = 15.

questions.prompt: The toy CPU spends one cycle on every byte it reads or writes in memory. What does `ADD #5` cost?
options: 2 cycles, because it reads two bytes
1 cycle, because it is a single instruction
5 cycles, because the operand is 5
15 cycles, because that is the result left in A
questions.explanation: The opcode and the operand are each read once. Counting cycles is how the emulator knows how long the real chip would have taken.

questions.prompt: Nothing in memory marks where one instruction ends. How does the CPU find the start of the next one?
options: The opcode gives the instruction's length, and fetching its bytes moves PC past them
A special marker byte follows every instruction, and the CPU scans for it
The emulator keeps a table of every instruction's address, which it reads in order
Each instruction is padded to the same length, so PC always moves by two
questions.explanation: Some instructions carry an operand byte and some do not. Because the opcode tells the CPU how many bytes to fetch, PC lands on the next instruction automatically.

questions.prompt: A loop of five guest instructions runs 1,000 times. How many instructions does an interpreter decode, compared with a dynamic recompiler?
options: 5,000 against 5, since the recompiler translates the block once and then runs it
5,000 against 1,000, since the recompiler decodes once per pass of the loop
1,000 against 5, since the interpreter decodes only the loop's first instruction
5 against 5,000, since the interpreter keeps stored translations of each block
questions.explanation: The interpreter pays 5 x 1,000 = 5,000 decodes, although only five different instructions exist. The recompiler pays 5 decodes and then runs the stored host code 1,000 times.

questions.prompt: Why must an emulator on a console or some phone platforms fall back to interpreting instead of recompiling?
options: A recompiler writes machine code to memory then runs it, which those platforms refuse to allow
A recompiler needs the platform's graphics driver, which these platforms do not provide at all
A recompiler needs more RAM than those platforms can offer to run the original game
A recompiler can only run code for processors that were built back in the 1980s era
questions.explanation: Code that a program writes for itself at run time was never signed, so these platforms generally do not allow it to run.

questions.prompt: In the toy console, RAM is `0x00` to `0xEF`. How many bytes is that?
options: 256, since eight bits name 2^8 addresses
239, since the range stops one short of `0xF0`
15, since `0xEF` is a single hex digit pair
questions.explanation: The 8-bit address space has 256 addresses, but not all of them are RAM. `0xF0` onward are the display, the buttons, and unused addresses.

questions.prompt: On the toy console, the CPU stores A at address `0xF0`. What happens?
options: The byte goes to the display, because the address alone picks the device
The byte goes into RAM at `0xF0`, and a later instruction copies it to the screen
The byte vanishes, because `0xF0` lies outside the RAM range of the console
The CPU stops, because storing to a device needs a special I/O instruction first
questions.explanation: This is memory-mapped I/O. In hardware, address-decoding circuits choose the device. In an emulator, the write function does the same job.

questions.prompt: How does an emulator imitate a console's address-decoding circuits?
options: Every access goes through a read or write function that picks the target by address
The emulator gives each device its own host thread, which watches the address lines
The emulator maps each device into the host's own address space for the host to decode
The game code is rewritten to call each device by name, instead of by address
questions.explanation: In the lesson's diagram the bus checks which range holds the address and sends the access to RAM, the display register, the buttons register, or nothing.

questions.prompt: The toy console's clock runs at 1.2 MHz and the screen redraws 60 times a second. How many cycles does each frame last?
options: 20,000, from 1,200,000 divided by 60
72,000,000, from 1,200,000 multiplied by 60
2,000, from 1,200,000 divided by 600
1,200, from 1.2 MHz read as 1,200 cycles
questions.explanation: The emulator runs instructions until the frame's 20,000 cycles are used, draws the frame, and then waits until 1/60 of a second of real time has passed.

questions.prompt: A game changes a picture-chip register partway down the screen. What goes wrong if the emulated CPU reaches that write too early?
options: The split lands on the wrong line of the screen
The game's save file is corrupted when the frame ends
The picture chip skips the next frame to catch up
The host's GPU refuses to draw the texture
questions.explanation: Older games depended on exact timing, so emulators run the CPU for a slice of cycles and advance the other chips by the same amount of time.

questions.prompt: For an 8-bit or 16-bit console, what does the emulator do with the pixels its picture-chip imitation produces?
options: It writes them into a framebuffer array and hands that array to the host's GPU as a texture
It sends each pixel to the host display directly, one at a time, as the CPU writes it
It compiles them into shaders, which the host GPU then runs to draw the frame
It stores them in the guest's RAM, where the host operating system reads them
questions.explanation: The emulator imitates the chip's rules for tiles and sprites. A 3D console is harder because the emulator must translate the guest's GPU commands into Vulkan or Direct3D.

questions.prompt: Why can an emulated 3D game stutter the first time a new effect appears on screen?
options: The emulator translates the guest's shaders at that moment, then caches the result
The emulator has to decrypt that effect's data from the disc image first
The host GPU must warm up to the guest's clock speed before it draws a new effect
The guest's sound chip pauses the video until enough samples have been made first
questions.explanation: The original console never had this problem, because its games shipped shaders already compiled for its one GPU.

questions.prompt: A host plays 48,000 audio samples per second and the emulator runs at 60 frames per second. How many samples must it produce every frame?
options: 800, from 48,000 divided by 60
80, from 48,000 divided by 600
8,000, from 48,000 divided by 6
1,200, from 48,000 divided by 40
questions.explanation: If the samples run out, the speakers click and crackle, while a late video frame just leaves the previous picture up a moment longer. That is why many emulators pace themselves by the audio device.

questions.prompt: How does a save state differ from a game's own save file?
options: A state captures the whole machine at any instant; a save file holds what the game chooses
A state holds only RAM contents; a save file holds registers and RAM together as one
A state works only at the start of a frame; a save file can be written at any instant
A state is stored in the game's own format; a save file uses the emulator's own format
questions.explanation: A save state includes every register, all of RAM, the I/O registers and the emulator's own timing position, so it works for any game, even in the middle of a frame.

questions.prompt: Why must a save state include the CPU's registers as well as RAM?
options: A new value may exist only in a register and not yet in memory
The registers hold the game's graphics, which RAM does not contain at all
RAM is rebuilt from the registers whenever a state is loaded
The registers record which version of the emulator saved the state
questions.explanation: A snapshot of RAM alone would lose such a value. Emulators also store a version number, because the layout changes as the emulator does.

questions.prompt: A RAM search on an NES game covers 2 KiB of guest RAM. How many bytes is that?
questions.explanation: A RAM search is the scan of Lesson 1.9 run over the guest's RAM, so it covers a few thousand bytes instead of the gigabytes a PC game can occupy.

questions.prompt: How can an emulator provide a watchpoint on a guest variable without any debug registers?
options: An `if` in the write function checks the address and records PC
The emulator pauses the host operating system and lets the debugger read the host's registers
The emulator rewrites the game's code so it calls a debugger routine before each store
The emulator scans the guest's whole RAM after every frame and compares it with the last scan
questions.explanation: Every guest memory access passes through the emulator's read and write functions, so a check there sees every store.

questions.prompt: How did a Game Genie differ from an Action Replay or GameShark code?
options: It changed the byte read from a cartridge address; the others wrote a value to RAM each frame
It wrote a value to RAM each frame; the others changed the byte read from a cartridge address
It replaced the console's BIOS with its own copy; the others left the BIOS in place
It decrypted the game from its package; the others ran the encrypted package as it was
questions.explanation: A RAM-writing code is just an address and a value. Such a code can lose a race if the game stores its own number back over the cheat's.

questions.prompt: Which statement matches the lesson's description of the legal line around emulators?
options: Writing an emulator is legal in many countries; downloading a BIOS or games is generally infringement
Writing an emulator is generally illegal, though downloading BIOS files is allowed for owned games
Emulators are legal only when they ship the original firmware inside the same download file
Emulating a console is legal only when the emulator is promoted as a way to play pirated games
questions.explanation: Sony v. Connectix held that copying the BIOS during reverse engineering was fair use. Several emulators avoid needing original firmware by replacing it with their own code.

questions.prompt: A guest runs on an Intel processor with hardware virtualization and second-level address translation. Which of these guest actions causes a VM exit?
questions.explanation: Ordinary instructions and system calls run natively inside the guest, and a fault on a page the guest's own tables do not map is delivered to the guest kernel, which handles it as it would on real hardware. `cpuid` always exits on Intel processors, so the hypervisor controls what the guest learns about its processor.
options: A `cpuid` instruction asking about the processor
An `add` instruction on two registers in a guest program
A system call from a guest program into its own guest kernel
A page fault on a virtual page the guest kernel has not mapped yet

questions.prompt: In virtualization vocabulary, what is the guest?
options: The operating system running inside the virtual machine
The real computer whose hardware is being shared out
The software that creates machines and shares the hardware
The file on the host that holds the virtual disk
questions.explanation: The guest is the OS inside the VM and the host is the real computer. The hypervisor, also called a virtual machine monitor, is the software that creates VMs and shares the hardware.

questions.prompt: Hyper-V is turned on, and the PC is restarted. What has happened to the user's own Windows installation?
options: It has become the root partition, a privileged guest that manages the other guests
It keeps running straight on the hardware, with Hyper-V as an ordinary application
It has been replaced by Hyper-V's own kernel, and the old files are unreachable
It has become a normal guest with no more rights than any other virtual machine
questions.explanation: Hyper-V is type 1: the hypervisor starts first at boot and everything runs above it. Windows is still there, but as the root partition with extra privileges for managing guests.

questions.prompt: How does a hypervisor's virtual machine differ from the Lua virtual machine in Lesson 10.8?
options: It offers the same instruction set as the real processor, so guest instructions run directly on it
It translates every guest instruction into Lua bytecode before running it on the real processor
It offers a smaller instruction set than the real processor, which the hypervisor expands at run time
It runs only the guest's kernel code natively, and interprets every ordinary program instruction
questions.explanation: Lua's VM carries out bytecode that no processor runs in silicon. A hypervisor's VM offers x86-64 itself, so the hypervisor steps in only when the guest touches something the host must control.

questions.prompt: With Intel VT-x, in which ring does the guest's kernel run, and why does that help?
options: In the guest's own ring 0, so it runs unmodified and each instruction behaves as it expects
In ring 3, with the hypervisor emulating every privileged instruction that faults
In ring 1, a middle ring that the guest kernel was written to expect on virtual machines
In the host's ring 0, shared with the hypervisor but separated by the page tables
questions.explanation: VMX non-root operation gives the guest its own complete set of rings 0 to 3. Running the kernel in ring 3 is the old approach that failed because some instructions did not fault there.

questions.prompt: The hypervisor keeps a VMCS (Intel) or VMCB (AMD) for each virtual processor. Which list matches what it holds?
options: The guest's saved state, the host's state, and the exit controls
The guest's disk blocks, the delta file, and the snapshot index
The stage-2 tables, the guest's RAM, and the list of host processes
The guest's registers and a log of every instruction it has executed
questions.explanation: The structure holds the guest's registers, the host state to reload when the guest stops, and the list of guest actions that must hand control to the hypervisor.

questions.prompt: Which instruction does a hypervisor on an Intel processor use to start a guest for the first time?
options: `vmlaunch`, with `vmresume` used to continue a guest that has run before
`vmrun`, which Intel and AMD processors both use to enter guest mode
`cpuid`, which switches the processor into VMX non-root operation
`vmexit`, issued by the hypervisor whenever it wants the guest to start
questions.explanation: `vmlaunch` and `vmresume` are the Intel entries, while `vmrun` is the AMD one. `cpuid` is an instruction a guest executes that causes an exit, not one that starts a guest.

questions.prompt: After handling an exit caused by a guest instruction, what does the hypervisor usually do before the VM entry?
options: It moves the guest's saved instruction pointer past the instruction it just handled
It restarts the guest at the beginning of its boot code with a clean register set
It rewrites the guest's own page tables so the instruction cannot exit again
It clears the exit reason so the guest can read that the exit happened
questions.explanation: The exit saves the guest's state and gives the hypervisor an exit reason. After dealing with the cause, the hypervisor steps the saved instruction pointer forward so that, from inside the guest, the instruction just seems to have taken effect.

questions.prompt: A guest network driver writes 1 to its virtual card's START register and a VM exit follows. What caused the exit?
options: The register's guest-physical page has no second-stage mapping, so the processor hands the address to the hypervisor
Every memory write from a guest exits, so the hypervisor can check each one before it happens
The guest's own page table marks the page not present, so the guest's kernel reports the error to the host
The write is a ring-0 instruction, which always faults in the guest and is passed up to the host
questions.explanation: A missing stage-2 entry is how the hypervisor catches accesses to a device's memory-mapped registers. Ordinary memory writes and a page missing from the guest's own tables never leave the guest.

questions.prompt: Why does a guest's `hlt` instruction cause a VM exit?
options: The virtual processor has nothing to do, so the hypervisor can hand the real core to other work
`hlt` is a privileged instruction that would stop the real core if it ran inside the guest
`hlt` writes to a memory-mapped register, which has no second-stage mapping in the guest
The guest must be told that every core in the host has now been stopped
questions.explanation: Exits are listed in the exit controls. `hlt` is one because an idle virtual processor lets the hypervisor give the real core to something else, rather than wasting it.

questions.prompt: On an Intel processor `cpuid` always causes a VM exit. What does this let the hypervisor do?
options: Decide what the guest is told about its processor
Measure how fast the real processor is running
Stop the guest from reading the real processor's cache
Switch the guest from ring 3 into ring 0 for a moment
questions.explanation: `cpuid` describes the processor. Because it exits, the hypervisor can answer with whatever description it chooses instead of the real one.

questions.prompt: What does stage 1 of second-level address translation translate?
options: A guest virtual address into a guest physical address, through the guest's own tables
A guest virtual address into a host physical address, in a single combined lookup
A guest physical address into a host physical address, through the hypervisor's tables
A host virtual address into a host physical address, through the host kernel's tables
questions.explanation: Stage 1 belongs to the guest kernel, which writes the tables and switches them with its own `cr3`. Stage 2, written only by the hypervisor, turns guest physical into host physical.

questions.prompt: A guest kernel loads a new value into `cr3`. Which tables does that choose, and can it reach the stage-2 tables this way?
options: Its own stage-1 tables; stage 2 is the hypervisor's and the guest cannot name it
The stage-2 tables for the guest, since those are the ones that place its RAM
Both stages at once, because the processor treats `cr3` as pointing to a combined table
Its own stage-1 tables, and the guest can also edit stage 2 once it runs in ring 0
questions.explanation: `cr3` picks the guest's own page tables exactly as on real hardware. Stage-2 tables are out of the guest's reach altogether, which is where isolation comes from.

questions.prompt: A guest page is read-only in the hypervisor's stage-2 entry, but the guest's own page-table entry says read-write. The guest writes to it. What happens?
options: The access fails, because an access succeeds only if both stages allow it
The write succeeds, because the guest's own tables decide permissions for its pages
The write succeeds, and the hypervisor copies the page so it can be written
The write succeeds, because stage 1 overrides stage 2 for writable pages
questions.explanation: Stage-2 entries carry their own read, write and execute permissions, and the hardware needs both stages to agree. The guest cannot override the hypervisor's restriction by editing its own tables.

questions.prompt: A guest kernel can write any page-table entries it likes. Why can it still not reach another guest's memory?
options: Its entries only produce guest physical addresses, and only pages mapped in stage 2 exist for it
The processor rejects any guest page-table write whose frame number is above the guest's RAM size
Another guest's memory is encrypted with a key that only the hypervisor holds
The guest's own page tables are checked by the host kernel before each translation
questions.explanation: Memory that belongs to the host or to another guest has no guest physical address at all, so no instruction can name it. The guest's own tables can say anything, but they feed into stage 2.

questions.prompt: The disk figure shows blocks 1 and 4 written since the snapshot. A guest now reads block 3. Where does the data come from?
options: The frozen base, because the delta holds no newer copy of block 3
The delta, because every read after a snapshot is served from it
The memory file saved with the snapshot, which holds the latest disk contents
Neither; block 3 is merged from base and delta before it is returned
questions.explanation: A read checks the delta first and falls back to the base. Only blocks 1 and 4 have entries in the delta, so block 3 still comes from the base.

questions.prompt: Why is restoring a snapshot quick, while deleting a snapshot can be slow?
options: Restoring discards the delta, but deleting has to merge the delta's blocks into the base
Restoring only reads the frozen base, but deleting must rewrite the saved RAM file
Restoring skips the processor state, but deleting must save it into the base disk
Restoring copies back only the changed blocks, but deleting must copy back every block
questions.explanation: Nothing is copied back on a restore: the hypervisor simply throws the delta away. Deleting has to fold the delta's blocks into the base, so it is the slow direction.

questions.prompt: Which of these can restoring a snapshot not undo?
options: A message the guest already sent over the network
A file the guest deleted from its own virtual disk earlier
A driver that crashed the guest's kernel during a lab test
A setting the guest changed in its own registry hive
questions.explanation: Snapshot restores bring back the guest's disk, memory, processors and devices. Anything that left the machine, such as a sent message, an online account change or a copy on the host, stays out of reach.

questions.prompt: What is a VM escape, and why does it undercut the value of a snapshot?
options: A bug that lets guest code run on the host, putting the attacker beyond any snapshot's reach
A guest that crashes the hypervisor, erasing the delta file so the snapshot cannot be restored
A restore that stops partway through, leaving the guest half in one state and half in another
A snapshot being copied to another host, where the attacker can read the guest's memory
questions.explanation: A snapshot only resets what is inside the guest. If guest code can run on the host, the damage is outside what is restored. Such bugs usually sit in device-emulation code.

questions.prompt: Why does Lesson 1.7 keep shared folders, the shared clipboard and USB passthrough turned off until needed?
options: They are extra paths between guest and host, which a VM escape or a stray file copy could use
They add one VM exit to every guest instruction, which would slow the lab to a crawl
They make the delta file grow without limit, since every host file is copied into it
Windows refuses to enable them while the hypervisor is running with memory integrity on
questions.explanation: Every shared channel is a way for something to cross the isolation boundary. A snapshot cannot take back what crosses it.

questions.prompt: In virtualization-based security, what runs in VTL1, the secure world?
options: A small secure kernel and a few isolated processes, such as a secrets guard
The normal Windows kernel and drivers, with the games running up in ring 0
The hypervisor itself, together with all of the host's real device drivers too
A second complete copy of Windows that takes over if VTL0 ever crashes
questions.explanation: VTL0 is the normal world, with the usual kernel, drivers and programs. VTL1 is small, and it exists so that the most sensitive checks can run where VTL0 cannot tamper with them.

questions.prompt: Why can ring-0 kernel code in VTL0 not change its own stage-2 permissions?
options: VTL0 cannot reach the stage-2 tables at all; only VTL1 can ask the hypervisor to change them
The kernel is mapped read-only after boot, so no function in it can write any page table
VTL0's ring 0 has lower privilege than ring 3 in VTL1, so VTL1 wins any dispute at all
The permissions sit in firmware ROM, which cannot be written once the hypervisor has started
questions.explanation: The hypervisor keeps separate stage-2 permissions per trust level, and they are out of VTL0's reach even for ring-0 code. VTL1 is the only side that can request changes.

questions.prompt: On a PC with memory integrity on, a reader's lab VirtualBox runs a bit slower than a friend's. What is the right reaction?
options: Keep memory integrity on; the guests run through Windows' hypervisor, which costs some speed
Turn memory integrity off, because its slowdown is the only way VirtualBox can be sped up
Disable virtualization in the firmware settings, so VirtualBox falls back to running directly
Stop using the VM and run the labs on the host, since lab speed matters more than isolation
questions.explanation: With the Windows hypervisor running, VirtualBox and VMware run guests through it, which can be somewhat slower. The lesson does not treat that as a reason to turn off a protection; memory integrity also needs virtualization enabled.

questions.prompt: The keypad driver receives the control code `0x8000_6007` instead of `0x8000_6004`. What changed, and what should the driver do?
questions.explanation: `0x7` is `0111` and `0x4` is `0100`, so only bits 0 and 1 differ: the method went from 0, buffered, to 3, which passes the caller's raw user-mode addresses instead of a safe kernel copy.
