Each snapshot is written to disk before it is used
questions.explanation: A live Windows observer and a replay reader can both implement it, so automation can be tested without a process handle.

questions.prompt: What does `collect_for_lua` do when a snapshot has more than 256 entities?
options: Returns an error that names the published limit
Silently drops every entity beyond the limit
Splits the snapshot into several smaller Lua tables
Passes it along but tags the snapshot as large
questions.explanation: `anyhow::ensure!` fails the call with a message, enforcing a published bound instead of quietly truncating.

questions.prompt: Entity 7 despawns at sequence 42, but a script sends a request with `based_on = 41`. What does the host do?
options: Refuses it, because entity 7 no longer exists
Accepts it, since entity 7 was alive in snapshot 41
Selects whichever entity now has ID 7
Accepts it and logs the sequence mismatch
questions.explanation: The script did nothing wrong; it was right at snapshot 41. The `based_on` field lets the host see that the request describes a moment that has passed.

questions.prompt: Why is `game.request({ kind = "select_entity", id = target.id })` better than `game.execute("select " .. target.id)`?
options: It is structured data matched against an explicit enum
It runs faster because a table is smaller than a string
It lets the script pick any console command it likes
It makes checking the entity ID unnecessary
questions.explanation: A built command string is a command-language injection boundary. A structured request has a fixed shape, and unknown `kind` values fail.

questions.prompt: Why must the host validate again when it processes a request?
options: Checking at snapshot time says nothing about later state
Checks made at snapshot time are skipped for speed
Scripts are unable to see the values that were checked
The first check always ran against a different map
questions.explanation: This is a time-of-check/time-of-use issue: an entity may disappear between the snapshot and the request. Check recency, existence, state, finite numbers, bounds, and budget.

questions.prompt: How should the host handle permissions for an observer script versus an automation script?
options: The host picks the API first; observers get no requests
The script names its own permission level at the top
One API for all scripts, which agree to behave
Permissions come from the script's file name
questions.explanation: Do not decide permissions from a script-provided name. An observer gets snapshot and log only; automation gets those plus two bounded requests.

questions.prompt: Which input belongs in a test of the Lua-to-host request boundary?
options: A coordinate of `0/0` or infinity
A request that the host has approved before
A snapshot with every field filled in
A script that only logs one line
questions.explanation: The tests should send missing IDs, non-finite coordinates, unknown actions, too many actions, and expired sequences. The host must reject each usefully and stay alive.

questions.prompt: What is wrong with `while true do game.request({ kind = "select_entity", id = 1 }) end`?
options: No state, confirmation, or stop rule exists
It uses the wrong request kind for a selection
Lua forbids a loop that contains a function call
It sends one request, then ends the script silently
questions.explanation: The loop has no named phase, no way to see whether the request worked, and no stop condition, so it can flood the host and never respond to a stop signal.

questions.prompt: In the lesson's state machine, what does one update compute?
options: Next state, plus maybe a request, from state and input
A fresh Lua interpreter built from the script text
A new snapshot built from the host's raw memory reads
A final score built from the number of requests sent
questions.explanation: Formally the update maps (current state, validated snapshot or event) to (next state, optional request).

questions.prompt: Which job belongs to the host rather than the state machine?
options: Delivering a request and checking the target
Deciding that a living candidate was found
Moving the bot from Choose to Request
Counting down the `wait_ticks` value each update
questions.explanation: The state machine is policy: whether a request is appropriate. The host is mechanism: how it is delivered and whether the current target allows it.

questions.prompt: Why is `WAITING_FOR_SELECTION` a better state name than one that includes the selected entity's ID?
options: A state names a phase; the ID is separate data
IDs cannot be written inside any Lua string
Long state names are rejected by the host
A state name must match the entity's own name
questions.explanation: A state describes the bot's control phase. The selected entity ID, request sequence, and remaining timeout are data owned by that phase.

questions.prompt: Why does the lesson build a `State` table of constant strings?
options: Lua has no enum, so a table cuts spelling mistakes
The host reads that table to decide permissions
Strings stored in tables run faster than numbers
A script must declare every state to the interpreter
questions.explanation: A table of constants gives one place to see all states, and a typo like `State.WAT` yields nil instead of a silently wrong string.

questions.prompt: How much work does one call of `update` do?
options: One transition and at most one proposed action
Everything until the bot reaches the Stop state
One full pass through every state in turn
As many requests as the snapshot has entities
questions.explanation: Bounded work makes scheduling visible. The host can measure it, stop between calls, and keep a script from starving rendering or input.

questions.prompt: Who owns the loop that calls `update` in the lesson's design?
options: The host, which calls it at a controlled rate
The script, which loops until it is stopped
The snapshot, which wakes the script on change
The operating system, once per mouse click
questions.explanation: The script has no infinite loop, so it cannot flood actions between frames. The host chooses when each update runs.

questions.prompt: In the REQUEST state, which two values are set before the bot moves to WAIT?
options: `request_sequence` set and `wait_ticks = 20`
`selected` set to nil and `wait_ticks = 0`
`snapshot` cleared and `state = State.OBSERVE`
`wait_ticks = 1` and `selected = bot.snapshot`
questions.explanation: The request is tagged with the stored snapshot sequence, then the timeout counter starts at 20 and the state becomes WAIT.

questions.prompt: The bot enters WAIT with `wait_ticks = 20` and no confirmation ever arrives. After how many WAIT updates with `wait_ticks` still above zero is it at 0?
options: 20 updates; the next one goes to Stop
19 updates; the next one goes to Observe
21 updates; the next one sends a new request
1 update; the counter then resets itself
questions.explanation: Each unconfirmed WAIT update subtracts one: 20 updates take it from 20 to 0. On the next update `wait_ticks == 0`, so the bot stops safely.

questions.prompt: Why does the bot keep `bot.snapshot` from OBSERVE separate from the snapshot passed to later WAIT calls?
options: A stale choice cannot silently become authority
The host only lets scripts store one snapshot at a time
The WAIT state cannot read any snapshot at all
Older snapshots are sent back to the game automatically
questions.explanation: REQUEST tags its action with the stored sequence, and WAIT uses the latest snapshot to look for confirmation. Keeping them apart makes the host's staleness check meaningful.

questions.prompt: Which description fits `choose_nearest_living` as a pure function?
options: It reads input and returns a choice, nothing else
It logs each candidate and sends one request too
It edits the snapshot so the best entity is first
It sleeps until the player moves nearer to a target
questions.explanation: Pure here means reading input and returning a choice without side effects, which makes it easy to test with fixed tables.

questions.prompt: Entity 1 is the local player. Living candidates at distances 5.0 and 3.0 appear before a dead entity at 1.0. Which does `choose_nearest_living` return?
options: The living entity at distance 3.0
The dead entity at distance 1.0
The living entity at distance 5.0
The local player
questions.explanation: The loop skips entity 1 and any entity with `alive` false. Of the living candidates, 3.0 beats 5.0, so it returns that one.

questions.prompt: Which of these should move the host to Stopped even if the Lua script wants to continue?
options: The user pressing the stop hotkey
The script choosing a new state name
The bot finishing its CHOOSE phase
A snapshot containing a living entity
questions.explanation: The script is a guest, not the authority over shutdown. Hotkey, process exit, profile mismatch, an error limit, a rejected action, or an invalid snapshot all stop it.

questions.prompt: What should the update function do on an unknown state string?
options: Raise an error containing the bad state name
Treat it as Observe and carry on quietly
Move to Request to retry the last action
Return true without changing anything at all
questions.explanation: The final `else` calls `error("unknown bot state: " .. tostring(bot.state))`. A readable error is better than silently continuing from a nonsense state.

questions.prompt: What stance should an embedded interpreter take toward script failure?
options: Treat it as a normal result; keep the game running
Treat it as impossible once scripts pass a review
Close the whole game so the error cannot spread
Retry the failing line until it finally succeeds
questions.explanation: One script error should not crash the game, leak resources, or leave input stuck.

questions.prompt: A script has an `if` with no `end`. At which stage does the failure appear?
options: Syntax check; no runnable function is made
Lua runtime, once the `if` line first executes
Host function, once the game API is called
Gameplay, after a wrong action is requested
questions.explanation: A syntax error means the source never became a runnable function. Runtime, host-API, and gameplay errors all need code that already compiled.

questions.prompt: A script runs without raising any error but selects the wrong unit. Which kind of error is this?
options: A gameplay error, where nothing is raised
A syntax error, caught when the file loads
A runtime type error, from unsuitable values
A host-API error, from a broken contract
questions.explanation: Every layer ran correctly; the requested action was simply wrong. It needs a test that asserts expected behavior, not an error message.

questions.prompt: A script calls `game.request` with a missing required field. Which stage fits best?
options: Host-API error: the call broke the contract
Lexing error: the file had an unclosed quote
Gameplay error: the unit chosen was the wrong one
Syntax error: the grammar of the line was wrong
questions.explanation: The script called the engine but violated its contract. Syntax was fine, and a gameplay error would raise nothing at all.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a separate budget the lesson lists besides VM instructions?
options: Maximum call-frame depth
Global names a script may define
Comments in the script's source
Length of each string literal
questions.explanation: The lesson separates source and bytecode size, Lua memory, instructions, frame depth, host callbacks, wall-clock work, and queued actions or log output.

questions.prompt: When a budget is exceeded mid-update, what should the host do with the update's queued actions?
options: Discard them and report which budget was hit
Commit them, since they were valid when queued
Keep them for the script's next update
Commit the first half and discard the rest
questions.explanation: Do not quietly continue with half-produced output. Stop the update, drop uncommitted actions, and name the exact budget.

questions.prompt: What does `lua.set_memory_limit(4 * 1024 * 1024)` set in bytes?
options: 4,194,304 bytes (four mebibytes)
4,000,000 bytes (four megabytes)
4,096 bytes (four kibibytes)
1,048,576 bytes (one mebibyte)
questions.explanation: 1024 × 1024 = 1,048,576 bytes is one mebibyte, so four of them is 4,194,304 bytes. The multiplication converts mebibytes to bytes.

questions.prompt: Does the Lua memory limit cover everything a host callback allocates?
options: No; only Lua-managed memory, so callbacks need bounds
Yes; any allocation during a script call counts
Yes; Rust heap memory is counted through `mlua` too
No; it covers only the size of the script's source
questions.explanation: The limit applies to Lua-managed memory. A host function can allocate other memory, so it needs its own limits.

questions.prompt: The hook fires every 1,000 instructions and the script is stopped once `calls > 100`. Roughly how many instructions can one update run?
options: About 100,000
About 1,000
About 10,000
questions.explanation: 100 allowed hook calls × 1,000 instructions between calls is roughly 100,000 VM instructions before the budget stops it.

questions.prompt: Why does the hook use `Arc<Mutex<u32>>` for its counter?
options: The closure shares one counter and guards it
Lua stores every counter inside an `Arc` itself
The mutex makes the counter reset on each call
`Arc` copies the count into each separate hook call
questions.explanation: `Arc` shares ownership and `Mutex` protects one update at a time. `Arc::clone` shares the same counter and does not reset the budget.

questions.prompt: Why is an instruction-count hook not a stopwatch?
options: Instruction costs differ, and callbacks run between hooks
The hook counts seconds instead of instructions
Hooks fire only once, at the moment a script ends
Instructions always cost the same number of nanoseconds
questions.explanation: Different instructions cost different real time, and host callbacks can do work between hooks, so the hook is one defense against runaway bytecode, not a timer.

questions.prompt: Who should reset the instruction allowance?
options: The host, at a controlled boundary
The script, when it runs low
The hook, after each call
The user, by restarting the game
questions.explanation: Reset from the host side, not from inside the script, which could otherwise grant itself unlimited work.

questions.prompt: What should happen when `scripts/budget_failure.lua` (`while true do end`) runs?
options: An error that names the script and the budget
The terminal hangs until you press a key
The script ends quietly and prints nothing
The host exits its own process to stay safe
questions.explanation: Expected result is a contextual error. If the terminal hangs forever, the limit is not working.

questions.prompt: Which item belongs in a host callback's input checks?
options: Numeric finiteness, range, and referenced IDs
Whether the script file is long enough to run
Which Lua version wrote the script's comments
The colors the log output will be shown in
questions.explanation: Validate argument types, string lengths, sequence lengths, numeric finiteness and range, referenced IDs, permissions, and rate budgets.

questions.prompt: Which detail should NOT appear in a public error report?
options: Account tokens or dumps of process memory
The script path or a stable identifier
The line number and the traceback if known
The validation rule that failed on the call
questions.explanation: Development builds should report path, traceback, API function, and rule. Do not leak memory, tokens, private logs, or arbitrary host paths.

questions.prompt: In the lesson's failure policy, what happens on the first error in an update?
options: Stop this update and report it
Disable the script for the session
Reset the script and retry at once
Stop all scripted actions immediately
questions.explanation: The first error stops that update and reports it. Only repeated errors disable the script, and a host invariant failure stops all scripted actions.

questions.prompt: Why should the host not catch a script error and keep going from the same state?
options: Host state may be half-changed; commit only afterward
Lua errors always repair themselves by next frame
Lua requires every error to close the interpreter
Catching errors always makes the script run faster
questions.explanation: Lua requests should be queued and committed only after the script returns successfully, so a failure cannot leave half-mutated host state.

questions.prompt: Which list names the four parts of a Turing machine as the lesson describes it?
options: Tape, head, state, and rule table
Tape, stack, heap, and compiler
Memory, register, bus, and clock
Input, parser, lexer, and output
questions.explanation: A tape of cells, a head reading and writing one cell, a current state, and a rule table. The other lists mix in ideas from other lessons.

questions.prompt: What does one step of a Turing machine do?
options: Look up a rule, write, move one cell, switch state
Read the whole tape, then rewrite every cell at once
Jump to any cell by its address and swap two symbols
Compile the rule table and then run the compiled result
questions.explanation: One step is lookup, write, move one cell or stay, and a state change. The head walks one cell at a time; it does not jump.

questions.prompt: How does the lesson's machine halt?
options: No rule matches the state and the symbol
The tape runs out of blank cells on the right
The head reaches the leftmost cell of the tape
The machine enters a state that is named `carry`
questions.explanation: Halting is stopping. In the incrementer, `done` has no rules, so reaching it halts the machine.

questions.prompt: The incrementer starts in `carry` on the rightmost digit of `1011`. What is on the tape when it halts?
questions.explanation: The head reads 1, writes 0, moves left; reads 1, writes 0, moves left; reads 0, writes 1, stays, and halts. That turns eleven (1011) into twelve (1100).

questions.prompt: On `111`, what does the third rule (`carry`, blank) do?
options: Writes a new leading 1, giving `1000`
Writes a 0 and keeps moving left
Halts without changing the tape
Writes a 1 on the right end instead
questions.explanation: The carry runs past the leftmost digit into a blank cell. The machine writes a 1 there, so seven becomes eight (`1000`).

questions.prompt: Which pair matches a Turing machine part to its closest counterpart in a real computer?
options: The tape and memory
The head and the power supply
The rule table and the file system
The state and the monitor
questions.explanation: Tape maps to memory, head position to an address, state to registers including the instruction pointer, rules to the program, and a step to an instruction.

questions.prompt: Why does a real computer only approximate the Turing machine model?
options: Its memory is a fixed size; the tape never runs out
Its CPU cannot read a symbol before writing one
Its hardware can only use binary, never other symbols
Its programs cannot be stored as bytes in memory
questions.explanation: A finite machine eventually runs out of memory or states. The Turing machine says what could be computed with as much time and storage as needed.

questions.prompt: What makes a universal Turing machine special?
options: It reads another machine's rules from tape and imitates it
It runs any program on any input in one single step
It has an unlimited supply of different states to use
It never halts, whatever input sits on its tape
questions.explanation: A rule table is just symbols, so it can sit on a tape like data. To change what the machine does, change the tape, not the machine.

questions.prompt: What does 'stored-program computer' mean for the tools in this book?
options: Instructions and data are both bytes in memory
Programs live on a separate chip from the data
Programs cannot be changed once they are loaded
Data bytes are run whenever the CPU reads them
questions.explanation: Because code is bytes, tools can inspect code as well as data, subject to memory protections. Only bytes the instruction pointer reaches run as instructions.

questions.prompt: Which action treats code as data by writing it?
options: A debugger writing `0xCC` over an instruction byte
A disassembler naming the instructions it reads
A game loading a texture file in order to draw it
A script printing a log message to the console
questions.explanation: A software breakpoint is a one-byte write of `int3` (`0xCC`). The disassembler reads code as data; the other two are not about code.

questions.prompt: What stops a program from overwriting its own instructions?
options: Page protections set by the OS and enforced by the CPU
The Turing machine model, which forbids the write
Comments in the program marking its code read-only
The instruction pointer, which erases every change
questions.explanation: Nothing in the model forbids it. The OS marks pages readable, writable, or executable, and the CPU refuses forbidden accesses. A writable-and-executable page deserves a second look.

questions.prompt: What is true of a Turing-complete system, given enough time and memory?
options: It can compute anything a Turing machine can
It will halt on every program it runs
It can only run programs written in Rust or C++
It needs a graphical screen to work
questions.explanation: In idealized form Rust, C++, Lua, and assembly qualify, and so do Conway's Game of Life and redstone circuits. Real builds are limited by their actual resources.

questions.prompt: Why does the lesson treat a mod's script differently from a texture file?
options: A script is a program that computes within the host's limits
A texture is a program, so it can run by itself
A script cannot be inspected the way a texture can
A texture cannot contain a bug in the code that reads it
questions.explanation: A texture is read in one fixed way, so a strange one usually trips a reader bug. A Turing-complete script computes within resources, and the host's API limits what it can touch.

questions.prompt: In the halting-problem argument, what does `contrary` do when the checker says it halts?
options: It loops forever, so the checker was wrong
It halts at once, so the checker was right
It asks the checker a second, different question
It deletes the checker program before finishing
questions.explanation: `contrary` does the opposite of the answer for `contrary(contrary)`. Whichever answer the checker gives, it is wrong, so an always-right checker cannot exist.

questions.prompt: Which question is undecidable in general, per Rice's theorem as the lesson describes it?
options: Does this program ever write to a given address?
Does the file hold more than one hundred bytes?
Does the source text contain the word `while`?
Is the very first byte of the file `0x4D`?
questions.explanation: Questions about what a program does, rather than how its text is written, are undecidable in general. The other three are checks on the text or bytes.

questions.prompt: Why can a disassembler produce a plausible but wrong listing on x86?
options: Lengths vary, so a start one byte off misreads
Disassemblers cannot read bytes held in memory
Every x86 instruction is exactly four bytes long
Disassemblers run the program and guess output
questions.explanation: It must decide which bytes are instructions. Starting too early or late gives a convincing wrong listing, so check odd output against the debugger.

questions.prompt: Why can a signature scanner miss code it has never seen?
options: It matches known patterns, not behavior
It scans only files under one megabyte
It runs each file and waits for a halt
It cannot read executable files at all
questions.explanation: Since behavior is undecidable in general, scanners use known byte patterns and behavior. They can miss the unknown and occasionally flag something harmless.

questions.prompt: In the lab's `run` loop, a machine reaches `done` on its very last budgeted step. How is it reported?
options: Halted, since the rule lookup comes before the budget check
Out of budget, since all the steps are now spent
An error, since both limits were hit at the same moment
Still running, since it used every step it was given
questions.explanation: The loop looks up the rule first and returns `Halted` if none exists, then checks the budget. The order matters for this edge case.

questions.prompt: Why does the lab feed the simulator a malformed rule table at the end?
options: To show that a program-as-data still needs validation
To prove the simulator can read any text file at all
To make the step budget run out on purpose again
To show how to flip every digit of a binary number
questions.explanation: A rule table is only data, but running it is running a program, so it needs validation before it runs.

questions.prompt: A two-rule machine flips every digit of `1011` starting at the leftmost digit. How many rule steps does it take?
options: 4, then it stops at the blank
5, because the blank is also flipped
3, because the last digit is skipped
2, because there are only two rules
questions.explanation: It applies a rule to each of the four digits, turning `1011` into `0100`. At the blank no rule matches, so the machine halts without a fifth step.

questions.prompt: In what order do the interpreter stages process `total = 5 + 2`?
options: Lexer, parser, compiler, virtual machine
Parser, lexer, virtual machine, compiler
Compiler, lexer, parser, virtual machine
Lexer, compiler, parser, virtual machine
questions.explanation: Characters become tokens, tokens are checked against the grammar, the meaning becomes bytecode, and the VM executes it.

questions.prompt: What is the lexer's job in the pipeline?
options: Group characters into tokens like name or integer
Check the token order against the grammar
Turn the program's meaning into bytecode steps
Run the bytecode using a stack of values now
questions.explanation: The lexer produces tokens like name, equals, integer, plus, integer. Grammar checking is the parser, and compiling and running are later stages.

questions.prompt: Does every interpreter use the lexer, parser, bytecode, VM pipeline?
options: No; one may walk a syntax tree or add a JIT
Yes; bytecode is part of the definition of Lua
Yes; every interpreter must emit native code
No; only compiled languages have a parser
questions.explanation: The stages are common but not definitional. The language's meaning can stay the same while its implementation changes.

questions.prompt: Which is a language rule, as opposed to an implementation detail?
options: `+` adds two numbers and produces a number
Pop two VM values, check variants, push the sum
The host's native code runs on the CPU
A bytecode listing has eleven instructions
questions.explanation: The source rule is the contract. Stacks, bytecodes, and native instructions are replaceable ways to carry it out.

questions.prompt: What does `Constant(2)` mean in the lab's bytecode?
options: Copy constant number two from the pool onto the stack
Add the integer 2 to the value on top of the stack
Jump to bytecode position two in the program
Print the constant at the top of the stack
questions.explanation: Instructions refer to pool constants by index. In the example pool, index 2 holds 6.

questions.prompt: In the lab's listing, `JumpIfFalse(9)` sends a false condition where?
options: Index 9, where the else branch begins
Index 9 of the constant pool
The end of the program, at the `Halt`
The instruction right after the `Print`
questions.explanation: Jump operands are positions in the bytecode vector. Index 9 is `Constant(4)`, the start of the else branch.

questions.prompt: What does `Jump(11)` at index 8 do for the then branch?
options: Carries it past the else branch to `Halt`
Repeats the `Print` instruction at index 7
Restarts the program at index 0
Pushes the integer 11 onto the stack
questions.explanation: After printing 1, the then branch must not run the else branch. Jumping to 11 lands on `Halt`.

questions.prompt: Why does the VM add one to `instruction_pointer` right after fetching an instruction?
options: It sets the next default; jumps overwrite it
It skips every other instruction, for speed
It counts how many values the stack holds
It resets the step budget before each fetch
questions.explanation: The increment sets the default next location. A jump overwrites it, and bounds checks stop corrupt bytecode from leaving the program.

questions.prompt: Which item is NOT part of the tiny VM's state as the lesson lists it?
options: The Windows process handle of the game
The instruction pointer into the bytecode
The value stack of temporary values
The remaining step budget for the run
questions.explanation: The state is instruction pointer, bytecode, constant pool, value stack, remaining budget, and output so far. A process handle belongs to the host, not this VM.

questions.prompt: After `Constant(0)`, `Constant(1)`, `Add`, what is on the value stack?
options: The single value 7
The two values 5 and 2
The single value 2
The single value true
questions.explanation: Constants 5 and 2 are pushed, then `Add` pops both and pushes 7.

questions.prompt: After `Constant(2)` pushes 6 on top of 7, what does `GreaterThan` leave on the stack?
options: true
questions.explanation: It pops 6 and 7 and compares 7 > 6, so the one value left is the Boolean true, which `JumpIfFalse` then tests.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between the constant pool and the value stack?
options: The pool holds constants; the stack holds temporaries
The pool holds temporaries; the stack holds constants
Both hold identical values, just in a different order
The pool holds code; the stack holds output text
questions.explanation: Adding two values removes both from the stack and leaves one result, while the pool is only read.

questions.prompt: Why does `Add` pop the right-hand side first?
options: It was pushed last, and the stack is last-in first-out
The right side is always the larger of the two integers
Add reads the pool before it ever reads the stack
Lua defines addition so that it starts from the right
questions.explanation: The stack hands back the most recently pushed value first, the same basic idea as a call stack.

questions.prompt: What happens if the tiny VM is told to add a Boolean to an integer?
options: A VM error from the variant check
The Boolean quietly becomes the integer 1
The integer quietly becomes the Boolean true
The VM adds the two values' raw bytes
questions.explanation: `pop_integer` checks the variant. Dynamic typing means the check happens at run time, not that types do not exist.

questions.prompt: A script's jump target points outside the program. Which kind of failure is this?
options: Bytecode validation
Lexing of the source
Parsing of the grammar
Execution of the code
questions.explanation: The lesson separates lexing, parsing, bytecode validation, and execution failures. A jump outside the program is invalid bytecode, a different stage from a type error at run time.

questions.prompt: Why keep the four failure kinds separate in error messages?
options: The host can tell bad Lua from a budget stop
Short messages make every script run faster
Lexing errors can only be fixed by the host
Each stage writes its errors to a different file
questions.explanation: If everything becomes 'script failed', no one can tell whether the author wrote invalid Lua, the compiler made bad code, or a valid script exceeded resource policy.

questions.prompt: In the VM's loop, what does `if self.steps_left == 0` check before each instruction?
options: Whether the instruction budget is spent
Whether the value stack is empty
Whether the program contains an `Add`
Whether the instruction is a jump
questions.explanation: Every instruction consumes one step, so a program like `Jump(0)` ends in an error instead of looping forever.

questions.prompt: Why does each interpreter value carry a tag beside its payload?
options: An operation reads the tag to learn the value's type first
The tag stores the value's address in memory
The tag makes the payload immune to garbage collection
The tag lets the host skip type checks in Rust
questions.explanation: Lua decides many operations at run time, so `+` checks both tags before touching payloads. Two Integer tags can add; an Integer with a Table is a type error.

questions.prompt: What is the `TableId` inside `Value::Table(TableId(3))`?
options: A handle into storage the VM owns
The address of the table in the game process
The number of fields the table currently holds
The table's line position inside the script file
questions.explanation: Handles keep interpreter objects under one memory manager and avoid giving scripts raw native pointers.

questions.prompt: In `{ "red", "green", "blue", name = "palette", selected = 2 }`, which keys use the array-like part?
options: Keys 1, 2, and 3
Keys `name` and `selected`
Keys 1, 2, 3, and `name`
None; all keys are hashed
questions.explanation: The three dense integer keys fit the array part, while the named keys use the hash part. These are implementation strategies behind one table value.

questions.prompt: Why does `pairs` promise no meaningful order?
options: It walks the array part, then hash nodes by hash
It sorts the keys alphabetically before each loop
It picks a new random order every time it runs
It follows the order in which the fields were set
questions.explanation: Node order follows the keys' hash values, not the order they were written, so a script must not depend on it.

questions.prompt: What does it mean to intern strings?
options: Keep one canonical copy and let values carry an ID
Make every string a fresh copy for each table
Store each string inside the table that uses it
Convert each string into its integer length
questions.explanation: Repeated names and keys share one stored string, so values hold a small ID or shared reference.

questions.prompt: Why is comparing two interned strings fast?
options: It is one integer comparison, whatever the length
The text is compared one letter at a time
Interned strings are always one letter long
The collector compares them while it is running
questions.explanation: If both values carry `String(0)`, equality is `0 == 0`. The cost moves to lifetime work: the VM must know when no live value still needs the string.

questions.prompt: After `a = {}`, `b = {}`, `a.friend = b`, and `b.friend = a`, what are the counts of table A and table B?
questions.explanation: A is held by `a` and `b.friend`. B is held by `b` and `a.friend`, so each has 2.

questions.prompt: After `a` and `b` leave scope in that cycle, what do the counts settle at?
options: Each stays at 1, held up by the other
Each drops to 0 and is freed at once
A drops to 0, but B stays at 1
Each rises to 3 for a short while
questions.explanation: Dropping `a` and `b` removes one count from each table, leaving the friend field of the other. Neither can be reached, yet neither is freed.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between unreachable and unreferenced?
options: Unreachable means no root path; unreferenced means count zero
Unreachable means count zero; unreferenced means no root path
Both mean the same thing for a table
Unreachable is for strings; unreferenced is for tables
questions.explanation: In a cycle the objects are unreachable from any root but still referenced by each other, and counting alone cannot tell those apart.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a root in a tracing collector?
options: The global environment, which holds live names
A table that is found only through an unreachable cycle
A string whose reference count has already hit zero
A function that the script never defined anywhere
questions.explanation: Roots include the global environment, active frames, VM stack values, open upvalues, and intentionally retained host references. The collector marks everything reachable from them.

questions.prompt: What does a tracing collector do with objects the mark step did not reach?
options: It sweeps them, cycles included
It keeps them until the script ends
It counts them and frees any whose count is 0
It moves them to the nearest root
questions.explanation: It asks about reachability, not owner counts, so two tables in an unreachable cycle are both reclaimed.

questions.prompt: What risk comes from a host API that retains a Lua table?
options: It may keep a large graph of objects alive
It stops the script from using that table
It converts the table into a string
It forces a collection every frame
questions.explanation: Anything reachable from a retained table stays alive, which is why limits should measure interpreter memory and not the source size.

questions.prompt: Why does the lesson call the `game` table a capability container?
options: If `os.execute` is absent, scripts cannot call it
The table is where all the game's save data lives
It makes every call in it run with admin rights
Lua requires a separate table for each function
questions.explanation: Table construction is part of the security boundary: a script can call only what its environment contains.

questions.prompt: In a debug build of an embedded VM, which structure hints at a VM instruction pointer separate from the CPU's?
options: An index into an array of bytecodes
A pointer into the Windows kernel's thread list
A string table that holds only file paths
An array of GPU shader constants
questions.explanation: The lesson suggests looking for tagged-value dispatch, a central table lookup, a VM instruction pointer, bytecode or constant arrays, roots, and callbacks under readable names.

questions.prompt: A reader assumes the PE entry point is the developer's `main` function. What is wrong with that?
options: Windows first runs startup code that prepares the runtime, then that code calls `main`
The entry point is a data table, so the CPU does not execute anything there
The entry point is the loader's own routine and runs before the game's EXE is mapped
The entry point calls `main` on 64-bit builds; 32-bit builds skip startup code
questions.explanation: Startup code can set up security state, global constructors, and thread-local storage before `main`. Labeling the first code address `main` hides that chain of responsibilities.

questions.prompt: Which pair of things do all threads of one process share?
options: The virtual address space and the handle table
The instruction pointer and the general-purpose registers
The stack and the saved return addresses
The thread ID and the thread-local storage slots
questions.explanation: Address space and handles are process-wide. Each thread needs its own registers, stack, and TEB so Windows can pause and resume it independently.

questions.prompt: Why does every thread need its own registers and stack?
options: So Windows can pause it and later resume exactly where it stopped
So the process can hold a separate address space for each thread
So each thread can keep its own private copy of every loaded DLL
So each thread has a separate handle table that other threads cannot see
questions.explanation: A paused thread's place in the code and its call history live in registers and the stack. The address space and handle table stay shared.

questions.prompt: What does the PEB (Process Environment Block) mainly describe?
options: Process-wide user-mode data: image base, loader lists, process parameters
The registers, stack bounds, and error code of the one thread that is running now
The kernel-mode page tables Windows uses to translate this process's addresses
The list of files on disk that the game's installer copied into its folder
questions.explanation: The PEB is a root for process-wide metadata. Per-thread details such as stack boundaries live in each thread's TEB.

questions.prompt: How do the TEB and PEB relate?
options: Every thread has a TEB, and each TEB leads to the one shared PEB
Each process has many PEBs, one per thread, and the TEB is the shared copy
The PEB sits inside the kernel while the TEB sits inside the game's EXE file
The TEB lists the loaded modules and the PEB lists the current thread's stack
questions.explanation: TEB is one per thread, PEB is one per process. Thread-specific facts such as stack boundaries come from the TEB, and the loader lists hang off the PEB.

questions.prompt: Disassembly of a 64-bit Windows program contains `mov rax, qword ptr gs:[0x60]`. What is this most likely doing?
options: Fetching the PEB pointer through the current thread's segment data
Reading a health value from the game's player object at offset 0x60
Loading the address of the next instruction so the function can return
Copying 0x60 bytes of the game's save file into register rax
questions.explanation: On x86-64 Windows, `gs` helps locate thread state, and the PEB pointer sits at `0x60` there. It is not ordinary game data, which is why the segment prefix stands out.

questions.prompt: The 32-bit PEB pointer offset is `0x30` and the 64-bit one is `0x60`. What should a learner conclude?
options: Each layout has its own offsets; no rule says to double them on 64 bits
Every structure offset doubles on 64-bit Windows because pointers are twice as wide
Offsets stay identical in both layouts and `0x60` was a typing error in the lesson
Offsets add 0x30 for each extra register that the 64-bit CPU provides over 32-bit
questions.explanation: Wider pointers and alignment help explain why layouts change, but the real offsets come from the layout under examination. Treat them as observations for one architecture and Windows build.

questions.prompt: A tool copies a PEB field offset from an old 32-bit article and uses it on a current 64-bit process. What is the main risk?
options: Layout depends on architecture and Windows build, so it may hit another field
Windows will refuse to run any program that uses a number copied from an article
The offset will be too small by exactly one pointer width, so a +4 fix works
The PEB is encrypted on 64-bit systems, so every read returns random bytes
questions.explanation: PEB and TEB internals are not a stable public API contract. An old offset can still read plausible-looking bytes, which is what makes the mistake hard to notice.

questions.prompt: Why does the course's module tool use `CreateToolhelp32Snapshot` instead of walking loader lists by hand?
options: It is a documented, read-only way to get a moment-in-time copy of the module list
It is the only call that can read memory belonging to a different 32-bit process
It freezes every thread in the game so the module list cannot change at all
It returns undocumented loader structures that are faster to decode than the PEB
questions.explanation: Walking internal loader pointers is fine for learning in a debugger, but ToolHelp gives a supported copy. The copy is a snapshot, not a freeze of the running game.

questions.prompt: What is `dwSize` in `MODULEENTRY32W` for?
options: It tells Windows which size and version of the output structure the caller prepared
It stores the number of bytes the module occupies once it is loaded in memory
It records how many modules the snapshot found when the list is complete
It limits how many characters of the module name Windows is allowed to return
questions.explanation: The lesson compares forgetting it to handing someone a form without saying which form it is. The module's size is a different field, `modBaseSize`.

questions.prompt: Right after a module appears in a ToolHelp snapshot, a read at its base address fails. Which explanation fits the lesson?
options: The process kept running, so the DLL may have unloaded after the snapshot
Snapshots return placeholder addresses that were not mapped in the target process
ToolHelp reports the preferred base, which differs from the live base
Windows blocks every read of a module until the snapshot handle is closed
questions.explanation: A snapshot is stable but the process is not frozen. A later read must still be allowed to fail, and `Result` makes that failure visible.

questions.prompt: What does 'enumeration tells you what existed during the snapshot' mean for later reads?
options: An address seen earlier may still fail to read and should give a normal error
Any address seen in the snapshot stays valid until the program exits
A read should be retried in a loop until Windows finally allows it
The tool should cache the address and skip checking the result next time
questions.explanation: Seeing an address earlier does not guarantee it is valid now. The tool reports an error rather than assuming a previously seen address must remain valid.

questions.prompt: In the `module` function, `Module32NextW` fails with the 'no more files' error. How should the loop treat it?
options: As the normal end of the list, so it stops and reports the module as not found
As a crash in the game, so it should retry the whole snapshot from the start
As a sign the module was found, so it returns the last entry it looked at
As a security block, so it should request more access rights and continue
questions.explanation: That error is the documented end of enumeration. Other errors are returned as real failures, and only a name match returns a base and size.

questions.prompt: `pe_inspector` shows a preferred base of `0x400000` and `module_inspector` shows a live base of `0x520000`. Where does RVA `0x3CCD91` sit in this run?
options: `0x8ECD91`, because the live base plus the RVA gives the live address
`0x7CCD91`, because the preferred base plus the RVA gives the live address
`0x3CCD91`, because an RVA is already the final address in the process
`0x9ECD91`, because the shift between the bases is added twice to the RVA
questions.explanation: The module moved by `0x120000`, and every byte inside moved with it. The RVA is measured from the module start, so live base `0x520000` + `0x3CCD91` = `0x8ECD91`.

questions.prompt: If ASLR moves the whole module, why does the same RVA still name the same position?
options: It is measured from the module's start, which moves along with every byte inside
It is an absolute address that Windows rewrites in the lab tool's output
It is stored in the PEB, and the PEB is left unchanged when a module moves
It is a file offset on disk, which does not depend on where the module loads
questions.explanation: An RVA is a relative position. That is why the lab adds it to the live base instead of reusing a displayed absolute address after a restart.

questions.prompt: What does the lesson say about editing PEB flags or unlinking modules from the loader lists?
options: Do not; it can break loader assumptions or hide activity from diagnostic tools
Do it after the game is closed, because then the loader lists are unused
It is the preferred way to speed up ToolHelp when a process has many DLLs
It is safe on 64-bit Windows because those structures are protected copies
questions.explanation: The lesson uses the structures to explain Windows, then relies on documented APIs. Tampering is called out as both fragile and something that conceals activity.

questions.prompt: Which pairing correctly separates mechanism from policy?
options: A context switch is mechanism; picking the next ready thread is policy
A context switch is a policy; the thread's saved registers are the mechanism
A handle is a policy; the access check on a request is the mechanism
Choosing the next thread is a mechanism; stopping one thread is a policy
questions.explanation: A mechanism is how something is done and a policy decides what should be done. Mixing them makes an implementation detail sound like a guarantee.

questions.prompt: Why does copying `wesnoth.exe` not copy a running match?
options: The process also holds live memory, thread contexts, and handles the file lacks
Windows encrypts the EXE so a copy cannot contain the game's logic and assets
A running match is stored inside the PE header and a copy resets that header
The EXE keeps its own scheduler, so a copied file schedules threads differently
questions.explanation: The EXE supplies code and initial data; the process is that plus address space, register contexts, handles, and bookkeeping. This is also why a crash dump reveals more than the file.

questions.prompt: Which of these can make a live process differ from its EXE file?
options: Applying relocations, resolving imports, and zero-filling data
Rewriting the PE section names so they match the process's heap names
Deleting the import table from the file once the game starts running
Renumbering every function so RVAs match the preferred base exactly
questions.explanation: The process is not simply a copy of the file. Windows may place sections at different virtual addresses and also creates private memory that never existed in the EXE.

questions.prompt: Why is walking the PEB's live loader lists risky compared with a snapshot?
options: Another thread may load or unload a module while the list is being walked
The lists are stored encrypted and each entry needs a key from the TEB
The lists exist while a debugger is attached to the process
The lists contain 32-bit modules, so 64-bit DLLs would be missed
questions.explanation: The loader lists are live linked lists. A walker needs the correct layout at every step and must tolerate the list changing underneath it.

questions.prompt: x86 processors define four privilege levels. Which two does Windows actually use, and for what?
options: Ring 0 for the kernel and drivers, ring 3 for games, browsers, debuggers, and every tool in the book
Ring 0 for games and debuggers, ring 3 for the kernel and the drivers that talk to hardware
Ring 1 for drivers and ring 2 for services, with ring 3 for the kernel's scheduler and memory manager
Ring 0 for administrator programs and ring 3 for standard user programs, with the kernel in between
questions.explanation: Windows uses ring 0 (kernel mode) and ring 3 (user mode). Administrator versus standard user is a security-token matter, not a processor ring: an administrator's game tool still runs in ring 3.

questions.prompt: Why does the user/kernel privilege rule have to be enforced by the processor instead of by ordinary operating-system code?
options: A restricted program could overwrite protections kept in ordinary code or data, so the rule must live beyond its reach
Ordinary operating-system code runs too slowly to check every instruction a program executes on a busy core, so hardware must
Software checks cannot read the page tables, so only the processor knows which memory belongs to which running program
Every game is compiled with its own copy of the rules, so a shared software rule could not apply to all of them
questions.explanation: If the protections were just code and data, the program being restricted could rewrite them, the way a debugger rewrites an instruction. Only the processor sits beyond a ring-3 program's reach. Speed and page-table visibility are not the reason.

questions.prompt: A ring-3 program executes `cli`, which turns interrupts off. What happens?
options: The processor raises a general-protection fault instead of running it, and the kernel normally ends the program
Interrupts go quiet for that program's threads only, while the kernel's timer keeps ticking for everyone else
The instruction runs, but Windows turns interrupts back on at the next system call the program makes
The processor ignores the instruction silently and continues with the next one, so nothing visible happens
questions.explanation: Privileged instructions such as `cli`, `hlt`, `wrmsr`, and writes to `cr3` are refused at ring 3 with a general-protection fault (vector 13). The kernel turns it into an exception that normally ends the program. Silencing the timer would let a program keep the processor forever.

questions.prompt: What does the privileged instruction `mov cr3, rax` change, and why is it kept from ring 3?
options: It switches to a different set of page tables, which selects a process's whole view of memory
It changes which core the current thread runs on, which would let a program dodge the scheduler
It switches the processor between user and kernel mode, which would let a program promote itself
It rewrites the table of interrupt handlers, which would let a program redirect the timer
questions.explanation: `cr3` holds the address of the top-level page table, so loading it changes what every virtual address means. Allowing that at ring 3 would let a program view memory it was never given. The scheduler loads it for you during a context switch between processes.

questions.prompt: A page-table entry for a present page has its user/supervisor bit (bit 2) set to 0. A ring-3 instruction tries to read that page. What happens?
options: A page fault occurs, because the page is reserved for ring 0 even though it is present
The read succeeds, because a present page can be read by any code that knows its address
The processor sets the page's dirty bit and then lets the read finish normally
The kernel copies the page into the program's own memory so the read can finish
questions.explanation: Bit 2 equal to 0 on a present mapping means supervisor-only, so a ring-3 access causes a page fault. Being present only says the page is in memory; it does not say who may use it.

questions.prompt: On x86-64, the `syscall` instruction copies the address of the next instruction into `rcx`. Why does it do that?
options: So the kernel can return to the user program later, resuming right after the `syscall`
So the kernel can see which arguments the user program passed in its first register
So the processor knows which service number the program wants the kernel to run
So the kernel can check whether the call came from inside `ntdll.dll` before running it
questions.explanation: `syscall` saves the return address in `rcx` and the flags in `r11`; `sysret` later resumes there. The service number travels in `eax`, not `rcx`.

questions.prompt: When the processor executes `syscall`, where does it jump?
options: To an address held in a processor setting that only ring 0 can change, written by the kernel during boot
To the address in `rcx`, which the calling program loaded with the routine it wants to run
To the address given by the service number in `eax`, which the program picks from a public table
To the start of `ntdll.dll`, where the stub decides which kernel routine to enter
questions.explanation: The target comes from a processor setting the kernel wrote at boot with `wrmsr`. A program chooses when to request a service, never which kernel instruction runs. That is what makes the crossing controlled.

questions.prompt: In the `ntdll.dll` stub for `NtReadVirtualMemory`, what is the value placed in `eax` before `syscall` for?
options: It is a service number telling the kernel which of its routines to run
It is the number of bytes the program wants to copy out of the other process
It is the process ID of the game whose memory is being read
It is the privilege level the processor should switch to once the call starts
questions.explanation: The stub is only a few instructions: put the service number in `eax`, then `syscall`. The kernel uses it to pick the routine. The byte count and the target are ordinary arguments.

questions.prompt: A tool holds a handle with full rights to the game and calls `ReadProcessMemory` on an address in the kernel's half of the address space. Why does it fail?
options: The kernel checks that both address ranges lie in user space, whatever rights the handle carries
The handle's rights do not include `PROCESS_VM_READ` for addresses above the halfway point
The user/supervisor bit stops the kernel's own copy, because the copy runs at ring 3
The game process has no page tables for the kernel half, so the copy cannot find the pages
questions.explanation: The kernel validates both ranges itself before copying; that check is why `ReadProcessMemory` cannot read kernel memory with any handle. The copy runs in ring 0, so the supervisor bit would not stop it.

questions.prompt: A handle was opened with only query and read rights. The tool calls `WriteProcessMemory` on it. What does the kernel do, and can the tool fix it afterward?
options: It denies the write at the rights check, and no later call can add rights to the existing handle
It allows the write once, then drops the handle's read right for being used in an unexpected way
It denies the write for now, but running the tool as administrator adds the missing right to the handle
It allows the write, because query and read rights together imply permission to change memory
questions.explanation: A write needs `PROCESS_VM_WRITE`, which this handle lacks. Rights are fixed when the handle is opened. Administrator status can affect what `OpenProcess` grants for a new handle, not what an old one holds.

questions.prompt: Which instruction reverses `syscall`, dropping the level back to ring 3 and resuming the thread after its `syscall`?
options: `sysret`, with the status already placed in `eax`
`iretq`, with the status pushed on the user stack
`hlt`, which waits until the next interrupt returns control
`int3`, which raises vector 3 and hands control back
questions.explanation: The kernel puts its status code in `eax` and runs `sysret`, which returns to ring 3 at the saved address. `int3` is the breakpoint exception and `hlt` stops the processor until an interrupt.

questions.prompt: A tool's `ReadProcessMemory` fails and `GetLastError` reports 5. What most likely happened underneath?
options: The kernel returned an access-denied status, and `kernelbase.dll` turned it into error 5
The kernel returned `STATUS_SUCCESS`, which is 0, and `kernelbase.dll` added 5 to it
The processor raised a page fault inside the tool, which the kernel reported as error 5
The `ntdll.dll` stub put the wrong service number in `eax`, which the kernel reports as 5
questions.explanation: On failure the kernel returns a status and `kernelbase.dll` converts it to the number `GetLastError` reports, such as 5 for access denied. A page fault in the tool would be an access-violation exception, not an error code.

questions.prompt: A game is running when the player presses a key. Which way does execution reach the kernel's key-handling code?
options: An interrupt from the device arrives between two of the game's instructions
A `syscall` that the game must execute first before the key press is noticed
An exception raised by the game's own instruction, such as a page fault
The kernel polls the keyboard by running its own loop in the middle of the game's code
questions.explanation: The three ways into the kernel are system calls, exceptions raised by the running instruction, and interrupts that arrive between instructions whether or not the program expects them. A key press is a device interrupt.

questions.prompt: The interrupt descriptor table is indexed by a one-byte vector number. How many entries can it have at most, and what is vector 14?
options: 256 entries, numbered 0 to 255; vector 14 is the page fault
128 entries, numbered 0 to 127; vector 14 is the page fault
256 entries, numbered 0 to 255; vector 14 is the breakpoint
65,536 entries, numbered 0 to 65,535; vector 14 is the page fault
questions.explanation: One byte holds 2⁸ = 256 values. The processor fixes vectors 0 to 31: 3 is the breakpoint (`int3`), 13 the general-protection fault, 14 the page fault. Devices get vectors from 32 up.

questions.prompt: What does the kernel do during a context switch to a thread of a different process?
options: Saves the old thread's registers, loads the new thread's, and puts the new process's page-table address in `cr3`
Copies the old process's memory out to disk, then reads the new process's memory back into the same pages
Saves only the old thread's `rip`, because the other registers are rebuilt when the new thread starts
Pauses every other thread on all cores while the new process's page tables are written out from scratch
questions.explanation: A context switch saves the old registers, loads the new ones, and, if the process differs, loads its top-level page-table address into `cr3`. The program never sees the switch because its registers come back exactly as they were.

questions.prompt: After a page is committed, Windows may assign its physical frame only on first access. Why does the kernel hand the game a zeroed page then?
options: So old data from another process cannot leak into the new page
So the first read always returns a recognizable pattern that the game can test for
So the page fault finishes faster than if the kernel copied real data
So the game's variables start at the default values written in its executable file
questions.explanation: The first access faults, and the kernel supplies a zeroed page, updates the mapping, and retries the instruction. Zeroing prevents data left in a reused frame from showing up in another process.

questions.prompt: Why must interrupt handlers be short?
options: Other work on that core waits while they run, so long handlers delay everything
The processor ends any handler that runs for longer than one timer tick
Interrupt vectors are only 32 bytes apart, so handler code cannot be longer
A handler's registers are kept only in a small buffer that overflows if it runs too long
questions.explanation: While a handler runs, other work on that core waits. Lesson 12.4 shows how drivers split the work so the urgent part stays brief. There is no hard time cut-off that ends handlers.

questions.prompt: A game follows a bad pointer in user mode. What is the normal outcome?
options: The kernel handles the page fault and raises an access violation for that one process; everything else keeps running
The kernel stops the whole computer with a bug check, since a bad address cannot be told apart from kernel damage
The processor silently fixes the pointer by mapping a zeroed page, and the game carries on unaware
The kernel ends every process that shares a module with the game, because they might hold the same pointer
questions.explanation: At ring 3 the kernel checks its records, finds nothing valid at that address, and turns the fault into an access-violation exception for that process. The program's handler, a debugger, or Windows Error Reporting deals with it; at worst that one process ends.

questions.prompt: Why does Windows stop the whole machine on an unexpected fault inside kernel code, rather than just ending the offender?
options: Kernel code and drivers share data structures, and a fault mid-update leaves records Windows cannot trust
The kernel cannot tell which process was running when the fault struck, so it has no single process to end and must stop everything
Ending a driver would require restarting the hypervisor, and that takes the whole machine down anyway
Windows cannot write a crash dump unless the whole system stops completely first
questions.explanation: Kernel state such as scheduler lists, page records, and locks is shared, and a fault may leave one half updated with a lock held. Windows cannot generally prove what is still sound, and carrying on could write corrupted data to disk.

questions.prompt: A machine shows a blue screen with stop code `0xD1` DRIVER_IRQL_NOT_LESS_OR_EQUAL. What is that screen?
options: A bug check: a deliberate stop with a stop code, a crash dump if possible, and a restart
An access violation in one process, which Windows Error Reporting shows on a full screen
A system call that returned an error status, which the kernel prints before it returns
A debugger breakpoint in the kernel, which waits until a developer chooses to resume the machine
questions.explanation: A bug check, better known as the blue screen, is a deliberate stop after an unrecoverable kernel failure. It differs from an access violation, which ends only one process.

questions.prompt: How can a kernel-mode anti-cheat make a tool's `ReadProcessMemory` on the game fail, even though the tool asked for read rights?
options: A handle-operation callback can strip rights, so the handle lacks `PROCESS_VM_READ` and the rights check fails
It edits the tool's page tables so the game's addresses point at zeroed pages in the tool's own view of memory
It rewrites the service number in `ntdll.dll` so the tool's calls reach a different kernel routine instead
It lowers the tool's privilege to ring 4, below user mode, where all memory reads are refused outright
questions.explanation: Handle-operation callbacks run while a process opens a handle to the game and may remove rights. The tool then gets a handle without read rights, and its read fails at the rights check. There is no ring 4.

questions.prompt: What is a real cost of putting anti-cheat code in the kernel?
options: Its bugs become bug checks on players' machines, and a flaw in it exposes every installed machine
It makes the game slower only while the player is not in a match, so the cost is easy to avoid entirely
It cannot see process creation, because only user-mode code receives such notifications from Windows
It lets cheat tools run at ring 0 as well, because Windows lowers its checks for every signed driver
questions.explanation: Kernel code has the authority of the whole kernel, so its mistakes are bug checks and its vulnerabilities spread widely. It also asks players to trust a company with ring-0 code. Process notifications are in fact one of the things it gains.

questions.prompt: Why does this book keep its labs in user mode and inside a virtual machine?
options: A user-mode crash ends one process, and a bug check inside a virtual machine stops only that machine
User mode is the only mode in which a debugger is able to read the memory of another process
A virtual machine runs at ring 0, which makes every instruction in the lab run noticeably faster
Windows refuses to write crash dumps for any programs that do not run inside a virtual machine
questions.explanation: Failures in user mode are contained to one process, and a bug check inside a VM stops only that VM. A debugger can attach in the way the book describes without needing a VM.

questions.prompt: A dump from a crashed game shows the failing thread. A teammate asks what happened ten seconds earlier. What can the dump tell you?
options: Little, because it records one instant; pair it with logs or an ETW trace when history matters
Everything, because a dump keeps a timeline of every call the process made before it was captured
The last ten seconds, because dumps always include a rolling buffer of recent events
Only the earlier module loads, since those are the one event type a minidump records over time
questions.explanation: A dump saves selected state at one capture moment, not a timeline. The history must come from logs or an event trace.

questions.prompt: A teammate wants to post a `.dmp` file in a public chat to ask for help. What is the right concern?
options: It may hold file paths, arguments, and stack data, so treat it as private diagnostic data
None, because a minidump is only a harmless text log of function names and module versions, with no values
It will be far too large to post, since every dump includes a full copy of the process's memory
It will not open on another machine, because dumps are valid only on the computer that captured them
questions.explanation: The word mini describes a selectable subset, not a harmless log. Paths, arguments, and stack data can be private. Dumps are also not full copies by default.

questions.prompt: A reader opens a dump and cannot find a particular heap object. What is the safest conclusion?
options: It may not have been captured, since the dump type decides which streams and pages are saved
The object never existed, because a dump lists every object that was alive at the capture time
The object was freed just before the capture, because dumps list every freed object by name too
The dump is corrupt, since a valid minidump must always contain the whole heap of the process
questions.explanation: A missing object or exception record can mean not captured, not never existed. The dump type chooses the optional streams.

questions.prompt: `MiniDumpWithThreadInfo` is `0x1000` and `MiniDumpWithUnloadedModules` is `0x20`. What does the lab's `dump_type` equal when they are combined with `MiniDumpNormal`?
options: `0x1000`, because `MiniDumpNormal` clears the other bits
questions.explanation: `0x1000` is 2¹², `0x20` is 2⁵, and `MiniDumpNormal` is 0, so `|` sets both bits: 4,096 + 32 = 4,128 = `0x1020`. `|` adds bits; it does not clear them.

questions.prompt: In the lab's `dump_type`, what does `MiniDumpNormal` contribute to the value?
options: Nothing: it is 0, sets no bit, and names the baseline dump
Bit 0, because the first flag in the list always takes the lowest bit
Bit 12, because the baseline dump is built on the thread information stream
Bit 1, since the baseline dump asks for full memory and the other flags trim it
questions.explanation: `MiniDumpNormal` is 0, so OR-ing it in changes nothing. The other two flags are the bits that add streams.

questions.prompt: `MiniDumpWithFullMemory` is `0x2`, bit 1. Why does the lab leave it clear?
options: A normal dump with thread info is enough; full memory would copy every private page
Full memory is valid only for dumping another process, and this lab dumps itself instead
Full memory makes the file smaller, which would hide the stack the lesson wants the reader to see
Bit 1 is reserved by Windows for its own use, so the lab cannot set it from Rust
questions.explanation: The lab only needs the workflow, so it avoids copying every private page in the process. Nothing stops the flag from working on the current process.

questions.prompt: Why does the course's dumper call `GetCurrentProcess` and `GetCurrentProcessId`?
options: So it can dump only itself, never searching for a game PID or opening another handle
So the dump can include the game's memory without needing a handle that has read rights
So the file handle it writes to is shared with the running game for the length of the call
So Windows treats the dump as a crash and records an exception record inside it
questions.explanation: Scoping the lab to the current process keeps it from touching any other process. No game handle is requested.

questions.prompt: What does `create_new(true)` do in the self-dump lab's file open?
options: Makes a repeat run fail safely instead of overwriting the first capture
Creates a fresh handle each time, which lets several dumps share one file
Makes the dump file smaller by skipping streams that were already saved
Lets the dumper write to a file owned by another process without asking
questions.explanation: `create_new(true)` fails if the file already exists, so an earlier capture is never replaced by accident. It has no effect on dump size or file ownership.

questions.prompt: In the lab, why does `drop(file)` come after the `MiniDumpWriteDump` call?
options: The `File` owns the handle; closing it earlier leaves `file_handle` stale
`MiniDumpWriteDump` closes the file itself, so `drop` only waits until that closing is done
The dump is buffered in `file`, and `drop` is what flushes that buffer out to disk first
`drop` releases the process handle, which the call needs only after the dump is finished
questions.explanation: `AsRawHandle` only borrows the number. The `File` must stay alive until the Windows call returns, so the drop belongs after it.

questions.prompt: In WinDbg, which command lists loaded modules and their address ranges?
options: `lm`
`!analyze -v`
questions.explanation: `lm` lists modules, `~` lists threads, `~* k` shows every thread's stack, `r` shows the registers, and `!analyze -v` summarizes an exception if the dump has one.

questions.prompt: The self-dump is captured during a normal function call, not a crash. Why is that useful for learning?
options: You can practice module, thread, register, and stack navigation without any undefined behavior
`!analyze -v` can only run on dumps that were written by a healthy, non-crashing process
WinDbg refuses to open any dump that holds a real exception record from a crash
A dump from a crash is always smaller, so it gives the learner less to practice on
questions.explanation: With no crash exception in the file, `!analyze -v` has nothing to summarize, but the navigation commands all work. No crash is needed to learn them.

questions.prompt: A `k` listing for the self-dump thread shows `MiniDumpWriteDump` on top and Windows thread start-up at the bottom. What does the top frame show?
options: Where the thread was when captured, with callers below it
The function that started the thread, with later calls listed beneath it
The most recent module to load, with older modules listed beneath it
The function that crashed, with unrelated threads listed beneath it
questions.explanation: The top frame is the thread's position at capture; frames below are its callers. Reading from the bottom up replays the calls in order.

questions.prompt: With no symbols, WinDbg shows `self_minidump+0x1234`. What does that name?
options: The byte `0x1234` past the start of `self_minidump.exe` as loaded, in one exact build
A function called `0x1234`, which is a name that the module's symbol table always provides
The value `0x1234` stored in the module's version field at the time that it was built
The thread number `0x1234` that was running when the dump file was captured
questions.explanation: It is a module name plus an offset from where the module loaded. Paired with the exact build hash and module base, it picks out one specific instruction.

questions.prompt: A reader wants a crash dump to practice on. What does the lesson suggest?
options: Write a tiny separate program that crashes on purpose, with local dumps enabled in a disposable VM
Corrupt a running game's memory with a tool, since the crash will be caught and recorded
Run the game with `MiniDumpWithFullMemory` enabled so that it produces a dump at start-up
Attach a live debugger to a system process, then let it fault deliberately inside the kernel
questions.explanation: Do not corrupt a running game's memory just to obtain a dump. Use your own test program in a VM.

questions.prompt: A Rust program built with the default settings panics with a message and exits with code 101. Why is there no dump from Windows Error Reporting?
options: The default panic is caught by the runtime and ends as an ordinary exit; nothing crashed
Windows Error Reporting only watches programs that return an error from `main` with code 1
Exit code 101 is reserved for programs that ran out of memory, so no dump is ever allowed
The panic message goes to the console instead, and the console process blocks dump capture
questions.explanation: Returning an error from `main` exits with code 1 and a default panic exits with 101; both are ordinary exits, so there is nothing to dump.

questions.prompt: A program built with `panic = "abort"` panics. How does that differ from the default?
options: It ends in a fail-fast exception, code `0xC0000409`, which Windows Error Reporting captures
It exits with code 101 like a normal panic, but the message is hidden from the console
It raises an access violation, and `!analyze` always reports it as an access violation
It still exits cleanly, but the runtime writes a dump file of its own just beforehand
questions.explanation: A panic that aborts ends in a fail-fast exception, which Windows Error Reporting does capture. `!analyze` reports that exception rather than an access violation.

questions.prompt: Why can a dump help with a crash that disappears when a debugger is attached?
options: It saves state close to the failure without a debugger attached, so timing is left alone
It lets the process keep running while the debugger sets a breakpoint on the failing line
It replays the crash from the beginning, so the debugger sees the same timing as before
It forces the crash to happen again whenever the dump file is opened in WinDbg
questions.explanation: Attaching a debugger can change timing and hide a reproducible crash. A dump saved near the failure keeps the state with no debugger. A dump does not replay events.

questions.prompt: A game folder contains `<Game>_Data/Managed/Assembly-CSharp.dll`. What is the very likely runtime?
options: Unity using the Mono backend
Unity using the IL2CPP backend
Unreal Engine with a shipping build
Godot with a packaged `.pck` file
questions.explanation: That managed assembly is the Mono-backend clue. IL2CPP builds ship `GameAssembly.dll` instead, because their C# was compiled ahead of time.

questions.prompt: Which pair of files suggests a Unity game built with IL2CPP?
options: `GameAssembly.dll` and `il2cpp_data/Metadata/global-metadata.dat`
`Assembly-CSharp.dll` and `_Data/Managed/UnityEngine.dll` files
`coreclr.dll` and a `.runtimeconfig.json` file in the folder
`jvm.dll` and a `.jar` file placed beside the executable
questions.explanation: IL2CPP turns the C# into C++ and compiles it into `GameAssembly.dll`, with metadata kept in `global-metadata.dat`. The other pairs point to Mono, .NET, and Java.

questions.prompt: A large `.pck` file sits beside a small executable. How should you treat that clue?
options: A starting hypothesis for Godot, checked against loaded modules and a behavior
As proof of Godot, because no other engine ever ships a package with that extension
As proof of purely native code, because packages cannot hold script files
As a sign the game runs on the JVM, because packages are the Java equivalent of a jar
questions.explanation: Folder clues start the investigation but a game can add native extensions or use another arrangement. Verify with the loaded-module inventory before deciding.

questions.prompt: Why confirm a folder-based guess against the process's loaded-module list?
options: The folder shows what is installed; the module list shows what the running process mapped
The module list is generated before launch, so it matches the folder in every case
The folder lists files ending in `.dll`, which hides any executable beside them
The loaded modules appear for native games, so they separate native from managed
questions.explanation: A launcher can start a different executable than the one you inspected. The module list reflects the real process, not the install directory.

questions.prompt: What changes for a Unity Mono build compared with a native one?
options: A decompiler shows near-original C#, like a `health` field and the `TakeDamage` that writes it
The code is encrypted at rest, so the sole evidence is offsets found by scanning memory
The collector moves objects so often that field names can be read after a pause
The assemblies hold plain C++ source files, so no decompiler step is needed
questions.explanation: `Assembly-CSharp.dll` holds intermediate language that keeps class, method, and field names. The Chapter 3 recovery skills become confirmation rather than discovery.

questions.prompt: Why can you not simply open a decompiler on `Assembly-CSharp.dll` for an IL2CPP game?
options: That DLL is absent; the C# became C++ and ships as native code in `GameAssembly.dll`
That DLL exists but is split into pieces that the Unity editor can reassemble
That DLL is replaced by a `.jar` file that must be opened with a Java decompiler
That DLL is present but its metadata is stripped, leaving zero-filled data
questions.explanation: IL2CPP compiles the logic ahead of time, so at first glance you are reading disassembly again. Metadata may still help with names and types.

questions.prompt: How far can you trust names found in `global-metadata.dat`?
options: They can help, but stripping may remove some, so check them against native code
Every original class, method, and field name survives, so they are a full source of truth
None of them can be used, because the file stores image compression settings
They are exact for the current build and for each later build of the same game
