They would raise the process's integrity level, which the labs deliberately keep fixed at one value
They only work on 64-bit games, so the 32-bit lab games could not show the effect at all
questions.explanation: The course observes and baselines modules; it does not alter loader state, which other tools read too.

questions.prompt: What is the loader lock for, and when does Windows call `DllMain` relative to it?
options: It stops other threads from seeing a half-initialized module, and `DllMain` runs while it is held
It stops two games from loading the same DLL at once, and `DllMain` runs after it is released
It guards each module's exports from being patched, and `DllMain` runs before it is taken
It protects the game's own locks from deadlock, and `DllMain` runs only when no thread holds it
questions.explanation: Windows serializes important parts of loading with a process-wide lock so no thread observes a half-initialized module. `DllMain` is called while that lock is held.

questions.prompt: Which list best describes what the loader does while loading a DLL?
options: Maps sections, applies relocations, resolves imports, sets up TLS, updates bookkeeping, calls entry points
Copies the file into the game's folder, signs it, resolves imports, then asks the game to call its entry
Reads the export table, deletes the relocation data, hands the module to the kernel, and waits for a reply
Maps the first page only, resolves imports lazily at each call, and never runs an initialization entry point
questions.explanation: Loading is a coordinated operation, not a byte copy. Initialization entry points such as `DllMain` are part of it.

questions.prompt: Which `DllMain` reason announces that a new thread has started in the process?
options: `DLL_THREAD_ATTACH`
`DLL_PROCESS_ATTACH`
`DLL_THREAD_DETACH`
`DLL_PROCESS_DETACH`
questions.explanation: `DLL_PROCESS_ATTACH` is for the DLL joining the process, `DLL_THREAD_ATTACH` for each new thread, and the two detach reasons for a thread ending or the DLL or process unloading.

questions.prompt: On whose thread does `DllMain` run when a DLL is loaded with `LoadLibrary`?
options: The thread that caused the load, with notifications serialized
A new thread created by the loader for each notification, running in parallel
The game's main thread, always, even when a different thread was the one that called `LoadLibrary`
A system thread in the kernel, which then returns to the caller's thread
questions.explanation: The code runs in the context of whichever thread caused the load or unload. These are loader notifications, not general application events.

questions.prompt: Thread A holds `game_lock` and wants the loader lock; Thread B holds the loader lock inside `DllMain` and wants `game_lock`. What happens?
options: Neither can continue, since each waits for a lock the other holds; no timeout makes that ordering correct
Thread B wins because it holds the loader lock, and Thread A gets an error code after a short delay
The loader lock is released automatically after a few seconds, so Thread A eventually continues on
Windows picks the thread with the lower ID and lets it take both locks at once, so both continue
questions.explanation: A deadlock needs a cycle of waits. Remove the wait from the loader callback or follow one global lock order; a timeout only hides it.

questions.prompt: A `DllMain` calls `CreateThread` and then `WaitForSingleObject` on that thread. Why does it hang?
options: The new thread must run `DLL_THREAD_ATTACH` first, which needs the loader lock `DllMain` holds
The new thread starts at once but crashes, and `WaitForSingleObject` cannot wait on a crashed thread at all
`CreateThread` fails inside `DllMain`, so the wait is then made on a handle that is invalid for the call
The loader suspends every new thread until the whole process has fully exited its start-up phase
questions.explanation: `D` holds the loader lock and waits for `T`; `T` needs the same lock to start. The cycle is the hidden second lock.

questions.prompt: In that deadlock, `CreateThread` returned success. What does the new thread get to run before the hang?
options: Not a single line of the reader's code, because it blocks before reaching it
Its start function, which then hangs on its first lock inside the game's own code
The first part of its start function, up to the first call into another DLL
Its start function in full, which hangs only when it exits and detaches
questions.explanation: The thread exists, but the loader makes it run `DLL_THREAD_ATTACH` notifications first, which need the lock. So the wait never finishes and nothing looks wrong at the creation call.

questions.prompt: Which work is acceptable inside the course DLL's `DllMain`?
options: Calling `DisableThreadLibraryCalls` on attach, which only turns off notifications and never waits
Loading a helper DLL with `LoadLibraryW`, since the loader is already running and can finish that load
Initializing COM, so later worker threads can use it without waiting on any lock held by the game
Parsing the configuration file, since it is small and does not touch any of the game's own locks
questions.explanation: The course entry point stays tiny. Loading DLLs, initializing COM, parsing configuration, scanning memory, and installing hooks all belong in later stages.

questions.prompt: What does `DisableThreadLibraryCalls` do in the course DLL?
options: It turns off per-thread attach and detach notifications that the library does not use
It stops the DLL from creating threads of its own while the loader lock is held
It blocks other DLLs from calling the course DLL's exports until `gha_start` has run
It releases the loader lock early, so the rest of start-up can run without it
questions.explanation: It is a documented optimization during process attach: no allocation, waiting, or scanning. It does not release any lock.

questions.prompt: Why does the course DLL do its real start-up in the exported `gha_start` rather than in `DllMain`?
options: The injector calls it only after `LoadLibraryW` has finished, so the work runs outside the loader lock
`DllMain` can run only once per process, so a second function is needed for each later load of the DLL
`gha_start` runs at a higher privilege level than `DllMain`, which lets it install the hooks safely
Exported functions are loaded before `DllMain`, so they can set things up in the right order first
questions.explanation: The injector waits for `LoadLibraryW` to return, then calls `gha_start`. Complex work then begins on an ordinary worker thread, with the failure of each stage visible on its own.

questions.prompt: A second injector call reaches `gha_start` while the first worker is running. What happens?
options: The `OnceLock` is already set, so it returns 1 and no second worker is created
It starts a second worker that shares the first one's hooks, which is the intended design
It returns 0 and silently restarts the worker, so every patch is applied again
It returns 2, since a second thread can never be created for the same DLL
questions.explanation: `OnceLock` prevents duplicate startup; a second worker would race over the same hooks and cleanup state. Return 1 means already running, 2 means the thread could not start.

questions.prompt: Why does `gha_stop` only set a flag and return, instead of waiting for the worker to finish?
options: Waiting there could recreate the loader-lock deadlock; the worker restores patches at its next checkpoint
The worker thread cannot be stopped by a flag, so `gha_stop` has to terminate it from the outside instead
A flag is faster than a wait, and speed matters because hooks run once per frame in the game loop
`WaitForSingleObject` is not available inside exported functions of a DLL that was loaded by an injector
questions.explanation: A request-only stop keeps waiting out of loader callbacks. The worker owns restoration and drops owned patches so original bytes come back.

questions.prompt: Shutdown should reverse ownership. Which order does the lesson give?
options: Reject new work, request worker stop, join outside the loader lock, restore patches, release resources, allow unload
Release resources, restore patches, join inside the loader lock, request worker stop, then reject new work
Allow unload, request worker stop, release resources, restore patches, then join the worker
Restore patches, allow unload, reject new work, join inside the loader lock, then release resources
questions.explanation: Ownership order matters: stop new work first, join without the loader lock, restore patches before releasing resources, and only then allow unload.

questions.prompt: A tool with a lock-order bug passes ten test runs. What does that prove?
options: Very little, because deadlocks depend on timing and may need an unlucky ordering to appear
The lock order is correct, since ten clean runs on one machine rule out a cycle of waits
The bug is limited to 32-bit builds, since a 64-bit run would have shown it already
The loader lock is released early on that machine, so the bug cannot occur anywhere else
questions.explanation: “It worked on my machine” does not prove the ordering is safe. Write the lock edges down and check for cycles instead.

questions.prompt: A game hangs while loading the DLL. A teammate suggests adding a ten-second timeout to the wait. What is the better first step?
options: Inspect lock order and the work in entry points, since a timeout hides a deadlock instead of repairing it
Raise the timeout to a full minute, since the hang is just slow disk access and will end by itself
Retry the load in a loop until it works, since the deadlock depends on timing and may not recur
Move the wait into `DLL_THREAD_ATTACH`, which runs after the loader lock has already been released
questions.explanation: A timeout leaves the wait cycle in place. Remove the wait from the loader callback or establish one global lock order.

questions.prompt: Which step is part of the lesson's lifecycle test for each DLL profile?
options: Verify `gha_start` returns zero, then stop and confirm patches restore and input is released
Skip `gha_stop` so patches stay in place, then close the game without restoring them
Call `gha_start` twice in a row and check that both calls return zero
Inject the 64-bit build into the 32-bit game to see which stage fails first
questions.explanation: The test injects the exact 32-bit build, checks `gha_start` returns 0, enables a feature, stops, confirms restoration, closes the game, and repeats to catch one-run assumptions.

questions.prompt: Verification of the target fails before any patch is installed, and the DLL starts cleanup. What should cleanup do?
options: Skip restoring the patch, since nothing was installed and the lifecycle makes that state visible
Restore the patch's original bytes anyway, to be safe, even though nothing was ever written there
Wait for the loader lock and then retry the verification, since the failure is probably just timing
Call `gha_start` again, so the lifecycle begins from the first step and every patch is rechecked
questions.explanation: An explicit lifecycle makes partially initialized states visible. Cleanup should not pretend a patch exists when it was never installed.

questions.prompt: In the startup order the lesson draws, which step comes right after the DLL is mapped?
options: Finish the loader notifications, and only then call the explicit start
Create the worker resources, so the target can be verified from inside the worker
Verify the target first, so the loader notifications know which hooks to install
Install the owned features straight away, since the loader finishes them in the background
questions.explanation: The arrows are dependency claims: a step may begin only after the one above has completed. Map, finish loader notifications, call explicit start, verify target, create resources, install features.

questions.prompt: Which sequence matches the lesson's four steps for dynamic API resolution?
options: Get a handle to the system DLL, look up the export, convert to one proven pointer type, then call or fall back
Look up the export, patch the import table, call the function by its ordinal, then restore the original table
Load every system DLL, scan memory for the function's bytes, call the first match, then check the result
Read the Windows version, pick the matching function by name, call it directly, then discard the pointer
questions.explanation: Dynamic resolution turns an optional API into a checked capability. Nothing is patched or scanned for.

questions.prompt: Why should a tool not decide that an API exists just because the Windows version string is new enough?
options: Compatibility settings, servicing changes, and alternative implementations can make version checks lie
Version strings are stored in the PE header and are changed whenever a DLL is loaded dynamically at run time
Version strings only describe the 64-bit kernel, so a 32-bit tool cannot learn anything useful from them
Windows publishes the version string only after the export has been resolved, so it cannot guide the lookup
questions.explanation: Look up the documented export, validate the result, and take the fallback when it is absent.

questions.prompt: `QueryFullProcessImageNameW` resolves successfully. Does that guarantee a later call will succeed?
options: No: the handle may lack rights, the buffer may be too small, or the target may exit
Yes, since a resolved export is proof that every call to it will work for the same process
Yes, as long as the buffer is at least 260 units long and the flags argument is zero
No, but only on 64-bit builds, where the resolver cannot check the signature
questions.explanation: Feature detection chooses a code path; normal error handling still applies inside that path.

questions.prompt: On 32-bit x86, `extern "system"` means stdcall. Who removes the arguments from the stack afterward?
options: The function itself, using a `ret` that also pops the arguments off the stack
The caller, using an `add esp` instruction right after the call returns to it
The loader, once the module is unloaded and its stack frames are discarded
The kernel, at the next system call that the thread makes after it returns
questions.explanation: In stdcall the caller pushes arguments from last to first and the function removes them before returning. For four 4-byte arguments that is `ret 0x10`.

questions.prompt: In 32-bit stdcall, `QueryFullProcessImageNameW` begins with `[esp]` holding the return address. Where is its fourth argument, `size`?
options: `[esp+0x10]`, since each argument slot is 4 bytes and the arguments start at `+0x04`
`[esp+0x0C]`, since the first argument sits at `[esp]` and each slot is 4 bytes
`[esp+0x20]`, since each argument slot is 8 bytes on a 32-bit stack
`[esp+0x04]`, since the arguments are pushed first to last and the last sits next to the return address
questions.explanation: The return address occupies `[esp]`; `process` is at `+0x04`, `flags` at `+0x08`, `name` at `+0x0C` (12), and `size` at `+0x10` (16).

questions.prompt: On x86-64 Windows, where does the function expect its fourth argument, `size`, and where does the `BOOL` result come back?
options: `size` in `R9`, with the result in `EAX`
`size` in `RDX`, with the result in `RCX`
`size` on the stack at `[rsp+0x20]`, with the result in `R10`
`size` in `R8`, with the result in `RAX` as a full 64-bit value
questions.explanation: The first four integer or pointer arguments go in `RCX`, `RDX`, `R8`, `R9`; the result returns in `EAX`, which is enough for a 32-bit `BOOL`.

questions.prompt: A 32-bit caller uses a type alias with only three parameters for a function that really takes four and ends with `ret 0x10`. What goes wrong?
options: The caller pushes 12 bytes but the function removes 16, leaving the stack pointer 4 bytes off
The caller pushes 16 bytes but the function removes 12, leaving the stack pointer 4 bytes off
The caller pushes 12 bytes and the function removes 12, so nothing goes wrong
The function reads a fourth argument from `R9`, which holds whatever it held before
questions.explanation: The mismatch of 16 − 12 = 4 bytes shifts the stack pointer from where the caller expects it. The `R9` problem happens on x86-64, not on 32-bit x86.

questions.prompt: On x86-64, the same wrong three-parameter alias is used. What goes wrong?
options: It still reads a fourth argument from `R9`, whatever it holds, and writes the length through that pointer
The function removes 16 bytes from the stack, which leaves the stack pointer 4 bytes off after the call
The loader refuses to call a function whose alias has fewer parameters than the export it was built for
The function puts the result in `EAX`, but the caller reads it back from `RCX` and sees another value
questions.explanation: Registers are not cleared between calls, so the function writes through whatever `R9` contained. A close-enough signature fails regardless of pointer size.

questions.prompt: `GetProcAddress` returns no address for an export. How should the resolver treat that?
options: As a supported compatibility state, returned as `None` so the caller chooses a fallback
As a fatal error, since a missing export means the Windows installation is broken
As a reason to guess a similar name, since exports are often renamed between versions
As a cue to resolve the name from a second DLL and call whatever address comes back
questions.explanation: “Export absent” is a supported state, not necessarily fatal. The `Option` is intentional so the caller handles the missing case.

questions.prompt: A plug-in resolver caches a function pointer from a module that can later unload. What is the risk?
options: The address becomes invalid once the module unloads, so keep module ownership and pointer lifetime together
The pointer is valid only until the next `GetProcAddress` call, which overwrites the previously stored address
The cached pointer is read-only, so a later call from another thread will write through it and fault at once
The module's exports are renumbered at unload, so the pointer calls the wrong function when it loads again
questions.explanation: System modules used for the whole process lifetime are simpler. A module that can unload leaves the cached address dangling.

questions.prompt: The lab passes `length` = 32,768 into the call, and the process path is a 35-character string. What is `length` after a successful call?
options: 35, the number of UTF-16 units written, not counting the terminator
36, the number of units written including the NUL terminator
32,768, since the call leaves the buffer size in `length`
34, since the call counts from the last index of the buffer's text
questions.explanation: Going in, `length` is the buffer size; coming back it is the units written without the terminator, so `buffer[..35]` is exactly the path.

questions.prompt: The lab's buffer is `vec![0_u16; 32_768]`. Why that number?
options: It is 2¹⁵, room for the longest extended-length path, 32,767 characters, plus a terminator
It is 2¹⁶, double the longest possible path, so a path can never need a second call to the API
It is 260, the classic maximum path length, rounded up to the next power of two for the allocator
It is the number of bytes in a 4 KiB page times 8, which matches the size the allocator hands out
questions.explanation: 32,768 = 2¹⁵ = 32,767 + 1. The count is units, not bytes, so it is 65,536 bytes in memory.

questions.prompt: Why does the lab check `used <= buffer.len()` before slicing?
options: Slicing past the end would panic, so a returned length larger than the buffer is rejected first
The API always returns `used` as zero unless this check has been run on the buffer beforehand
The check removes the terminator from the buffer before the string is built from the units
`String::from_utf16_lossy` only accepts a slice that fills the whole buffer from start to end
questions.explanation: The length is untrusted after every call. An invalid length is an error, not a slice.

questions.prompt: The export is present but the call fails because the handle lacks rights. What should the code do?
options: Handle the call error, because a failed call does not automatically choose the fallback
Take the fallback anyway, since a failed call proves the API is not really available
Resolve the export again under another name, since the first lookup was wrong
Panic at once, since a failed call means the function pointer type is wrong
questions.explanation: The API can exist while the handle, buffer, or target state is invalid. Keeping those cases apart stops compatibility logic from hiding an ordinary error.

questions.prompt: The ToolHelp fallback supplies the main module path through `szExePath`. How should it be presented?
options: As a different observation, labelled with its source and limits, since it can fail and go stale
As identical to the full-path API, since both return the same path text for any process in the system
As more reliable than the dynamic API, since a snapshot is taken in a single instant of time
As valid only for the game's own process, since ToolHelp cannot read any other process at all
questions.explanation: A fallback is not simply a shorter path. Enumeration can fail across architecture or protection boundaries, and a snapshot is a moment-in-time view.

questions.prompt: Which action does the lesson explicitly forbid?
options: Calling an unresolved address, or replacing `None` with address zero
Looking up an export from a module that is already loaded in the process
Testing the resolver with a deliberately misspelled export name
Comparing the result against an ordinary imported call
questions.explanation: Never call an unresolved address, never replace `None` with zero, and never pick a close-enough signature because pointer sizes match. The other three are the lesson's recommended tests.

questions.prompt: In a reversed game, a string names an API, `GetProcAddress` returns a pointer, and a later instruction calls through it. What is the benefit of spotting that chain?
options: It turns anonymous control flow into a documented contract with a known signature
It shows the game is hiding imports, which proves the code is malicious
It lets you skip reading the code, since the API name gives the whole behavior
It proves the pointer is safe to patch, since resolved addresses never change
questions.explanation: Dynamic resolution explains a common pattern. Reconstructing the chain links the indirect call to the documented API. It is not evidence of bad intent.

questions.prompt: Why does Windows not let two programs drive the same disk controller directly?
options: Devices hold shared state, so one program could overwrite another's command or aim a copy engine at it
Disk controllers run only in 16-bit mode, so a user-mode program cannot form the commands the hardware needs
Programs would be too slow at setting registers, so the controller would time out and lose the request
Each controller has a unique signature, and only the kernel is allowed to carry a certificate to use it
questions.explanation: If programs shared the controller, one could change the sector another had just chosen, or aim the copying engine at another process's memory. The operating system coordinates who may operate devices and which buffers they may reach.

questions.prompt: The I/O manager has checked that a caller's handle may write to a device. Why must the driver still validate the request?
options: A handle check does not prove the operation, lengths, and buffers inside the request are safe for the device
The handle check happens only for read requests, so every write arrives with no check of any kind
The I/O manager forgets the handle once it builds the IRP, so the driver has to look it up again
Handle rights apply only to user-mode drivers, so a kernel-mode driver must do all the checks itself
questions.explanation: The I/O manager checks the handle; the driver must still validate the operation, lengths, and buffers it uses. An access check does not prove the request's contents are safe.

questions.prompt: In a driver stack, which driver knows the device itself and does the real work?
options: The function driver
The bus driver
A filter driver
The I/O manager
questions.explanation: A bus driver talks to the bus (USB or PCI Express), the function driver knows the device and does the work, and optional filter drivers watch or adjust requests. The I/O manager is part of the kernel, not a driver in the stack.

questions.prompt: A program wants to send a numbered, device-specific command to a driver. How does it do that?
options: It opens the device like a file and calls `DeviceIoControl` with a control code and buffers
It calls a function inside the driver by address, since drivers export functions like DLLs do
It writes the command to the device's registers using an `out` instruction from user mode
It sends a window message to the driver, which reads it from the message queue
questions.explanation: The driver is in ring 0, so a program cannot call into it. It makes requests through a handle, using `ReadFile`, `WriteFile`, or `DeviceIoControl` for everything else.

questions.prompt: What is an I/O request packet (IRP)?
options: A kernel data structure serving as a request's work order, with its operation, buffers, and result
A hardware signal on the interrupt line that tells a device the next queued request is ready to start
A processor instruction that switches from user mode into the driver's dispatch routine for the call
A file on disk that stores each driver's list of supported control codes and the rights they require
questions.explanation: The I/O manager builds an IRP, which travels down the driver stack and comes back up carrying the result. It is a data structure, not a signal.

questions.prompt: A driver's dispatch routine receives a read IRP, but no key events are ready. What does it do?
options: Keeps the IRP, returns `STATUS_PENDING`, and completes it later from the interrupt-driven code
Completes the IRP at once with zero bytes, so the program can simply retry the read when it likes
Spins in the dispatch routine, reading STATUS repeatedly until an event finally arrives from the device
Hands the IRP back to the I/O manager to be rebuilt and re-sent when a key is pressed
questions.explanation: If the dispatch routine has to wait for the hardware, it parks the IRP and returns pending; the program's thread waits inside `ReadFile` until the DPC completes it.

questions.prompt: In what sense is a `DeviceIoControl` request checked twice?
options: The I/O manager checks the control code's rights against the handle; the driver distrusts the parameters
The I/O manager checks the buffer lengths, and then the driver checks the handle's rights again on arrival
The kernel checks the caller's signature, and then the driver checks the device's own signature as well
The driver checks the request once on arrival and again when the IRP is completed and handed back up
questions.explanation: Each control code declares required rights, and the I/O manager refuses a mismatching handle before the driver runs. The driver then compares the whole control code and keeps writes within the buffer.

questions.prompt: What does memory-mapped I/O mean for a driver?
options: The registers answer to physical addresses, which the driver maps and uses with ordinary loads and stores
The registers are copied into RAM once at boot, so the driver reads a stored snapshot of them instead
The driver reads registers with the `in` and `out` instructions, which use their own special port numbers
The registers are stored in the driver's `.sys` file and are loaded into memory together with its code
questions.explanation: Most modern devices expose registers as a range of physical addresses; the kernel maps it into kernel virtual addresses. Port I/O with `in` and `out` is the older mechanism.

questions.prompt: The toy keypad has four 4-byte registers in order: CONTROL, STATUS, DATA, ACK. Where does ACK sit, and how big is the block?
options: At `+0x0C`, in a block of 4 × 4 = 16 bytes
At `+0x0C`, in a block of 4 × 4 = 12 bytes
At `+0x10`, in a block of 4 × 4 = 16 bytes
At `+0x08`, in a block of 4 × 2 = 8 bytes
questions.explanation: Each register starts 4 bytes after the last: 0x00, 0x04, 0x08, 0x0C (12). Four of them fill 16 bytes.

questions.prompt: Why is reading the keypad's DATA register different from reading ordinary memory?
options: Reading it removes the event it returns, so the next read gives the next event
Reading it flips the device off, so the driver must write CONTROL again afterward
Reading it always returns the A key's scan code, `0x1E`, whatever key was pressed
Reading it is slower than ordinary memory but changes nothing inside the device
questions.explanation: DATA holds the front event; a read removes it. A tool that read DATA just to look would silently swallow a key press.

questions.prompt: STATUS can change between two consecutive reads with no instruction in between. Why does that matter for how reads are compiled and mapped?
options: The device changes it, so accesses must never be cached, merged, or skipped; the memory is uncacheable
Windows rewrites it between reads, so the driver must lock the page that holds the register in memory
The compiler may reorder reads freely, since the device checks the order of the values on its own side
It only changes when interrupts are off, so the driver turns them off around each of the register reads
questions.explanation: Register accesses are never cached, merged, or skipped. Drivers use dedicated read-register and write-register routines that the compiler must carry out exactly as written.

questions.prompt: Why does the keypad driver use interrupts rather than polling STATUS over and over?
options: Polling wastes a processor core on a device that sits idle almost all the time
Polling is not possible, since STATUS can be read only from inside an interrupt handler
Polling would let two programs read the same event, which the keypad does not allow
Polling needs port I/O, and the toy keypad has only memory-mapped registers
questions.explanation: An interrupt makes the processor stop between instructions and run the registered handler when the device has news.

questions.prompt: How is the work split between the ISR and the DPC for the toy keypad?
options: The ISR confirms the interrupt and writes ACK; the DPC drains events, fills the buffer, and completes the IRP
The ISR drains events and completes the IRP; the DPC runs later and does nothing except write to ACK
The ISR runs at low priority and does the real work; the DPC runs first and only queues up the ISR
Both run at the same priority at once, and each of them handles one half of the waiting key events
questions.explanation: The ISR runs immediately while other work waits, so it does the minimum. The DPC runs moments later at lower priority with interrupts enabled again.

questions.prompt: Why does the ISR read STATUS before doing anything else?
options: Several devices can share one interrupt line, so it must confirm its own device raised the interrupt
STATUS holds the IRP's buffer address, which the ISR needs before it can fill it
Reading STATUS turns the interrupt line off, so the ISR can safely enable interrupts again
STATUS tells the ISR which process owns the key press, so it can wake that process directly
questions.explanation: Because an interrupt line can be shared, the ISR reads STATUS to confirm the interrupt came from its device, then writes ACK so the device lowers the line.

questions.prompt: A user presses and releases A. How does the DPC complete the parked read?
options: It collects two events, A pressed and A released, and completes the IRP with 2 bytes
It collects one event, A pressed, and completes the IRP with 1 byte, leaving the release for the next read
It collects two events and completes the IRP with 8 bytes, the size of the program's buffer
It completes the IRP with zero bytes and lets the program read DATA itself
questions.explanation: The lesson's example: the DPC collects *A pressed* and *A released* and completes the read with those 2 bytes, even though the program's buffer was 8 bytes.

questions.prompt: Why do a disk or network card use DMA instead of register reads?
options: They move megabytes, and copying them by register reads would keep a core busy doing only that
They have no registers at all, so DMA is the only way that a driver can tell them what to do
DMA lets them skip the driver stack entirely, so the program talks to the hardware directly instead
DMA lets the device write to any virtual address in the program, so that no buffer has to be set up
questions.explanation: With DMA the driver gives the device a buffer's address and size; the device copies the data into or out of RAM and interrupts once when the transfer is done.

questions.prompt: What kind of address does a driver give a DMA device?
options: A physical address or, with an IOMMU, a device address that the IOMMU translates and limits
A virtual address from the process's page tables, which the device resolves on its own
A segment number, which the device combines with the process's `cs` value
A handle to the buffer, which the device exchanges for an address through the I/O manager
questions.explanation: A device has no access to any process's page tables. The IOMMU limits it to the buffers the driver approved.

questions.prompt: A USB host controller asks a keyboard for news 125 times a second. How often is the keyboard asked?
options: Every 1,000 ÷ 125 = 8 milliseconds
Every 125 ÷ 1,000 = 0.125 milliseconds
Every 125 × 8 = 1,000 milliseconds
Every 1,000 × 125 = 125,000 milliseconds
questions.explanation: A USB device never speaks first; the host asks on a schedule. Many gaming keyboards are asked every millisecond.

questions.prompt: Where in the key-press path does HID usage `0x04` become scan code `0x1E`, and what is the later virtual-key code on a US layout?
options: In `KBDHID.SYS`; the raw input thread then yields `VK_A`, `0x41`, which is 65
In `KBDCLASS.SYS`; the raw input thread then yields `VK_A`, `0x1E`, which is 30
In the game's message loop; `GetMessage` then yields `VK_A`, `0x41`, which is 64
In the host controller; the mapper driver then yields `VK_A`, `0x04`, which is 4
questions.explanation: The keyboard mapper driver `KBDHID.SYS` converts usage to scan code; the raw input thread uses the layout to produce the virtual-key code. `0x41` = 4 × 16 + 1 = 65, also the ASCII code of A.

questions.prompt: Synthetic input from `SendInput` enters the path at the raw input thread. What follows for tools that watch input?
options: Programs watching at that level can tell it from key presses that arrived through a keyboard driver
It looks identical to real key presses at every level of the path, so no tool can tell them apart
It enters below the keyboard drivers, so the drivers see it first and mark it before anything else
It skips the message queue and is delivered straight to the game's window procedure by the kernel
questions.explanation: `SendInput` joins above every driver in the diagram, so input observed at lower levels does not include it.

questions.prompt: A driver carries a valid digital signature. What does that tell you?
options: Who published it and whether it has changed since signing, but not whether its code is safe
That its code is safe, since Microsoft reads and tests every signed driver before signing
That it can never be on the vulnerable driver blocklist, since that list holds only unsigned code
That it runs at ring 3, since only user-mode drivers need signatures
questions.explanation: A signature answers who published it and whether it changed. A correctly signed driver can still expose a control code that reads or writes any memory.

questions.prompt: What is the vulnerable driver blocklist for?
options: It lists signed drivers known to be exploitable, which Windows refuses to load
It lists unsigned drivers that Windows allows for testing on disposable machines
It lists drivers that Secure Boot has already loaded, so they can be unloaded in order
It lists devices that cannot use DMA, so their drivers are loaded with the IOMMU off
questions.explanation: Attackers load old, legitimately signed drivers to borrow their bugs. The blocklist is Microsoft's answer; it is always enforced when memory integrity is on.

questions.prompt: A cheat seller says to turn off Secure Boot and memory integrity before loading their driver. What does that advice cost the user?
options: It lowers the machine's defense against all kernel malware, not only against cheats
It affects only the game, since those protections guard games and nothing else on the machine
It costs nothing once the cheat has loaded, since both features re-enable on the next restart
It lowers the defense only for 32-bit drivers, so 64-bit software stays protected as before
questions.explanation: Each of those protections protects the machine against all kernel malware. Turning one off lowers the defense for everything, and the driver's author is anonymous.

questions.prompt: The lesson says the key model is which invariants a component can break. What does that mean for a driver compared with a game tool?
options: Kernel code helps enforce the checks, so it can change mappings, device state, and security decisions system-wide
Kernel code is checked by the same page-table rules as a game, so it can break only its own invariants
User-mode code can change process state for every program on the machine, but kernel code can touch only devices
A driver breaks invariants only by crashing, since it cannot change anything while it is running correctly
questions.explanation: User-mode code is confined by page-table and privilege checks. Kernel-mode code participates in enforcing those checks.

questions.prompt: A user-mode program follows a bad pointer, and a driver follows a bad kernel pointer. How do the outcomes usually differ?
options: The user-mode crash normally ends one process; the kernel one can crash the computer or corrupt any process
Both end only the program that made the mistake, since Windows isolates each of them from the rest equally
The user-mode crash takes the computer down, while the kernel one is contained by the driver stack above it
Both end one process, but the driver's process always restarts itself automatically afterward in the kernel
questions.explanation: A bad kernel pointer can take the whole machine down, or corrupt data belonging to any process.

questions.prompt: A teammate says moving a tool into a driver makes it better engineering. What is the lesson's response?
options: More privilege enlarges both its authority and the damage a bug can cause; it is not better engineering
More privilege makes the tool more stable, since kernel code is protected from user-mode errors
More privilege only affects speed, since kernel code runs without the cost of system calls
More privilege is better only for games, since anti-cheat tools need it to see their own process
questions.explanation: Moving code into a driver enlarges authority and the damage of a bug alike.

questions.prompt: Why is the documented API boundary useful?
options: Callers get no kernel authority just by asking; the kernel checks the request and a sound driver checks again
Callers gain kernel authority for the length of each call, so they can then check the work for themselves
The kernel trusts the caller's handle completely, so the driver can skip any further checks of its own now
The boundary hides drivers from user mode, so callers never learn which drivers are loaded on the machine
questions.explanation: The kernel checks handles, rights, and buffers, and a sound driver checks again before touching device or privileged memory.

questions.prompt: Why do the course's offline lab games not need a driver?
options: They can be studied with documented Windows APIs, a debugger, a user-mode DLL, and reversible patches
Their code already runs in ring 0, so the course tools can reach it with ordinary calls and no driver at all
They are too old to load any drivers, so there is nothing that a driver could ever change inside them
Drivers cannot read the memory of 32-bit games, so a user-mode DLL is the only choice that is left to use
questions.explanation: The old open-source games in the book are offline processes, and the course avoids kernel-level capabilities.

questions.prompt: Which of these does the course deliberately not build?
options: Arbitrary kernel or physical-memory read/write commands
A read-only inventory of the drivers Windows has loaded
A user-mode DLL that is started in a separate, explicit second stage
A hash baseline of the modules a game has loaded
questions.explanation: The course avoids arbitrary kernel read/write, privilege escalation, security or anti-cheat bypasses, hidden drivers, and loaders for vulnerable drivers. The inventory is read-only and defensive.

questions.prompt: What design question does Microsoft's driver security guidance begin with?
options: Whether a kernel driver is actually required, since a service or application is the lower-risk boundary
Whether the driver can be signed by its developer, since unsigned drivers will not load on any Windows machine
Whether the driver can avoid using IOCTLs, since every IOCTL raises the privilege of the driver that serves it
Whether the driver supports 32-bit games, since most drivers for such games will have to run in ring 3 instead
questions.explanation: If a service or application can do the job, it is the lower-risk boundary.

questions.prompt: A driver is correctly signed. Why is that not enough to call it safe?
options: It may expose a badly protected command that lets another program read or write arbitrary privileged memory
Signed drivers are never checked at load time, so the signature only helps after a crash has already happened
The signature covers only the driver's file name, not its code, so changes to the code itself are missed
Signatures expire after a day, so every signed driver must be reloaded with a brand new signature each morning
questions.explanation: A signature says who published it and whether it changed; a signed driver can still be vulnerable.

questions.prompt: A new driver appears on a machine. Which order does the lesson give for looking into it?
options: Identify publisher and signature, compare hash with the baseline, check the block policy, find the installer
Delete it, compare the hash with the baseline, check the block policy, then ask who installed it on the machine
Check the block policy, unload the driver, identify the publisher, then update the baseline to include the new driver
Compare the file name with the baseline, restart the machine, then identify the signature of the driver it loaded
questions.explanation: Driver loading is a rare, high-impact event. Investigate the process and installer that introduced it.

questions.prompt: A teammate wants to load a suspicious driver on their daily computer to see what it does. What does the lesson advise?
options: Use an isolated, disposable virtual machine and vendor-provided analysis guidance instead
Load it on the daily computer, but only after turning off memory integrity to avoid conflicts
Load it with test-signing mode on, since that mode makes unknown drivers safe to inspect
Load it on a computer without a network, since the driver can only do harm over the internet
questions.explanation: Do not test a suspicious driver on a daily computer. A disposable VM contains the impact.

questions.prompt: Which Windows calls does the read-only driver inventory use to list loaded drivers?
options: `EnumDeviceDrivers` and `GetDeviceDriverBaseNameW`, with no API that changes anything
`LoadLibraryW` and `GetProcAddress`, with each driver loaded again to read its name
`DeviceIoControl` and `ReadFile`, with a handle opened to each driver's device object
`MiniDumpWriteDump` and `lm`, with a dump of the kernel and a list of its modules
questions.explanation: The inventory queries visible driver images and prints their base names. It enables no privileges and changes no driver state.

questions.prompt: The inventory starts with room for 256 pointers on a 64-bit build, and `EnumDeviceDrivers` reports `bytes_needed` = 3,000. What does `enumerate` do?
options: Computes 3,000 ÷ 8 = 375 pointers, which is more than 256, so it resizes to 375 and asks again
Truncates to 256 pointers and returns, since the buffer already holds as many as it can
Computes 3,000 ÷ 256 = 11 pointers, which fits, so it truncates to 11 and returns
Fails with an error, since a count above 256 means Windows returned an invalid size
questions.explanation: The count is `bytes_needed` divided by the pointer size, rounded up. If it exceeds the buffer length, the vector is resized and the call repeated.

questions.prompt: `enumerate` checks `count <= 16_384` before resizing. Why?
options: To refuse an unreasonable count from the API instead of allocating a huge buffer
To stay under the 16 KiB limit that Windows puts on every call from a user program
To make sure the count is a power of two, which `EnumDeviceDrivers` requires
To stop the loop after one retry, since a second retry is always an error
questions.explanation: The check guards against an absurd count. The loop otherwise keeps growing until the list fits.

questions.prompt: On a hardened Windows installation, the inventory shows fewer details. What should you do?
options: Treat it as the security boundary working, and do not weaken the machine to lengthen the list
Enable the debug privilege for the program so that it can see every driver on the whole machine
Turn off memory integrity for the run, since that feature hides driver names from user programs
Run the lab as ring 0 code inside a driver, so that the list matches what the kernel itself sees
questions.explanation: The program does not enable debug privileges. Fewer details are not a failure to fix by lowering defenses.

questions.prompt: Which item does a useful driver baseline record besides the file name?
options: Version, publisher, signature result, hash, why it is installed, and the approved update source
The driver's base address in memory, since that stays the same after every restart of the machine
The player's account name, since drivers are installed separately for each user of the machine
The game that was running when the driver was first loaded, and nothing else about the driver
questions.explanation: A baseline lists Windows build and capture time, file name, version, publisher, signature result, hash, reason, and update source.

questions.prompt: An old hardware driver conflicts with memory integrity. What does the lesson suggest?
options: Look for a supported update or remove the dependent software; trouble is no reason to leave it off
Turn memory integrity off for good, since the old driver is a fixed file that cannot be changed by anyone
Turn memory integrity off only while playing, and back on again when the game is closed afterward
Replace the driver with one from a forum, which is quicker than waiting for the hardware vendor to respond
questions.explanation: Memory integrity (HVCI) uses virtualization-based security to enforce kernel code-integrity rules. Do not turn off protections merely to run an experiment.

questions.prompt: Which Sysmon event can record a loaded driver's hash and signature information, and how should a hit be handled?
options: Event ID 6; confirm the file, service, signature, source, and owning software before acting
Event ID 1; delete the file with the unexpected name before looking at anything else
Event ID 6; assume it is malicious, since every driver load is a high-risk event
Event ID 3; block the network connection of the driver before checking its signature
questions.explanation: Alert on unknown publishers, missing signatures, hashes not in the baseline, and drivers introduced outside normal updates. Detection is not just deleting one weird filename.

questions.prompt: What does DMA stand for, and what does it do?
options: Direct memory access: a device moves data without the CPU copying each byte
Dynamic memory allocation: a program asks its allocator for space and gets an address
Debug memory analysis: a debugger reads the pages of another process
Data mapping array: a table the CPU uses to track free physical pages
questions.explanation: DMA is a hardware feature for device transfers. It shares the word memory with allocation, but that is a different operation done by a program's allocator.

questions.prompt: A classmate says any DMA transfer is automatically a cheat. What is the better statement?
options: It is a normal hardware feature; trouble starts when a device reaches memory it should not
It is an attack by design, since the transfer skips the CPU and so cannot be logged
It is harmless on every machine, so a device reaching extra memory is never a concern
It is used by storage controllers; network and graphics hardware copy bytes via the CPU
questions.explanation: Storage, networking, and graphics hardware all use DMA for speed. Security problems come from a device reaching memory it should not, or from software trusting a device too much.

questions.prompt: Two processes both use virtual address `0x1000` yet read different bytes. Why?
options: Each has its own page-table root, so the number maps to different pages
The OS adds a random per-process offset to each `0x1000` at the moment of every read
The CPU silently rewrites the second process's `0x1000` into `0x2000` before translating
Only one process may use `0x1000` at a time; the other receives a fault when it reads it
questions.explanation: A virtual address only has meaning together with an address space. Each process brings its own page-table root, so the translations differ.

questions.prompt: On an x86-64 system using four-level paging, what does `CR3` identify?
options: The physical base of the top-level translation table
The number of page faults since the process started
The virtual address of the process's first instruction
The size in bytes of the loaded capture file
questions.explanation: CR3 is where the walk starts: it names the physical location of the top table (PML4). Without the right value you walk some other address space.

questions.prompt: Which bits of a 48-bit virtual address select the byte inside a 4 KiB page?
options: Bits 11 to 0
Bits 47 to 39
Bits 20 to 12
Bits 63 to 48
questions.explanation: A 4 KiB page is 2^12 bytes, so the lowest twelve bits are the offset. Bits 20 to 12 pick the page-table entry instead, and bits 63 to 48 are the sign extension.

questions.prompt: How big is one translation table, and how are its entries laid out?
options: 512 entries of eight bytes each
256 entries of 16 bytes each
1,024 entries of four bytes each
512 entries of 16 bytes each
questions.explanation: Nine index bits select among 512 entries, and each entry is eight bytes, so a table fills exactly one 4 KiB page.

questions.prompt: How many bits of a 64-bit virtual address do the four table indices and the offset use together, and what about the rest?
options: 48 bits (4 x 9 + 12); the top 16 must copy bit 47
52 bits (4 x 10 + 12); the top 12 must copy bit 51
36 bits (4 x 9, no offset); the top 28 must be zero
64 bits (4 x 16); no bits are left over for copying
questions.explanation: Four 9-bit indices plus a 12-bit offset make 48 bits. The remaining 16 carry no information and must repeat bit 47, which makes an address canonical.

questions.prompt: How can a translation finish before reading all four levels?
options: A PDPT entry can map 1 GiB, or a page-directory entry can map 2 MiB
A page-table entry can map 2 MiB, or a page-directory entry can map 4 KiB
A PML4 entry with a clear present bit maps the whole address as one block
Large pages still walk four levels but use a 13-bit offset field instead
questions.explanation: Large pages stop the walk early at the PDPT (1 GiB) or page-directory (2 MiB) level, and the skipped index bits become part of the offset.

questions.prompt: Under the lab's `ensure_canonical`, what happens for `0x0000_8000_0000_0000`?
options: `NonCanonical`: bit 47 is 1, but bits 63-48 are all 0
`Ok`: the upper 16 bits are all zero, which is allowed
`NonCanonical`: bit 63 is set, which is never allowed
`Ok`: only the low twelve bits of an address are checked
questions.explanation: `0x8000_0000_0000` is 2^47, so bit 47 is 1 and the upper 16 bits would have to be `0xFFFF`. They are 0, so the function returns an error. Bit 63 is actually 0 here.

questions.prompt: Why does the lab reject a noncanonical address before reading the capture?
options: It gives a clear error instead of following meaningless offsets into the file
Such addresses are valid but slow, so they are rerouted to a cache first
The IOMMU must approve the address before any file read happens
CR3 cannot be loaded while a noncanonical address is pending
questions.explanation: Impossible input cannot lead anywhere real. Failing fast with a named error is clearer than reading nonsense bytes that look plausible.

questions.prompt: What does an IOMMU do for DMA-capable devices?
options: It translates device addresses so the OS can confine a device to approved regions
It compresses RAM pages so a device can fit much more data into each transfer it makes
It encrypts each transfer so a device cannot read the plain bytes that it fetches from RAM
It replaces the CPU's page tables so that processes stop using virtual addresses entirely
questions.explanation: An IOMMU does for devices what page tables do for processes: it sits between device and RAM and blocks requests outside approved regions.

questions.prompt: A protected machine blocks a DMA device during your experiment. What is the right response?
options: Treat it as the defense working and use the synthetic or offline capture
Turn off the IOMMU in firmware for the whole length of the experiment
Disable Kernel DMA Protection temporarily so the device can finish its work
Mask extra address bits in the walker until some output finally appears
questions.explanation: A blocked path is a successful defense, not a translation failure. The labs use synthetic or offline captures so no protection has to be weakened.

questions.prompt: Which statement about an offline capture is accurate?
options: Pages may have changed right after capture, and some may be absent or omitted
Threads keep running inside the image, so values update while you read
CPU caches and device memory are included in every RAM image
Any CR3 value works, because pages are stored by virtual address
questions.explanation: A capture is a frozen snapshot. It can miss pages, caches, and device memory, and you need the correct CR3 and architecture details to interpret it.

questions.prompt: Why do origin, build, capture time, and a hash travel with a capture file?
options: Numbers like CR3 only mean something for their source machine; the hash shows no changes
The hash lets the tool repair any pages that changed after the capture was taken
Provenance lets the walker skip the present-bit check when the file is trusted
The capture format requires a header holding the machine name and nothing else
questions.explanation: The file alone does not say where it came from. The record plus a cryptographic hash tells you what the numbers mean and whether the bytes are still the original ones.

questions.prompt: The lab is finished and a RAM capture is still on disk. What should happen to it?
options: Store it securely, then delete it, since it may hold private data
Share it with classmates for cross-checking, since it only holds plain numbers
Keep it on the desktop for good so that the lab stays reproducible
Delete only the provenance record and keep the raw bytes around for later
questions.explanation: A capture holds whatever was in RAM, including private data unrelated to the lesson. It is stored securely and removed when the lab no longer needs it.

questions.prompt: In the apartment-number analogy, what plays the part of the building?
options: The page-table root (CR3) chosen for the address space
The physical RAM chip that holds the final byte
The byte offset inside the final 4 KiB page
The access type: read, write, or instruction fetch
questions.explanation: Apartment 1000 means nothing without the building, just as `0x1000` means nothing without the page-table root. The analogy is limited, because real mappings can change and carry permissions.

questions.prompt: The lab walker returns a physical address for a virtual one. What does that show?
options: Present recorded entries lead there; a live access is not proven to be allowed
A user-mode write would certainly succeed, since every permission was evaluated
The page is executable, because the walker also checks the fetch permission bit
The process owns that page, because CR3 names the single owner of every byte
questions.explanation: The walker checks presence and file bounds but does not emulate every read, write, execute, and user/supervisor check the CPU makes.

questions.prompt: Why does the lab wrap addresses as `PhysicalAddress` and `VirtualAddress` instead of plain `u64`?
options: The compiler rejects mixing the two kinds unless you convert explicitly
The wrappers make each address take less memory than a bare `u64` would, saving space
The wrappers let the walker skip the bounds checks on every physical read it makes
Plain `u64` values cannot hold the 48-bit addresses that the x86-64 paging mode uses
questions.explanation: Both are 64-bit numbers underneath, so mixing them is an easy logic error. Distinct types turn that mistake into a compile error; they add no speed or extra range.

questions.prompt: In `read_physical`, which failure does the `checked_add` step guard against?
options: The start address plus the read length overflowing `usize`
The address being too large to convert into a `usize` at all
The final range ending beyond the last byte of the capture
The output buffer being empty when the read is requested
questions.explanation: The three checks are separate: a conversion to `usize`, an overflow in `start + length`, and the range lookup with `get`. `checked_add` is the overflow one.

questions.prompt: The first PML4 entry sits at `0x1000` and its bytes are `01 20 00 00 00 00 00 00`. What does it hold?
options: `0x2001`: the present bit is set and the next table is at `0x2000`
`0x0120`: the present bit is clear, so the entry is not present
`0x2000`: bit 13 is the present flag and the table is at `0x2000`
`0x0201`: the present bit is set and the next table is at `0x200`
questions.explanation: Entries are little-endian, so the first byte is the lowest. `0x20` in the second byte is worth `0x2000`, and the `01` below it sets the present bit. Clearing the flag bits leaves `0x2000`.

questions.prompt: Why does each table index take exactly nine bits?
options: A table holds 512 entries, and 512 is 2^9
A page is 4,096 bytes, and 4,096 is 2^9
Each entry is eight bytes, and eight is 2^9
Four levels share 36 bits, and nobody chose the split further
questions.explanation: Nine bits can choose among 512 entries. The 4,096-byte page size fixes the 12-bit offset, a different field.

questions.prompt: Which expression extracts the PML4 index from a virtual address `value`?
options: `(value >> 39) & 0x1FF`
`(value >> 12) & 0x1FF`
`(value >> 39) & 0xFFF`
`(value >> 48) & 0x1FF`
questions.explanation: The PML4 index lives at bits 47 to 39, so shift by 39 and keep nine bits (`0x1FF`). The mask `0xFFF` keeps twelve bits, which is the page offset, not an index.

questions.prompt: For the address `0x0000_7FF6_1234_0FF8`, which byte of the final 4 KiB page does the walk end up reading?
options: Byte 255 (`0x0FF`)
questions.explanation: The last twelve bits, `0xFF8`, are the page offset: 15 x 256 + 15 x 16 + 8 = 4,088. The other numbers are the table indices of the same address.

questions.prompt: The address `0x0000_7FF6_1234_0FF8` splits into six fields. Which PML4 entry number does it use?
options: Entry 255
Entry 472
Entry 145
Entry 320
questions.explanation: Bits 47 to 39 are `0 1111 1111` = `0x0FF` = 255. The values 472, 145, and 320 are the PDPT, page-directory, and page-table indices.

questions.prompt: A 32-byte read starts at virtual `0x0000_7FF6_1234_0FF8`. How many of those bytes lie in the first page?
options: 8, because the page ends at offset `0x1000` and 4,096 - 4,088 = 8
24, because the first page holds everything after the offset
4, because the walk reads in aligned chunks of four bytes
32, because a read never leaves the page it starts in
questions.explanation: The offset is 4,088, so only 8 bytes remain before the page ends. The other 24 bytes live in the next virtual page, which needs its own translation.

questions.prompt: A reader translates only the start address and then copies 32 consecutive physical bytes across a page end. What goes wrong?
options: The last 24 bytes come from whatever follows physically, maybe unrelated memory
The CPU raises a fault at the page boundary, so the read stops with an error code
The reader returns zeros for the second half until it later translates once again
The copy repeats the first page, because the offset wraps around back to zero
questions.explanation: Nothing warns you. The bytes look ordinary but belong to an unrelated allocation, another process's data, or nothing mapped at all.

questions.prompt: Why does the walk apply `& 0x000F_FFFF_FFFF_F000` to an entry before using it as the next table's address?
options: It keeps bits 12 to 51, dropping flag bits to leave a page-aligned address
It keeps bits 0 to 11, which hold the physical address of the next table, and the rest
It sets the present bit so that the next table can be read safely afterwards
It converts the whole entry from little-endian into big-endian byte order first
questions.explanation: Low bits of an entry store flags like present and writable, and high bits hold more flags. Only bits 12 to 51 are address.

questions.prompt: What is `value & 0xFFF` used for in the walk?
options: It keeps the twelve-bit offset inside a 4 KiB page
It keeps the nine-bit index of the page-directory entry
It removes the sign-extension bits from bits 63 to 48
It checks that the present bit of the final entry is set
questions.explanation: `0xFFF` is 4,095, so the mask keeps exactly twelve bits. That is the byte position within the final page, added to the page's physical base.

questions.prompt: How does the walk recognize a 1 GiB or 2 MiB page?
options: Bit 7 of the PDPT or page-directory entry is set, so the walk stops early
Bit 0 of the PML4 entry is clear, so the walk skips two levels
The virtual address has bit 47 set, which marks it as a large page
The capture file is larger than 2 MiB, so the reader switches modes
questions.explanation: Bit 7 (`0x80`) is the large-page flag at those two levels. When set, the index fields that were skipped become part of the offset.

questions.prompt: A PDPT entry maps a 1 GiB page (2^30 bytes). Which mask gives the offset inside it?
options: `value & 0x3FFF_FFFF`
`value & 0x1F_FFFF`
`value & 0xFFF`
`value & 0x7FFF_FFFF`
questions.explanation: Each offset mask is one less than the page size. 2^30 is `0x4000_0000`, so the mask is `0x3FFF_FFFF`; `0x1F_FFFF` belongs to a 2 MiB page.

questions.prompt: The synthetic capture is `0x7000` bytes. How many 4 KiB pages is that?
options: Seven pages, because 7 x 4,096 = 28,672 bytes in total
Twenty-eight, because 0x7000 is 28,672 bytes and each page is 1,024 bytes
Seventy, because each hex digit multiplies the size by ten
Four, because only four tables are used by the walk
questions.explanation: Each `0x1000` is one page, and `0x7000` is seven of them. Only four of the pages are tables, but the file still includes the data page and the zero pages.

questions.prompt: In the test fixture with `CR3 = 0x1000`, virtual `0x0123` becomes physical `0x5123`. Why?
options: Every index is 0, so the walk follows `0x2000`, `0x3000`, `0x4000`, `0x5000`, plus offset `0x123`
The walker simply adds `0x5000` to any virtual address that is smaller than `0x1000`, as a rule
Index 1 is used at every level, and that entry points at the data page at `0x5000`
The CR3 value `0x1000` is added to the virtual address, which gives the result `0x1123`
questions.explanation: Since `0x0123` is below `0x1000`, bits 12 to 47 are all zero, so each table's first entry is used. The final page base `0x5000` plus the offset gives `0x5123`.

questions.prompt: A walk fails with `NotPresent` at the PDPT level. Which is a likely meaning?
options: The page is absent, the CR3 is wrong, or the capture is incomplete
The virtual address is noncanonical, so it was rejected before the walk
The file is shorter than the entry address, so the read went out of range
The page tables were walked correctly and the data page is just empty
questions.explanation: A clear present bit says that level has no valid next table. Noncanonical addresses and out-of-range reads produce their own, different errors.

questions.prompt: A walk succeeds and returns bytes that look sensible, but the object is not the one you meant. What is a likely cause?
options: A wrong address space, a stale pointer, or a wrong build model
A noncanonical address that the reader forgot to reject
A present bit that the walker failed to check at the PML4
A bounds check that was too strict for the capture file
questions.explanation: A successful translation only says the page tables lead somewhere. The somewhere can still be the wrong object, which is why Lesson 12.9 adds provenance and independent checks.

questions.prompt: A translation fails with an error. Which response does the lesson recommend?
options: Compare entries with the manual, check the capture layout, keep the failure visible
Mask extra bits from each entry until some bytes finally come out of the other end
Retry with a different CR3 value until a plausible-looking object finally appears
Skip the present-bit check so that the walk always reaches some data page
questions.explanation: Forcing output by masking or skipping checks hides the real problem. A visible failure with context is more useful than bytes from the wrong place.

questions.prompt: Why does the command-line tool limit the byte count to 1 through 4,096?
options: A learning tool should make unexpectedly huge reads impossible
The page-table walk can only translate a single 4 KiB page per command run
The capture file format cannot store more than 4,096 bytes at one address
Larger reads would need CR3 to change partway through the printed output
questions.explanation: The limit is a deliberate safety choice, not a technical necessity. `read_virtual` does handle page crossings, so a limit is not there to avoid them.

questions.prompt: Why does `read_virtual` return a new byte vector rather than a borrowed slice of the capture?
options: The bytes may come from several physical places that are not adjacent
A slice cannot be created from a file that was opened as read-only data
Vectors are faster to hash than slices when checking provenance digests
The returned bytes must be converted from little-endian format first
questions.explanation: Neighbouring virtual pages can sit anywhere in physical memory, so the result has to be assembled from separate pieces and cannot be one slice.

questions.prompt: Why does a wrong CR3 value usually not make the page-table walk fail?
options: It is still a valid page-table root for some other address space
The walker silently falls back to the correct CR3 stored in the file
Every CR3 value leads to the same top-level table in the capture
The present bits are ignored whenever the CR3 does not match
questions.explanation: A clean walk only means the tables in the file lead somewhere. With the wrong root, the somewhere belongs to a different process.

questions.prompt: The capture's SHA-256 no longer matches the digest in its provenance record. What is the right move?
options: Stop, because every earlier translation assumed the recorded bytes
Continue, since the page-table walk will report any damaged pages itself
Recompute the digest and overwrite the old one in the record
Continue on a copy, since only the original file is affected by the change
questions.explanation: A changed file means the bytes are no longer the ones the record describes. Nothing translated from it can be trusted until the change is explained; overwriting the digest would hide the problem.

questions.prompt: Why keep the original capture read-only and experiment on a working copy?
options: A mistake then cannot change the only copy of the evidence
The walker refuses to open a file that is writable by anyone
A read-only file loads into RAM faster than a copy does
The hash can only be computed for a file that is marked read-only
questions.explanation: The original must keep matching its digest. Experiments on a copy leave the evidence intact.

questions.prompt: Which item belongs in a capture's provenance record?
options: The CR3 source and the process it belongs to
The current health value read from the first object found
The decoded `PlayerSnapshot` from the first translation
The names of all other files stored on the source machine
questions.explanation: Provenance records where and how the file was made: tool, build, architecture, UTC time, included ranges, CR3 source, and the digest. Decoded values come later and are not provenance.

questions.prompt: A capture translator and a debugger give the same physical address, yet the object is still wrong. Which mistake can remain?
options: Both translated the wrong thing correctly, such as a stale pointer
The first translator contains a bug that the debugger happens to share by luck
The hash of the capture file was computed using the wrong hashing algorithm
The IOMMU blocked one of the two translations while the capture was recorded
questions.explanation: A second translator catches a bug in the first. Agreement says the translation is right, not that the target is the intended object, which is what semantic structure checks are for.

questions.prompt: Why run several checks on different fields rather than trusting one plausible health value?
options: Random memory often holds small integers, yet several checks rarely all pass by chance
A single check cannot be written in Rust code without also writing all of the others
The health field is stored in a different physical page than the other fields are
Each additional check lowers the digest size, so the hash is faster to verify later
questions.explanation: One field can look right by accident. A wrong address usually fails at least one of several checks that examine different bytes in different ways.

questions.prompt: The toy `PlayerLayout` has an 8-byte vtable pointer, 4-byte health, three 4-byte floats, and three 8-byte container pointers. What is `SIZE`?
questions.explanation: 8 + 4 = 12, plus 12 for the floats makes 24, plus 24 for the pointers makes 48, which is `0x30`.

questions.prompt: What does the semantic check on the vptr verify?
options: That it points into the expected module's read-only section
That it equals the virtual address where the object was found
That it is a multiple of 4,096 so it sits at a page start
That it matches the CR3 value stored in the provenance record
questions.explanation: A vtable normally lives in read-only data of the expected module. A pointer elsewhere suggests the bytes are not the object you meant.

questions.prompt: Which relation should a container's three pointers satisfy in the layout check?
options: `begin <= end <= capacity`
`capacity <= begin <= end`
`end <= begin <= capacity`
`begin == end == capacity`
questions.explanation: A growable list starts at begin, holds items up to end, and has room up to capacity, so the three pointers must be in that order.

questions.prompt: The capture layer, layout layer, and presentation layer are kept separate. What is the main benefit?
options: A layout mistake cannot corrupt translation code; each layer tests alone
The presentation layer can skip decoding whenever the hash already matches the record
Page tables can be walked without any CR3 once the object layout is already known
The layout layer can repair the physical ranges that the capture tool omitted from the file
questions.explanation: The capture layer knows physical ranges and page tables; the layout layer knows fields and invariants; the presentation layer prints. Splitting them keeps each mistake local.

questions.prompt: Which step is part of defensive validation for DMA exposure?
options: Check Windows Security or System Information for the protection state
Turn off Kernel DMA Protection for a moment so the check runs faster and more simply
Plug in an unknown device and watch whether the machine reacts to the new hardware
Disable Secure Boot so the firmware reveals much more of its diagnostic output
questions.explanation: Defense means confirming protections are on, keeping software updated, and using trusted devices. The lesson says not to disable protections to make an experiment easier.

questions.prompt: Which lab test targets a time gap in a control?
options: Pause between validation and use, mutate a fixture, and expect rejection
Send labeled events through toy paths and compare the logs afterward
Feed bounded malformed fixtures into both the producer and consumer parsers
Restart the toy target and verify its identity is evaluated again
questions.explanation: A time gap is the assumption that trusted state stays the same between check and use, so the test changes the state in that interval. The other tests target coverage, parser, and identity gaps.

questions.prompt: In `validate_write_request`, the write policy is read-only and the build ID is also wrong. Which denial is returned?
options: `Denial::ReadOnly`, because that check runs first and its `?` exits
`Denial::WrongBuild`, because build mismatches take priority over policy
Both denials, in a list ordered by when each was checked
`Denial::StateChanged`, because the byte comparison runs last
questions.explanation: Each `?` is a separate exit, so the first failing check decides the named reason. The later checks never run once one has failed.

questions.prompt: The byte comparison is the last check, right before the toy write. What does that achieve?
options: It shortens the time gap but does not make a remote read and write atomic
It guarantees no other code can change the bytes before the write happens
It replaces the need for the build and range checks that came earlier
It proves the bytes belong to the intended process and object
questions.explanation: A tool needing a true guarantee must own the state exclusively, or have the owner validate and apply the request as one operation.

questions.prompt: How does the lesson define an invariant?
options: A condition that must hold every time
A value that never changes while the program runs
A check that runs once at program start
A log entry written after every state change
questions.explanation: Stating an assumption as an invariant makes it testable. A value that never changes is a constant, which is a different idea.

questions.prompt: Which assumption defines a telemetry gap?
options: A blocked action needs no event of its own
Every execution path passes the point being observed
The name or handle a control trusted cannot change
A crash cannot leave hooks or handles in a bad state
questions.explanation: The safer test asserts that every allow, deny, timeout, and parse failure produces an event. The other assumptions describe the coverage, identity, and recovery gaps.

questions.prompt: Which lab test targets an identity gap?
options: Restart or rebuild the toy target and verify identity is re-evaluated
Pause between validation and use, then mutate a fixture value
Exercise a fake broker with least-privilege test tokens
Inject worker errors and verify cleanup happens in reverse order
questions.explanation: An identity gap assumes the trusted name, signer, PID, or handle cannot change. Restarting the target tests exactly that. The other tests cover time, privilege, and recovery gaps.

questions.prompt: Which of these is an invariant?
options: An entity ID names at most one live entity in a snapshot
Entity 7's health changed from 6 to 0 during tick 900
The player pressed the heal button during tick 41 once
The damage routine was called twice within one frame
questions.explanation: An invariant is a statement that must be true in every valid state. The other options describe single events, which can happen and still leave the state valid or invalid.

questions.prompt: Health is 5 and a request asks for 20 damage. What should a correct damage routine produce?
options: Health 0, because the range rule `0 <= health <= max_health` must hold
Health -15, because the subtraction is exact and the bar clamps it later
Health 5, because a request larger than the current health is ignored
Health 20, because the larger number replaces the current one
questions.explanation: The invariant forbids negative health, so the control limits the transition and leaves 0. A display that hides -15 would not fix the stored value.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a detector rather than a control?
options: A scan that logs any entity whose health exceeds its maximum
A damage routine that stops health at 0 instead of going negative
A heal routine that applies `.min(max_health)` before storing
A command handler that refuses a change in read-only mode
questions.explanation: A control keeps an invariant true by limiting or refusing a transition. A detector only reports that the invariant may already have failed.

questions.prompt: A detector stays quiet for a whole play session. What can you conclude about the control it watches?
options: Nothing certain, since the control can still be incomplete
The control is complete, because the detector would have noticed any gap
The invariant is no longer needed, because nothing has broken it
The control must have run on the authoritative copy of the state
questions.explanation: Detector and control are separate code that fail separately. A quiet detector may simply not cover the path that was used.

questions.prompt: A state shows `health = 120` with `max_health = 100`. Which statement fits the lesson?
options: It is invalid whichever of the clamp, field, or log missed it
It is valid if the clamp instruction was never reached by the code
It is invalid once the log line has actually reported it to a reader
It becomes valid again once the health bar redraws itself showing 100
questions.explanation: The invariant is a property of the state, not of one address or one piece of code. A clamp, a `max_health` field, and a log line are places where it is kept or reported.

questions.prompt: What does the lesson call a bypass?
options: A path to an outcome that skips the control meant to guard it
A faster version of a control that skips the logging of its own decisions
A second copy of a state value that is kept just for drawing a health bar
A detector that keeps reporting a false positive for harmless debugging tools
questions.explanation: In this chapter a bypass is a mismatch between a convenient proxy and the real rule. It is about the path and the control, not about speed or false alarms.

questions.prompt: A menu button is greyed out unless the player may heal. In the proxy table, what real property does that button stand in for?
options: The engine policy actually permits the state change
The health bar's cache currently matches the entity
The game build matches the one the tool was made for
The telemetry queue has not dropped any events
