questions.explanation: A greyed-out button answers how the screen should look. Whether the simulation may perform the effect is a separate question that must be checked where the effect happens.

questions.prompt: A checksum over one field matches. Which real property does it fail to establish?
options: That the complete object relation is current and valid
That the field was copied from memory without any error
That the build number is recorded in the provenance file
That the entity is drawn on screen this frame
questions.explanation: A matching one-field checksum says only that field is unchanged. Other fields can still make the whole relation invalid.

questions.prompt: In a single-player game, which copy of health is usually authoritative?
options: The simulation's entity object
The health bar's cached copy
The snapshot handed to a script
The copy shown in a debugger window
questions.explanation: The authoritative copy is the one whose value decides what happens next. The others are copies that catch up afterward.

questions.prompt: In a networked game with an authoritative server, what is a client's copy of health?
options: A prediction that the server can overwrite
The record that the server must copy before each tick
A second authoritative value, equal in rank to the server's
An integrity tag the server checks against its record
questions.explanation: The server's record decides, and each client's value is only a prediction. That is why requests from clients are validated against the server's own record.

questions.prompt: Why does a server validate every client request against its own record?
options: Anything a client computed can be altered on its machine before sending
Clients send values in a binary format that the server cannot decode directly
Servers are faster than clients, so they can recheck every single computation
The network always changes numbers while they travel over the wire to the server
questions.explanation: The client's machine is outside the server's control, so the client's own check cannot be the rule. The server keeps the authoritative record.

questions.prompt: Two copies of health hold the same number. How does the lesson say you can tell which one is authoritative?
options: By timing: the authoritative copy changes first, the rest catch up
By address: the copy at the lowest address is always the authoritative one there
By size: the authoritative copy is stored in the widest integer type available
By value: the larger of the two numbers is the authoritative one of the pair
questions.explanation: Matching values do not reveal which copy was read. The order in which they change does.

questions.prompt: In the trace, `HealthWrite` to 0 is at tick 900 but the health bar reads 0 at tick 901. What explains the difference?
options: The bar draws from a copy that catches up one tick after the authoritative change
The bar read the value before the write, so it holds a stale number from tick 899
Two ticks passed between the write and the read, as a sequence number shows
The mode watch changed the health to 0 a second time at tick 901
questions.explanation: The health bar is a copy updated after the simulation. Reading 0 there confirms the value, but not that the bar is the place it changed first.

questions.prompt: Event 41 (health reaches 0) is logged just before event 42 (mode becomes Downed). What does log order prove?
options: It fits damage causing the change, but a shared cause or flush timing also fits
It proves the health write directly caused the mode change that came after it
It proves the mode watch ran on a different thread from the health watch
It proves the two events happened in two different game ticks of the clock
questions.explanation: Log order is not cause. Lesson 13.2 adds correlation IDs to tie events to one action even when order misleads.

questions.prompt: What advantage do typed event fields have over free-text log sentences?
options: A test can check that a `HealthWrite` to 0 precedes the `ModeChanged` to `Downed`
Typed events take up less space, so the log never needs a size bound at all
Typed events are written to disk automatically in order of the entity ID number
Free-text sentences cannot contain tick numbers or entity IDs in any form
questions.explanation: Fields such as `before`, `after`, and `entity_id` can be compared by code, so the order can be checked automatically.

questions.prompt: Which transition is not in the Alive / Downed / Removed state diagram?
options: Removed to Alive
Downed to Alive by revive
Downed to Removed by timeout
Alive to Removed by despawn
questions.explanation: Removed leads only to the end of the diagram. Revive, timeout, and despawn are all listed as allowed transitions.

questions.prompt: For hook installation, what must remain true, and where does the health analogy break down?
options: A call sees a complete original path or a complete hook path; a hook changes bytes other threads use
A call sees only the hook path; health is a copy while a hook is the authoritative original
A hook may be half installed if telemetry records it; health is a value checked only once
The original bytes are overwritten at once; health is held in a register that no thread shares
questions.explanation: Health is one value, but a hook changes executable bytes that other threads may be running, which is why Lesson 6.10 handles concurrency separately.

questions.prompt: A log says only that a write was refused. Which of the four recorded things is missing?
options: The reason: which specific check produced the refusal
The identity: which process, build, and object was touched
The outcome: whether the write finally happened
The decision: whether the answer was allow or deny
questions.explanation: The log shows a decision, but without a reason you can never learn why. Dropping the outcome instead would hide whether an allowed operation completed.

questions.prompt: A log records `Decision allowed=true` but nothing afterward. What can you not tell?
options: Whether the allowed operation actually completed
Which check allowed the operation to go ahead
Which build the operation was run against
Whether the decision was made before the effect
questions.explanation: Allowed is not the same as completed. The outcome field is what separates the two.

questions.prompt: Events in log order: seq 41 corr 7 denied; 42 corr 8 allowed; 43 corr 7 `changed=true`; 44 corr 8 `changed=true`. Which action did the effect at seq 43 belong to?
options: Action 7, which was denied
Action 8, which was allowed just before it
Neither, since effects have no correlation IDs
Both, since they ran in the same interval
questions.explanation: Pairing by correlation ID shows that a state change happened after a refusal. Pairing by adjacency would call both actions successful and miss it.

questions.prompt: Why did the adjacency reading of that log reach the wrong conclusion even though no events were missing?
options: Two actions interleaved, and the reader assumed they had not
Sequence numbers were reordered so that 43 came before 42
The monotonic clock jumped between events 42 and 43
A dropped event hid the real decision for action 7
questions.explanation: The evidence was complete. Ordering alone misled, which is why detection rules join on the correlation ID, not on neighbouring lines.

questions.prompt: What is a correlation ID for?
options: Connecting the events of one logical action, even across threads
Counting how many events were lost when a queue overflowed
Recording how long each event took to produce, in microseconds
Naming the build so a reader can reject unknown schemas
questions.explanation: The ID ties decision and effect events together without pretending they happened on one thread. Dropped counts, durations, and schema checks use other fields.

questions.prompt: Why use a monotonic clock for event ordering and durations within one run?
options: Wall-clock time can jump, while a monotonic clock only moves forward
A monotonic clock is more accurate to the calendar date than wall time
Wall-clock time cannot be stored in a `u64` field
A monotonic clock records which thread produced each event
questions.explanation: Monotonic time is for measuring elapsed time and order inside a run. Wall time is useful to humans but can be adjusted.

questions.prompt: What does the `sequence` field let a reader do?
options: Detect missing or reordered events
Join one request's decision to its effect
Reject fields from a newer event format
Identify which entity the event was about
questions.explanation: Sequence numbers run in order, so gaps and reordering show. The correlation ID does the joining, and `schema_version` handles format changes.

questions.prompt: What is the `schema_version` field for?
options: It lets a reader reject fields it cannot interpret
It joins a decision with the effect that followed
It marks the order in which events were produced
It names the build that generated the trace
questions.explanation: A reader that sees an unknown version can refuse the event rather than guess what the fields mean.

questions.prompt: Why must denied operations be recorded too?
options: Logging only successes leaves a blind spot where refusals hide
Denied operations change some state, so they have to be written down first
A denial record is what makes the decision take effect in the game engine
Logs without denials cannot be compressed or normalized by the analysis tool
questions.explanation: A silent refusal can preserve state while leaving diagnosis and coverage testing blind, because nobody can see the control working.

questions.prompt: Why prefer build ID plus entity ID plus generation to a raw pointer as an identity?
options: Allocations move and addresses can be reused by something else
Pointers cannot be written into an event on a 64-bit build
Entity IDs are always smaller, which saves queue space
Generation numbers are the only value a pointer can verify
questions.explanation: A pointer may later name a different object. A build, an entity ID, and a generation keep naming the same thing.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a detection rule from the lesson?
options: One entity's generation decreases
Health ever changes during a run
The correlation ID is larger than the sequence
A decision takes more than one event to log
questions.explanation: A useful rule is a query over explicit events that signals a contradiction. Ordinary changes in health are expected and do not mean an invariant failed.

questions.prompt: What does normalization do before comparing two traces?
options: Replaces unstable values such as addresses and timestamps so traces compare
Sorts all events by correlation ID value so that the two traces will match up
Deletes denied decisions, which would otherwise differ from run to run in a trace
Converts every event to the newest schema version that the reader currently uses
questions.explanation: Line-by-line text comparison is noisy because addresses and times differ every run. Normalizing exposes the first meaningful divergence.

questions.prompt: Fixture: an allowed command whose effect event arrives late, and the rule fires. How is it classified?
options: False positive: no invariant fails, yet the rule fires
True positive: the rule fired, so a real violation must exist
False negative: the late event somehow escaped the rule
True negative: allowed commands never fire this kind of rule
questions.explanation: A true positive needs the invariant to actually fail. Here the command was valid, only its event was delayed.

questions.prompt: The effect changed state, but the decision event was dropped, and the rule stayed silent. How is that classified?
options: False negative, or insufficient evidence
False positive, because the rule did not fire
True positive, because the effect changed state
True negative, because there was no decision event
questions.explanation: The invariant failed, but the rule could not see it. That is why dropped events lower confidence.

questions.prompt: A report says the rule 'detected 100%'. What is missing?
options: The counts and the exact fixture set that were tested
The wall-clock time at which the rule was written
The thread ID that produced each detection
The monotonic clock readings for every fixture
questions.explanation: A percentage means nothing without knowing what was tested. Report counts and the fixtures.

questions.prompt: A render hook cannot wait for a full log queue. What does the lesson say about lost events?
options: Never hide loss: record a counter, and treat the gap as lower confidence
Drop events silently, since the game must never slow down at all for logging
Block the hook until the queue frees up again so that nothing is ever missed
Delete the older half of the queue so that the final report stays quite short
questions.explanation: Bounded queues need a deliberate policy, but any policy must record that events were dropped so analysts can tell.

questions.prompt: What does a repair test built from the minimal regression trace need to show?
options: The effect stays unchanged after a denial while valid commands still work
Every event in the trace is written in a single frame, very quickly in order
The correlation ID is reused so that later runs can be compared to this one
The queue size is increased so that no event can ever be dropped in future runs
questions.explanation: A repair that disables everything would also pass the first half, so a separate valid-command test keeps the repair honest.

questions.prompt: Which of the five boundaries asks when bytes were measured and how long the result is reused?
options: Time
Bytes
Consumer
Failure
questions.explanation: Bytes asks what is covered, Time asks when and for how long, Identity asks which object, Consumer asks which operation trusts the result, and Failure asks what happens when verification cannot finish.

questions.prompt: For player 7, health 80, max health 100, generation 3, what does the lesson's `covered_checksum` return?
questions.explanation: The terms are 7 x 31 = 217, health 80, 100 x 128 = 12,800, and 3 x 8,192 = 24,576. The wrong options use a wrong rotation or drop a term.

questions.prompt: Why does `100u32.rotate_left(7)` equal 12,800?
options: 100 is seven bits wide, so nothing wraps and it is times 2^7 = 128
Rotation adds the count 7 to the value, repeated for each of 7 rotation steps
Rotation copies the lowest seven bits to the top, leaving the original bits in place
Rotation multiplies by 7 and then wraps around at 2^32
questions.explanation: Moving bits seven places toward the high end is a multiplication by 128 when no bit reaches the top. 100 x 128 = 12,800.

questions.prompt: A checksum was written without the `max_health` term and stores 24,873. Then `max_health` changes from 100 to 60 and nothing is recomputed. What happens?
options: The sum is still 24,873, so it matches while health 80 exceeds 60
The checksum changes to 32,553, so the verifier rejects the record at once
The checksum matches because health 80 is smaller than the old maximum of 100
The checksum changes by 40, the difference between the two maximum values
questions.explanation: The check reports honestly that every byte it covers is unchanged. The record is still impossible, because the damaged field was never looked at.

questions.prompt: With the complete `covered_checksum`, `max_health` drops from 100 to 60 and nothing is recomputed. What sum is computed now?
options: 37,673, because only the stored checksum field decides the result
24,873, because the max health term is no longer included
31,873, because the max term shrinks by exactly 40
questions.explanation: 60 x 128 = 7,680, so the sum is 32,553. That no longer equals the stored 37,673, so the edit is caught.

questions.prompt: Why does `verify` test both the checksum and `health <= max_health`?
options: The questions are independent: unchanged bytes versus a possible record
The range test is just a faster way to compute the same checksum value
The checksum already includes the range check, so the two always agree with each other
The second clause only runs when the first clause has failed to match anything
questions.explanation: A record can pass one and fail the other in either direction, so a check that asks only one question accepts states the game forbids.

questions.prompt: What kind of claim does the toy checksum make?
options: It signals accidental corruption; it is not cryptographic authentication
It proves that the record was written by the game itself, not by a tool
It prevents anyone from changing a record unless they hold the secret key
It encrypts the record so the health value stays secret from other programs
questions.explanation: Anyone who knows the formula can recompute it, so it detects accidents only. Defending against a deliberate editor needs an authenticated owner and key lifecycle.

questions.prompt: A hash of a byte range matches. What does that tell you?
options: Those bytes matched when measured, and nothing about anything outside them
The whole process stays unchanged for as long as the game keeps on running
Every operation that uses the object later on will see a valid state
The display cache and the simulation object hold the very same values now
questions.explanation: A hash proves something about the covered bytes and moment. It does not describe other objects, other fields, or later changes.

questions.prompt: A verifier approved generation 17, then the record changed to 18 before a later operation trusted the old `true`. Which repair fits?
options: The consumer compares the result's generation with the current one and refuses a mismatch
The verifier caches `true` for longer, so that the result also covers generation 18 later
The consumer skips verification whenever the record's generation is a larger number than before
The checksum is made longer, so that the old cached result can no longer match anything
questions.explanation: The result was correct for 17 but nothing tied it to that generation. Comparing at the last step catches the staleness.

questions.prompt: Why return an `IntegrityFailure` enum instead of a plain `bool`?
options: Read errors, wrong builds, and mismatches otherwise blur together or pass as 'valid'
A `bool` cannot represent more than one failed check at a time in a single value
Enums are checked by the compiler only when the results of verification are cached
Telemetry cannot record a `bool` return value that comes from any function at all
questions.explanation: Explicit variants make tests state exactly which promise failed, and keep an unreadable record from passing.

questions.prompt: A guarded read fails because memory could not be read. Which result should it produce?
options: `Unreadable`, and never treated as 'valid'
`ChecksumMismatch`, since nothing could be compared
`OutOfRange`, since the value is missing
`IdentityChanged`, since the read was refused
questions.explanation: The failure should say what actually went wrong. Treating an unreadable record as valid would be the worst outcome.

questions.prompt: Why is `apply_heal` easy to reason about?
options: It checks and changes the same object under one exclusive borrow
It runs on several threads at once, so the check can never possibly go stale
It recomputes the checksum before it verifies the record, so both always agree
It copies the record first, then edits that copy rather than the original record
questions.explanation: Check and effect share one mutable borrow, so nothing else can change the record between them. Across threads or processes that no longer holds.

questions.prompt: Why is a remote read followed by a remote write not atomic?
options: State can change in between; use versioned snapshots, expected bytes, or the owner
The write always starts running before the read has completed on the other process
Remote reads return stale cached bytes, which the later write then overwrites for good
Remote writes are checked by a different checksum function than the one the reads use
questions.explanation: Another thread or process can change the state between the two calls. The lesson suggests tying the write to a snapshot, comparing expected bytes, or sending a command to the owner.

questions.prompt: `apply_heal` runs on a valid record with health 95, max health 100, and amount 20. What is health afterward?
options: 100, because 95 + 20 = 115 and `.min(100)` limits it to the maximum
115, because the heal amount is simply added to health without any limit at all
20, because the heal amount replaces the current health value of the record
95, because any heal that would go above the maximum is refused outright by the function
questions.explanation: The code adds 20 to 95, then clamps with `.min(max_health)`. It also bumps the generation and recomputes the checksum.

questions.prompt: Which regression property does the lesson list for a display-only field?
options: Changing an uncovered display-only field leaves verification unaffected
Changing a display-only field must always cause verification to fail every time
A display-only field must always be included in the covered checksum as well
A display-only field must be changed again whenever the health value changes in the record
questions.explanation: Verification covers only the fields the checksum includes, so a field outside it changes nothing about the result. That is expected for display-only data.

questions.prompt: Why is `health > max_health` rejected even when the checksum is recomputed to match?
options: A matching checksum does not make an impossible value become meaningful
The checksum cannot be recomputed by anyone after the health value changes
The max health field is always protected from edits by the Rust compiler itself
Recomputed checksums are always rejected by the verifier as being stale results
questions.explanation: Checksum and range answer different questions. A consistent but impossible record should still be refused.

questions.prompt: What does flipping one bit in each covered field, one at a time, prove?
options: That the test suite notices missing coverage
That the checksum is cryptographically secure
That the generation field never wraps around
That the display cache matches the simulation
questions.explanation: If flipping a field's bit goes unnoticed, that field is not covered. The mutation test exposes the gap.

questions.prompt: In the lesson's vocabulary, what is an assessment?
options: An interpretation of signals, such as `NeedsAnotherSample`
One measured observation, such as a delay in microseconds from a sample window
An action chosen afterward, such as recording an event or refusing a command
A recorded range of ordinary behavior taken from earlier clean runs of a fixture
questions.explanation: A signal is measured data, an assessment interprets it, and a response is what the program then does. A baseline is the recorded ordinary behavior.

questions.prompt: Why does the lesson warn against folding signal, assessment, and response into one hidden boolean?
options: It hides false positives and makes the decision impossible to explain
A boolean cannot be written to a log file without extra conversion
It forces the detector to run once per frame regardless of its state
A boolean uses more memory than three separate enum values do
questions.explanation: With separate types, a test can show what was measured, what was concluded, and what was done. A single flag hides all three.

questions.prompt: What does a call like `IsDebuggerPresent` mostly amount to, according to the lesson?
options: Reading the `BeingDebugged` byte at offset `0x02` of the PEB
Timing a tiny operation and comparing it to a threshold
Scanning its own code for `0xCC` bytes with a checksum
Reading `DR0` through `DR3` from the current thread
questions.explanation: The loader writes that it was started for a debugger into the process, and the program reads the note. Nothing is measured.

questions.prompt: How can a program notice a software breakpoint in its own code?
options: A checksum over its code changes because a byte became `0xCC`
The `DR7` register shows a pending breakpoint address for the debugged thread
The heap `ForceFlags` value falls to zero after the process hits a break
The `PEB` removes its `NtGlobalFlag` field until the program resumes running
questions.explanation: A software breakpoint replaces an instruction byte with `0xCC`, which a checksum over the code sees. Hardware breakpoints leave no such change.

questions.prompt: Why does a checksum over a program's own code miss a hardware breakpoint?
options: It changes no code bytes; it lives in debug registers `DR0` to `DR3` and `DR7`
Hardware breakpoints rewrite the checksum along with the bytes that they change
The checksum runs before debug registers are loaded, so it never sees their values
Hardware breakpoints are removed from memory whenever a checksum starts running
questions.explanation: The two kinds of breakpoint leave traces in different places. Checking only bytes never sees a hardware one, and checking only debug registers never sees a software one.

questions.prompt: The lesson says `GetThreadContext` can inspect debug registers of which kind of thread?
options: A suspended target thread; on a running current thread the context can be invalid
Any running thread, since a success return code proves the register values are live
Only the main thread, since other threads do not have any debug registers at all
A thread in another process, which is the only case in which the call can fail
questions.explanation: Windows documents that a call on the current running thread can return success with an invalid context, so the return code alone is not evidence.

questions.prompt: Median 1.2 us, 99th percentile 8 us, maximum 412 us. What happens with a 10 us threshold?
options: Ordinary background activity trips it several times a minute
It flags only the single 412 us outlier and nothing else
It never fires, since 10 us is higher than the median
It fires only when a debugger is attached to the process
questions.explanation: The ordinary but unlucky samples overlap the paused ones. A low threshold makes false positives a constant occurrence.

questions.prompt: With the same numbers, what is wrong with setting the threshold above 412 us?
options: Almost nothing would trigger it, including the very condition you meant to catch
It would trip on ordinary samples several times each minute, just as 10 us does
It would change the median of the baseline measurements taken on the clean fixture
It would make the maximum value fall below the 99th percentile of the same samples
questions.explanation: No single number separates ordinary from paused cleanly. A very high limit is quiet because the rule is too blind to fire.

questions.prompt: Twenty slow samples in a row came from the same code path. What does that justify?
options: Evidence of a changed environment, though load or power policy may be the cause
A firm conclusion that a debugger must be attached to the game for the whole run
Proof that the game rules were violated by the player during these twenty samples
Permission to refuse every later command from the player after the twentieth sample
questions.explanation: Repetition is stronger than one sample, but it does not reveal intent. Persistent load, power policy, or an attached debugger can all do it.

questions.prompt: What does `assess_delay(8, 8)` return, with the limit being the recorded 99th percentile?
options: `Ordinary`, because the check is `delay_us <= ordinary_p99_us`
`NeedsAnotherSample`, because 8 is not strictly below the limit
`NeedsDiagnosis`, because two equal numbers form a signal
It does not compile, since both arguments are the same value
questions.explanation: The function returns `Ordinary` at or below the limit and `NeedsAnotherSample` above it. A delay of 9 would produce the latter.

questions.prompt: Which description names a response precisely?
options: After two samples over p99 it enters `Diagnosing`; no game state changes
The game detects a debugger as soon as a long delay is seen in a sample
The anti-debug routine reacts whenever it spots something that looks suspicious
The detector decides the player is cheating after repeated timing signals
questions.explanation: A precise description lists the trigger, the state reached, the event emitted, and the effect. Vague statements hide the decision.

questions.prompt: When reversing an unfamiliar anti-debug routine, what does tracing forward from the branch find?
options: Every response and shared sink that the branch can reach
The signals and stored history that fed the branch before it ran
The ordinary variation seen across a set of several clean runs
Whether the routine happens to run on a suspended thread
questions.explanation: Backward from the branch finds signals and history; forward finds responses and sinks. Clean runs estimate ordinary variation.

questions.prompt: The test matrix has an invalid health command with no environment signals. What is expected?
options: The environment is ordinary, the command is rejected, and health is unchanged
The command is accepted, since the quiet environment shows no sign of a debugger
The command is accepted but a diagnostic event is written
The environment is reported as suspicious, and health is unchanged
questions.explanation: A quiet environment must not turn an invalid operation into a valid one. State validity is enforced at the state-changing boundary.

questions.prompt: In the lesson's vocabulary, what does fail-closed mean?
options: Uncertainty leads to the effect being refused
Uncertainty leads to the effect being permitted
A failure closes the diagnostic log file for that run
A failure restarts the sampling window from scratch
questions.explanation: Fail-open and fail-closed describe whether doubt permits or refuses an effect.

questions.prompt: Which situation is a false negative for an anti-debug detector?
options: The target condition occurs without the expected signal appearing
An ordinary slow frame is classified as suspicious by the detector
A clean run is accepted as normal behavior by the detector
A debugger is attached and the detector reports it correctly
questions.explanation: A false positive is an ordinary condition classified as suspicious. A false negative misses the target condition.

questions.prompt: What is the lesson's target invariant for anti-debug behavior?
options: Observations may annotate or pause the run; validity is enforced at the effect boundary
A debugger signal may grant permission to change state, as long as it is recorded
Game state is treated as valid whenever no environmental signal has been observed
A response may change game state, provided telemetry reports the change afterward
questions.explanation: The environment is evidence about the setting, not a verdict about the game state. The state rule must hold whether or not any signal is present.

questions.prompt: In a table of timing measurements, how should the maximum be treated?
options: As one extreme event to inspect, not to generalize from
As the best estimate of the typical duration of a sample
As the threshold that should be used for the detector
As proof that an observer was attached to the process
questions.explanation: The median gives the typical duration, percentiles give ordinary tail latency, and the maximum is a single extreme.

questions.prompt: Which pair of the five terms involves a secret?
options: Authentication and encryption
Obfuscation and encryption
Compression and obfuscation
Serialization and authentication
questions.explanation: Only authentication and encryption need a secret key. Compression, serialization, and obfuscation do not, which is why mistaking obfuscation for encryption sends you hunting for a key that was never there.

questions.prompt: A stored value looks random in a memory viewer. Why is it a mistake to assume encryption?
options: Obfuscation also looks like noise, and there may be no key to find
Random-looking bytes are always plain integers stored in hexadecimal
Encryption cannot be applied to a game value held in memory
Every transform that changes the bytes is a form of compression
questions.explanation: Looking like noise says almost nothing. Obfuscation is a reversible representation, so a hunt for a key can waste days.

questions.prompt: Why should an integrity tag be verified before the decoded value is used?
options: Edited bytes still decode to a plausible number, so a clean decode proves little
Decoding fails whenever the stored bytes were changed, so the tag adds nothing new
The tag holds the very key that is needed to decode the stored value
A tag checked after decoding would no longer match the stored bytes at all
questions.explanation: A value that decodes cleanly is not the same as one nobody tampered with. The tag check is what looks for modification.

questions.prompt: Why does applying the same key a second time undo the XOR step?
options: Because `x ^ k ^ k == x`, as each bit is flipped twice
Because XOR with a key always sets all bits back to zero
Because the key is removed from memory after the first use
Because a second XOR rotates the bits back by seven places
questions.explanation: XOR flips the bits where the key has a 1. Flipping them again restores the original.

questions.prompt: In hexadecimal, what is the 32-bit value 100?
options: `0x00000100`, since the digits are written as in decimal
`0x000000FF`, since 255 is the largest value one byte holds
`0x00000046`, since 4 x 16 + 6 = 70 and the rest is padding
questions.explanation: Each hex digit is four bits. `0x64` is 96 + 4 = 100.

questions.prompt: What is `100 ^ 0x5A3C96E1`, that is `0x64` XORed with the key?
questions.explanation: The top six hex digits of 100 are zero, so the key's digits pass straight through. In the last byte, `0110 0100` against `1110 0001` differ in the bits that give `1000 0101` = `0x85`. The wrong options come from adding, OR-ing, or AND-ing.

questions.prompt: What does `rotate_left(7)` do to a 32-bit value?
options: Moves bits seven places up; the seven pushed off the top re-enter at the bottom
Moves every bit seven places up and fills the seven vacated bottom bits with zeros
Multiplies the whole value by 7 and then wraps the result around at 2^32
Adds 7 to each of the four bytes, wrapping each one of the bytes on its own
questions.explanation: A rotate loses nothing: bits that fall off the high end come back at the low end. A plain shift would drop them.

questions.prompt: With key `0x5A3C96E1`, `encode(100)` is `0x1E4B42AD` and sits in memory as `AD 42 4B 1E`. What does that do to a scan for the value 100?
options: Nothing matches, because no byte of the stored field is `64`
It still matches, because the first byte holds the plain low byte
It matches only after the program restarts, which reloads the key
It matches only at an address that is a multiple of four
questions.explanation: A plain 100 would be stored as `64 00 00 00` on a little-endian machine. The encoded field has no such bytes.

questions.prompt: `encode(100)` is `0x1E4B42AD` and `encode(101)` is `0x1E4B422D`. What does the one-bit difference tell you?
options: 100 ^ 101 = 1 becomes `0x80`, so the rotation is 7 and the key cancels
100 and 101 differ by 1, so the key must be exactly one less than a power of two
The top bit of the lowest byte must equal the lowest bit of the key itself
The one-bit difference shows that the transform is only a plain XOR with `0x80`
questions.explanation: Adding 1 to an even number flips only bit 0, so the encodings differ by `rotl(1, 7)` = 128 = `0x80`. The count falls out without knowing the key.

questions.prompt: Why does `encode(0)` expose the key in the toy transform?
options: `encode(0)` is the key rotated left by 7, so rotating right by 7 returns it
Zero XORed with itself leaves the key sitting unchanged in the stored memory bytes
Encoding zero always stores the key in plain bytes at the start of the field
Zero is the only value for which the rotation and the XOR step will agree with each other
questions.explanation: `0 ^ key` is just the key, so the stored value is the key rotated left by 7. Rotate it right and you have the key.

questions.prompt: The same plain value encodes to different stored bytes after a restart. What does that suggest?
options: The key is not constant; it is made per session or per object
The rotation count changes after every restart of the program, from 7 to a new number
The value is compressed in a different way on each run of the game
The integrity tag is being computed over a different build of the game program
questions.explanation: A fixed key gives fixed output. Differences suggest the key (or a nearby key field) has to be recovered for each session or object.

questions.prompt: For the XOR-and-rotate transform, what is `encode(a) ^ encode(b)` for any two plain values?
options: `rotl(a ^ b, 7)`; the key cancels
`rotl(a, 7) ^ key`; the key stays once
`rotl(a ^ b ^ key, 7)`; the key stays once
`a ^ b ^ key`; the rotation cancels
questions.explanation: Rotation only moves bits and XOR works bit by bit, so rotating then XORing is the same as XORing then rotating. The key appears twice and `key ^ key = 0`.

questions.prompt: `encode(100) ^ encode(0)` equals `rotl(100, 7)`. Since 100 is only seven bits wide, what number is that?
options: 700 (100 x 7), which is `0x2BC`
100, since the rotation does not move the bits
questions.explanation: No bit reaches the top, so the rotation is just a multiplication by 2^7 = 128, giving 12,800 = `0x3200`.

questions.prompt: Why must a decoder reproduce operand widths exactly?
options: An 8-bit rotate is not a 32-bit rotate, and truncation or byte order matters
Wider arithmetic is always more accurate, so a decoder should always prefer it to the narrow one
Narrow widths are required to keep the key secret from a debugger that is attached to it
The width only matters for compression of data, not for any obfuscation of its values
questions.explanation: Machine arithmetic happens at a width. The example only comes out right because the rotation is 32-bit and the bytes are read lowest first.

questions.prompt: For multiplication modulo 2^32, which multiplier can be undone?
options: Any odd multiplier, because each one has a multiplicative inverse here
Any even multiplier, because two even numbers cancel each other out when divided
Only a multiplier that is an exact power of two, such as 128 or 256
Only multipliers that are smaller than 256, since they fit in one byte
questions.explanation: Only an odd multiplier has an inverse mod 2^32. An even multiplier discards information, so the transform cannot be reversed.

questions.prompt: Why is the toy tag beside an encoded value not cryptographic authentication?
options: Anyone who knows the algorithm and key can recompute it
It is stored in plain bytes, and plain bytes can be copied
It is shorter than a hash, so collisions are certain
It is checked after decoding rather than before
questions.explanation: A toy integrity relation catches accidental changes. It does not stop a party who can reproduce the relation.

questions.prompt: Which test checks the recovered model?
options: `decode(encode(value, key), key) == value`, over edge values and keys
`encode(value, key) == value`, for every value and every key that is tested
`decode(value, key) == encode(value, key)`, using one fixed key throughout the test
`encode(encode(value, key), key) == value`, checked for just a single chosen value
questions.explanation: A round trip must restore the original. Edge values such as 0, 1, `u32::MAX`, and carry boundaries are good tests.

questions.prompt: What should a mutation test do with the toy tag?
options: Flip each encoded bit and confirm the tag check refuses the changed sample
Flip each plain bit and confirm that the decode of it still works as before
Delete the tag and confirm that the value still decodes unchanged afterward
Change the key and confirm that the stored bytes stay exactly the same as before
questions.explanation: If a flipped bit is not caught, the tag does not cover it.

questions.prompt: Which row of the comparison table describes authenticated encryption?
options: Nonces make repeated values encrypt differently, and a built-in tag detects changes
Repeated values may reveal obvious patterns, and any tag is an optional ad-hoc add-on to it
No durable secret is needed, and the analysis recovers the transform itself from reading it
The purpose is to change the representation, with no promise of secrecy made at all
questions.explanation: Authenticated encryption keeps data secret and detects modification. Reversible obfuscation only changes representation.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a useful clue in a read path that a stored value is encoded?
options: A conversion to float or a clamp right after the value is decoded
A call that prints the stored value to the console right before every use of it
A branch that always accepts the value without ever comparing it to a limit
A single store of the value at the very start of the program run, with no reads
questions.explanation: Clues include XOR, rotate, byte-swap, add, subtract, and odd multiplies, a nearby key or generation field, duplicate calculations before a comparison, a rejecting branch, and a float conversion or clamp after decoding.

questions.prompt: What does `weak_name_based_policy(LabCommand::ApplyPatch)` return?
options: `true`, since it blocks only the command named `WriteMemory`
`false`, since both state-changing commands are blocked by default
`true`, since `ApplyPatch` is classified as a read-only command
`false`, since a patch needs the write-enabled setting to pass
questions.explanation: The weak rule asks which command this is, and ApplyPatch is not on its denylist. It reaches the same state-changing effect the policy claimed to stop.

questions.prompt: What does the lesson mean by 'coverage by spelling'?
options: It covers only the names it recognizes, not every command with that effect
The control checks that command names are spelled correctly before running them
The control covers every command whose name starts with the same prefix
The control logs each command under its spelled-out name in the event list
questions.explanation: A denylist covers the spellings someone listed. Another name with the same effect slips through.

questions.prompt: Why is adding more forbidden names to the denylist not a real fix?
options: There are as many names as commands, so the list is never complete
Forbidden names slow down the policy, so the lab would run too slowly
The compiler rejects an enum with more than three blocked names
Extra names make `Observe` look like a state-changing command
questions.explanation: A question about names has as many answers as there are names. A question about effect has a fixed number of answers and can be answered completely.

questions.prompt: How many possible answers does 'what does this command do to state?' have in the lab's `Effect` enum, and why does that help?
options: Two, `ReadOnly` or `ChangesState`, so the question can be answered completely
Three, one for each command, so every name is handled by the match
Two, `Allowed` or `Denied`, so a policy has to run before each command
One, since every command in the lab ends in the same function call
questions.explanation: A fixed set of answers means the rule can be exhaustive. A rule about names can never be.

questions.prompt: What happens when a new variant is added to `LabCommand` but not classified in `effect_of`?
options: The code does not compile, because the `match` must cover every variant
The variant is treated as `ReadOnly` and allowed by default
The policy blocks the variant until a test is added for it
The variant is skipped, and a warning is written to the event list
questions.explanation: The `match` makes the classification decision unavoidable, so the denylist that would need extending forever becomes one decision made once.

questions.prompt: With `writes_allowed` set to false, which commands does `effect_based_policy` accept?
options: Only `Observe`, the read-only one
`Observe` and `ApplyPatch`, which is unnamed
`Observe` and `WriteMemory`, which is named
`WriteMemory` and `ApplyPatch`
questions.explanation: Only read-only effects pass in read-only mode. Both `WriteMemory` and `ApplyPatch` change state, so both are refused.

questions.prompt: What should the regression test for Recipe 1 do?
options: Loop over every state-changing variant and check each is denied in read-only mode
Run one `WriteMemory` command in the lab and confirm that this command is denied
Check that `ApplyPatch` appears in the policy's list of blocked command names
Compare the event list from two separate runs of the lab line by line
questions.explanation: Looping over every state-changing variant means a new variant has to be classified and tested.

questions.prompt: The weak patch function checks `build_id == 7`, then the fixture changes it to 8, and the write still happens. What is this gap called?
options: A time-of-check/time-of-use gap, a stale decision
A coverage-by-spelling gap, where a name was missed
A telemetry gap, where a decision left no event
A confusion-matrix gap, where outcomes were miscounted
questions.explanation: The decision was true when made and stale by the time it was used, so the write relied on an old check.

questions.prompt: Where does the repair for Recipe 2 put its validation?
options: Beside the write, checking both the build and the expected old byte
Before the program starts, checking the build only once for the whole run
After the write is done, undoing the change if the build ID differs
In the menu, so that the user can never select a stale command from it
questions.explanation: Checking right next to the write shrinks the gap and lets a changed byte be refused as `state changed`.

questions.prompt: Why can the toy's TOCTOU repair not fully close the gap in a real game process?
options: The target can still change between two calls, and another process cannot be frozen
Real processes ignore expected-byte comparisons for performance reasons in games
Real games encrypt the build ID, so that the check cannot read it at all
A real game has more than one build ID that must be compared at a given time
questions.explanation: So keep the interval small, compare expected bytes, report a mismatch as a normal refusal, and make the operation reversible.

questions.prompt: The old Recipe 3 code denies a write but records no event. Why is that still a problem?
options: A reader cannot tell 'nothing happened' from 'a request was blocked'
The denial lets the write go through without ever checking a policy at all
The event list overflows because every denial is counted twice in the lab
The policy returns `Allowed` for every later command that follows the denial
questions.explanation: It is a telemetry gap, not a control bypass: state is protected, but repeated mistakes are hidden and the control is hard to test.

questions.prompt: What is the fix for the missing denial event?
options: Compute the decision first, then log it whichever way it went
Log the command before the policy runs, then delete denied entries
Log only denied commands, since allowed ones are visible in effects
Return `Denied` early, then log in a separate cleanup step
questions.explanation: Both outcomes must produce an event, so decision and logging are separated.

questions.prompt: Which of these should an audit event not contain?
options: Raw memory contents, secrets, or giant payloads in events
The time and the operation category of the request, kept short
The allow or deny decision of the policy, kept as a short word
A bounded reason code that explains the decision made
questions.explanation: Useful events record time, category, verified target identity, the decision, and a bounded reason, while avoiding secrets, raw memory, keys, and huge payloads.

questions.prompt: In the lab's bypass anatomy, what did the weak control actually check?
options: One command name, and nothing else about its effect
The shared state-changing boundary that every command reaches
The expected old byte at the target, compared before writing
Every state-changing variant of the command enum in the lab
questions.explanation: The promise was that read-only mode prevents state change. The check covered one name, and an equivalent command reached the same sink.

questions.prompt: Why can a detector not read a player's intent?
options: It can only measure signals such as flags or timing and apply a rule
Intent is stored in a field that the detector is simply not permitted to read
Detectors run before the player ever acts, so that there is nothing for them to see
Intent can be read only for commands that the lab has already blocked earlier
questions.explanation: A detector observes proxies. A process name, timing gap, or flag often accompanies a violation without being the invariant itself.

questions.prompt: A rule fires on a legitimate debugger or profiler. How does the lesson classify this?
options: A false positive: a compatibility bug to fix, not proof of hostility
A true positive, since any observer at all indicates a violation of the rule
A false negative, since the observer program was not blocked from running
A true negative, since the rule behaved exactly as it was designed to
questions.explanation: Testing against a controlled fixture fills in the confusion matrix. A harmless tool producing the signal belongs in the false-positive row.

questions.prompt: In the four-outcome table, which row is 'the prohibited effect occurs without the expected signal'?
options: False negative
False positive
True positive
True negative
questions.explanation: A true positive has both signal and prohibited condition. A false negative has the prohibited condition but no signal.

questions.prompt: What do the three controls in this lesson have in common?
options: Each checks something near the property it cares about, not the property
Each checks the correct property but runs too late in the game frame to matter
Each protects a copy of the state that no code path of the game ever reads
Each depends on a timing threshold that the player can tune in the settings
questions.explanation: A greyed-out button, a one-field checksum, and a debugger flag are all easier to check than the real rule, and each can be true while the real property is false.

questions.prompt: What is the repair for all three weak controls?
options: Enforce the invariant at the effect boundary; keep the proxy as a clue
Add more proxy checks until every known path is covered by at least one of them
Make the proxy signal harder to change, so that it can be trusted as permission
Move the proxy check earlier in the frame, so that it runs before any input arrives
questions.explanation: The repair is never 'add more stand-ins'. It is to check where the effect becomes real and demote the stand-in to supporting telemetry.

questions.prompt: Why is `ui_button_unlocked` a poor basis for permission to change the score?
options: It answers how the button should look, not whether the engine may act
It is stored as a `bool`, which cannot be compared with the engine policy value
It is set only after the bonus has already been awarded during the frame
It changes too slowly to be read by the award function inside the same frame
questions.explanation: Presentation state is a copy used for drawing. Scripts, other inputs, and restored UI state can reach the same engine operation.

questions.prompt: In the repro, the engine policy is false, the UI flag is set to true, and `weak_award(25)` is called. What happens?
options: The event is allowed and `bonus` becomes 25, against engine policy
The event is denied with `UiFlagMissing` and `bonus` stays at zero afterward
The event is allowed, but `saturating_add` keeps `bonus` at zero in this case
The event is denied with `EnginePolicyDenied` and `bonus` stays at zero afterward
questions.explanation: The weak function reads only the UI flag, so it allows the award. `allowed = true` together with `bonus = 25` while policy is false is the evidence of the contradiction.

questions.prompt: What does the regression test for the repaired award method keep the UI flag at, and what must it prove?
options: The flag stays true, and the award is denied, `bonus` unchanged
The flag is set to false, and the award is then allowed with `bonus` raised
The flag stays true, and the award is allowed with the maximum value applied
The flag is removed entirely, and the award reports `UiFlagMissing` as its reason
questions.explanation: Keeping the old precondition (flag true) shows that the repaired method no longer trusts it. A second test shows that a valid engine policy still permits a bounded award.

questions.prompt: What does the weak checksum `health * 31` cover?
options: Only the health field
Health and maximum health
Every field in the record
Player ID and generation
questions.explanation: It answers only 'did the health field change?'. Changing `maximum_health` can break the relation while the stored checksum still matches.

questions.prompt: For `StatsRecord::new(7, 80, 100, 3)` with the maximum changed to 60 and no retagging, why is `completely_valid()` false while `weakly_valid()` is true?
options: The full relation also checks `80 <= 60`, which fails; the weak one ignores the maximum
The complete relation recomputes health with a larger multiplier, so the values mismatch
The weak relation fails first, but its result is later overwritten by the full check
The complete relation rejects any record whose generation field holds an odd number
questions.explanation: This is a coverage bypass: the mutation falls outside the measured bytes but changes the meaning of the protected state.

questions.prompt: What does the lesson call a meaningful change outside the data a control examines?
options: A coverage bypass
A time-of-check gap
A telemetry gap
An effect boundary
questions.explanation: A coverage bypass is a change the control never measured. The effect boundary is the point where a change becomes canonical.

questions.prompt: Which fields does the repaired relation cover?
options: Player ID, health, maximum health, and generation, plus a separate range check
Health only, with a much stronger multiplier so that changes are noticed more
Health and maximum health only, because identity is already checked somewhere else
Every field, with the range check removed since the checksum already covers that
questions.explanation: Coverage and the range rule answer different questions. Specific failures such as `ChecksumMismatch` or `OutOfRange` should be reported separately.

questions.prompt: What does the regression suite for the checksum repair do?
options: Mutates each covered field in turn, expects failure, and keeps a valid record passing
Mutates only health, because that is the field the old checksum already covered
Mutates every field together at once and asserts one single combined failure
Replaces the checksum with a larger number and then tests only the valid records
questions.explanation: Keeping a valid record shows verification is not permanently closed, so a repair that rejects everything would fail the suite.

questions.prompt: If a party can recompute an unkeyed checksum, what does the lesson say the system needs?
options: An authenticated owner and a key lifecycle, not a more obscure formula
A longer checksum, so that guessing the value takes more tries
A second checksum over the first, stored in a different place
A hidden formula, so that the party cannot work out the algorithm
questions.explanation: The checksum detects example-data corruption. Defending against a deliberate editor takes real authentication, not obscurity.

questions.prompt: When does `weak_set_health` refuse a request?
options: Only when the environment signal is `ObserverFlagged`
Whenever the requested value is above the maximum health
Whenever the engine policy is false for the request
Only when the value is zero or negative
questions.explanation: Otherwise it stores any number. The flag describes the environment, not the command.

questions.prompt: With health 80 and maximum 100, `weak_set_health(500, EnvironmentSignal::Ordinary)` runs. What results?
options: The event is allowed and health becomes 500, breaking `health <= maximum`
The event is denied as `ValueOutOfRange` and health stays at 80 after it
The event is allowed, but the stored health is clamped down to 100
The event is denied as `ObserverSignalRecorded` and health stays at 80 after it
questions.explanation: No signal is hidden or changed. The absence of one signal simply says nothing about whether the requested value is valid.

questions.prompt: The repaired health command creates two independent events. What are they?
options: An environment observation, and a decision validating `value <= maximum_health`
A snapshot event, and an effect event that records the changed health value
A denial event, and an allow event, so that both outcomes are always written
A checksum event, and a generation event for the record that was changed
questions.explanation: Keeping them separate means the environment record never grants or removes the health invariant.

questions.prompt: Which test coverage does the lesson ask for in the repaired health command?
options: All four combinations of ordinary or flagged signal with valid or invalid values
Only the flagged cases, since those are the ones the old code refused to accept
Only invalid values, tested in an ordinary environment, to see them rejected
One valid and one invalid value, with the environment signal left out of the test
questions.explanation: The repaired rule must hold whether or not the signal is present, so each combination must give the expected decision.

questions.prompt: In the repaired design, what role does the observer flag still play?
options: It helps diagnose a run; it neither grants nor removes the health rule
It grants permission to change health once it has been recorded in a log
It replaces the maximum health check whenever the environment is flagged
It decides whether the decision event is written to the telemetry log at all
questions.explanation: The flag is a clue, not the invariant, and the health relation holds regardless of it.

questions.prompt: What must a complete regression pair prove?
options: The old case is denied, state unchanged; a valid case is allowed and changes only what it should
The old failing case is logged with a reason code, and the valid case is skipped as a result
The valid case still works, and the old failing case is documented in the test notes
Both cases give the same decision and the same event, so that behavior is consistent
questions.explanation: The negative test reproduces the old preconditions and expects a refusal with the canonical state untouched. The positive test shows the repair has not disabled the feature.

questions.prompt: `offset` is `usize::MAX - 3` and `length` is 16 on a 64-bit machine. In a release build, what does `offset + length` evaluate to?
options: 12, so `12 <= 4096` is true and the bound check passes
16, so the check effectively compares only the length with 4096
A value just above `usize::MAX`, so the check fails and the read is refused
0, because the sum lands exactly on the wrap point of the counter
questions.explanation: The sum is computed modulo 2^64, so it wraps past zero to 12. Nothing panics in a release build, and the comparison on the wrapped number is simply true. A bigger integer type would not be the fix; refusing to answer when the sum has no valid value is.

questions.prompt: What does `offset.checked_add(length)` do when the true sum does not fit in a `usize`?
options: It returns `None`, which the repaired check turns into a denial
It returns the wrapped number along with a flag saying the add overflowed
It returns `Some(0)`, so the range is treated as empty and allowed
It panics in every build, so the program stops before reading
questions.explanation: `checked_add` returns an `Option`: `Some(sum)` when the sum fits and `None` when it does not. The repair maps `None` to `false`. Plain `+` is what wraps quietly in a release build.

questions.prompt: The check `request.starts_with("assets/")` allows `assets/../saves/profile.dat`. What is wrong with the check?
options: It tests the supplied text, but that text names a spot outside `assets/`
It is case-sensitive, so a request written as `Assets/` slips past it
It looks only at the first character of the request, which is a letter
It compares file sizes rather than names, so the folder is never checked
questions.explanation: The prefix test reads text, while the rule is about the resolved location. `assets/../saves/profile.dat` resolves to `saves/profile.dat`, outside the root. Case sensitivity is not the problem here.

questions.prompt: In the lab's path repair, what does `resolve` do when a `..` would climb above its own root?
options: It returns `None`, giving the caller a clear answer that the path escapes
It stops climbing at the root and carries on with the remaining segments
It drops the `..` segment and resolves the rest of the path as written
It panics, because climbing above the root is a bug in the lab itself
questions.explanation: The lab walks the segments and pops on `..`; when there is nothing left to pop it returns `None`. That is an answer the caller needs, so quietly clamping at the root would hide the escape attempt.

questions.prompt: Which three outcomes can `verify(...)` produce, according to its `Result<bool, VerifyError>` return type?
options: Matched, did not match, and could not tell
Matched, partly matched, and skipped as too large
Allowed, denied, and written to the audit log
Valid, expired, and revoked by the manifest author
questions.explanation: `Ok(true)` is a match, `Ok(false)` is a mismatch, and `Err(_)` means verification could not run. `unwrap_or(true)` folds the third outcome into the first, which is the bug.

questions.prompt: The repaired asset gate denies with `HashMismatch` in one branch and `VerificationUnavailable` in another. Why keep them as separate reasons?
options: One means a file changed, the other means verification is broken; people respond differently
The first covers mod assets and the second built-in assets, so they go to different logs
Rust requires every variant of an error enum to get its own match arm
Two separate reasons make the audit log shorter than one combined reason
questions.explanation: A mismatch says the asset changed; an unavailable check says your safeguard is broken, which is a larger problem. Collapsing both into one boolean throws that distinction away.

questions.prompt: What is wrong with `weak_apply_batch`, which loops over patches and calls `self.write(address, value)`?
options: It calls the private writer directly, so the policy check never runs and nothing is logged
It applies patches in reverse order, so later patches overwrite earlier ones silently
It copies the policy check but tests the wrong flag, so every write is allowed
It holds the policy lock for the whole loop, which blocks other callers
questions.explanation: The guard was never weakened; it was routed around. The batch path reaches the same effect without passing through the check, and records nothing, so the audit log shows no change while bytes changed.

questions.prompt: What is the lesson's repair for a batch helper that bypasses the write guard?
options: Make the batch helper call `apply_patch` for each item, so there is one entry point to get right
Paste a second copy of the policy check into the batch helper so both paths test the same rule
Make the private `write` function public so each caller can run its own check first
Remove the check from `apply_patch` so the two paths behave identically
questions.explanation: The repair is structural: one way in means one place to be correct. A second copy of the check is tempting but can drift out of step with the first.

questions.prompt: A command with a valid integrity tag, `weak_award(generation 1, amount 50)`, is submitted 4 times to the weak policy. What is the balance afterwards?
options: 200, because a valid tag says nothing about whether the command was used before
50, because the policy remembers the tag and refuses the three repeats outright
100, because the policy allows one replay and then stops to limit the damage
0, because four identical commands cancel each other out when summed
questions.explanation: A tag shows the bytes were not changed. It does not show the command was not already used, so each genuine copy pays out: 4 x 50 = 200. Integrity and freshness are separate properties.

questions.prompt: The repaired policy denies a command when `command.generation <= self.last_generation`. If generation 3 was just applied, which command is accepted?
options: One with generation 4, which is past the last applied one
One with generation 3 but a different amount than before
One with generation 2, provided it carries a larger amount
One with generation 3 and a freshly computed integrity tag
questions.explanation: Only a position strictly past the last applied one passes. Changing the amount or re-tagging does not change the generation, so those are still stale; the receiver has to remember the last generation.

questions.prompt: A design says it stops replay while remembering nothing between messages. What does the lesson conclude?
options: It has not stopped replay, since every such design must keep a counter, window, or timestamp
It can work if the integrity tag uses a much longer key, which makes copies detectable
It can work if every command amount is bounded, which caps the damage from copies
It works, because a valid tag already covers freshness as well as integrity
questions.explanation: The receiver has to remember something: a counter, a window of recent identifiers, or a timestamp with bounded skew. A longer key makes tags harder to forge but does not tell the receiver a genuine message was already used.

questions.prompt: The tool computes `let allowed = *self.cached_allowed.get_or_insert(self.writes_allowed);`. Writes are turned off after the first call. What happens next?
options: It keeps writing, because it reuses the answer stored on the first call
It stops writing at once, because `get_or_insert` re-reads `writes_allowed` every time
It panics, because the cached value and the setting now disagree
It writes once more, then refreshes the cache and stops
questions.explanation: The first call stores the answer and every later call returns that stored value. The tool keeps answering the question asked at start-up, so the repair is to re-read the setting where the write happens.

questions.prompt: A teammate says, "We are single-threaded, so we can skip reviewing for cached-decision bugs." What is the best reply?
options: Nothing raced in the lab; a stale answer needs only an input that changed afterwards
True for most code, but the lab's cache is shared with a background timer thread
One thread is enough, as long as the cache is cleared whenever the program starts
Single-threaded code is safe here, though an optimised build can reorder the cache reads
questions.explanation: The answer simply outlived the input it was computed from. No unlucky timing or second thread is needed, so single-threaded code can have this bug too.

questions.prompt: The movement rule has a maximum step of 400 cm and a tolerance of 5 cm. A player takes 405 cm steps for 600 ticks. How much free distance has been gained beyond the maximum?
options: 3,000 cm, which is 30 metres, with every single tick passing its own check
300 cm, which is 3 metres, because most ticks are rejected as over the limit
5 cm, because the tolerance is only granted once for the whole run
240,000 cm, because the 400 cm maximum is also added on each tick
questions.explanation: Each tick passes, and the excess is 5 cm per tick: 600 x 5 = 3,000 cm. No individual check was wrong; the tolerance simply accumulated.

questions.prompt: Why does the window budget cost honest players nothing when their jitter averages out?
options: A step at or below the maximum spends zero budget, because the excess is clamped at 0
Jitter is filtered out of each step before the step length is measured against the rule
The budget refills in full after every tick, so only a single tick can ever exceed it
Each tick's unused tolerance is subtracted from the next tick's step, cancelling the jitter
questions.explanation: The repair computes `(step - MAX).max(0)` and spends only that. Steps under the maximum spend nothing, while a steady lean in one direction runs the budget out.

questions.prompt: A repair is tested only with inputs that must be denied. What risk does the lesson give for a repair with only a negative test?
options: It tends to be over-tightened until ordinary behaviour breaks
It tends to drift back to the original weakness over time
It tends to run too slowly once the denial list grows
It tends to hide the original mismatch from the audit log
questions.explanation: A negative-only test pushes toward ever stricter rules, so honest use starts failing. A positive-only test is what lets a rule drift back. Both tests, or the repair will not hold.

questions.prompt: A weak batch has `[ {slot 0, value 7}, {slot 9, value 3} ]` and `slots` starts as four zeros. Slot 9 is invalid. After the call, what do the result and `slots` show?
options: `Denied(ItemInvalid)` with `slots = [7, 0, 0, 0]`
`Denied(ItemInvalid)` with `slots = [0, 0, 0, 0]`
`Allowed` with `slots = [7, 0, 0, 0]`
`Denied(ItemInvalid)` with `slots = [7, 0, 0, 3]`
questions.explanation: Slot 0 is written before slot 9 is rejected, so the denial is honest but the state is half-applied. Slot 9 is never written, since it fails validation first.

questions.prompt: What does the repair for a batch that fails halfway do?
options: It validates every item first and writes only once the whole request is known to be acceptable
It writes valid items as it goes and skips invalid ones, reporting `Allowed` for the batch
It validates only the first and last items, then writes the whole list in one pass
It writes every item, then tells callers in a comment to re-check the slots
questions.explanation: Two-phase apply means a denial genuinely means no change. Skipping bad items is tempting, but then the caller gets a state it never asked for. If atomic writes are impossible, the lesson wants an explicit rollback, not a comment.

questions.prompt: What shape do all eight patterns in this lesson share?
options: A control checks a stand-in, the stand-in drifts from the promise, and the effect happens
A cryptographic primitive is too weak, so values get forged by brute-force guessing
A race between two threads lets an action slip in between the check and the use
A control is missing completely, so every request is allowed from the very first
questions.explanation: In every row the control measured something true, but something true was not the same as the thing promised. The repair moves the check to the effect itself. Only one pattern (the check/use gap) involves timing at all.

questions.prompt: Why does the lesson suggest `region.get(offset..end)` as an even better repair than a hand-written comparison?
options: The slice knows its own length, so it returns `None` for every range it does not own
It uses a wider integer type internally, so the sum of offset and length cannot wrap
It copies the bytes first, so the original region is never exposed to the caller
It skips the bounds test in release builds, which makes the read faster
questions.explanation: Asking a value that knows the answer beats recomputing the answer yourself. The slice cannot be argued out of its own length. It does not widen integers, and it keeps its bounds checks in release builds.

questions.prompt: Which question does a debugger answer that a memory scanner cannot?
options: Which instruction just touched the value
Where might this value live in memory
Which value type the game uses for gold
How many copies of the value exist in RAM
questions.explanation: A scanner lists candidate locations for a value. A debugger pauses the program so you can see the instruction that accessed it.

questions.prompt: In the gold lab, what does a write breakpoint on the gold address ask the debugger to do?
options: Pause when an instruction stores to those four bytes
Block every write so the gold value cannot change
Pause when the game reads the gold value for display
Copy the four bytes into a register at each purchase
questions.explanation: A write breakpoint waits for a store to the watched bytes and pauses there. It does not prevent the write, and reads do not trigger a write-only watch.

questions.prompt: Why should you perform exactly one gold-changing action while the breakpoint is set?
options: So the pause can be tied to that action
So the debugger records fewer registers in its log
So the gold address stays the same after a restart
So Windows keeps the thread's context from expiring
questions.explanation: If several actions happen, you cannot tell which one caused a given pause. One action gives one clean cause and effect.

questions.prompt: A write breakpoint fires on a purchase. What does that pause establish?
options: One execution; a later test shows if other actions use it too
That the instruction handles recruiting units and nothing else
That the instruction is the only code that ever writes the gold
That the instruction subtracts the unit price in every build
questions.explanation: The pause is evidence of one execution. The same instruction could also run for other gold changes, which a later test can check.

questions.prompt: Which item can you inspect when a debugger pauses a process?
options: The condition flags used by branches
The source-code variable names of the game
The next game turn's gold amount
The compiler settings used to build the game
questions.explanation: At a pause you can see the next instruction, registers, call stack, nearby memory, and flags. Source names and future values are not there.

questions.prompt: In the register diagram, `rax` holds `0x1122334455667788`. What does `eax` hold?
options: `0x55667788`, the low 32 bits
`0x11223344`, the high 32 bits
`0x7788`, the low 16 bits
`0x1122334455667788`, a separate copy of it
questions.explanation: `eax` is the low half of `rax`, not a separate register. The low 16 bits are `ax` and the low 8 bits are `al`.

questions.prompt: What happens to the upper half of `rax` when an instruction writes `eax`?
options: It is cleared to zero
It is left unchanged
It is copied into `ax`
It is filled with the old `al` byte
questions.explanation: Writing `eax` also clears the upper half of `rax`. Writing `ax` or `al` leaves the rest alone.

questions.prompt: If `ebx` holds `0x5000` at the pause, which address does `[ebx+30h]` name?
options: `0x5030`, because 30h is 48 bytes past the base
`0x5300`, because the offset is shifted one digit
`0x4FD0`, because the offset is subtracted
`0x0030`, because the offset replaces the base
questions.explanation: The brackets name the address base plus offset, and `30h` is 48 in decimal. The offset is a distance, not a replacement address.

questions.prompt: What evidence makes `sub dword ptr [ebx+30h], eax` convincing as the instruction that spends gold?
options: Its address and `eax` match the gold address and price each time
The mnemonic is `sub`, and spending gold means subtracting it
The registers `ebx` and `eax` are the ones always used for gold
It is the first subtraction instruction in the disassembly view
questions.explanation: Register names alone prove nothing. Matching both the address and the price on repeated purchases is strong evidence, and recognizing `sub` alone is not.

questions.prompt: What question does the call stack answer at a pause?
options: Which chain of function calls brought this thread here
Which values were stored in every register earlier
Which instructions will run after the next branch
Which memory addresses the thread has written so far
questions.explanation: A low-level update function may be called from a recruit action, an AI simulation, or a save loader. The stack shows which one led here.

questions.prompt: How does a debugger learn that a thread reached a breakpoint?
options: Windows sends it a debug event after the process pauses
The game sends its own message through a shared file
The debugger polls the registers in a loop between frames
The CPU notifies the debugger directly, skipping Windows
questions.explanation: The debugger is a separate process, and Windows remains the gatekeeper that reports debug events such as breakpoints and DLL loads.

questions.prompt: In debugger terms, what is a thread's context?
options: A snapshot of its registers, with the instruction pointer
A copy of the whole process memory taken when it launched
A list of every function that the thread has ever called
The source file in which the thread's code was written
questions.explanation: The debugger asks Windows for the context of the stopped thread. It can also copy memory separately.

questions.prompt: Why can audio and rendering stop while you inspect a breakpoint?
options: The debugger pauses the whole process so reads stay stable
Breakpoints always lower the process priority for good
The game switches off its media threads after any exception
Windows frees those threads' memory while the pause lasts
questions.explanation: Pausing other threads stops them from changing registers and memory while you read. The cost is that their work waits too.

questions.prompt: Which fact can live debugging establish that disassembly alone cannot?
options: The path actually taken, with concrete register values
Which instructions might exist elsewhere in the file
The branch targets mentioned in a function
The constants referenced by the compiled code
questions.explanation: Disassembly shows possible instructions and paths. Dynamic analysis shows which path a real event took, and with which values.

questions.prompt: A decompiler names a value `player_health`. How should you treat that name?
options: As a guess until the program's behavior matches it
As a fact, because decompilers read the original source
As proof the field is a 32-bit signed integer
As a name recovered from the debug symbols
questions.explanation: A decompiler guesses structure, and machine code is the final record. A friendly name is only a hypothesis until behavior confirms it.

questions.prompt: How could you gather evidence for the rule "subtract 25 only if gold is at least 25"?
options: Try one affordable and one unaffordable purchase, then compare
Run affordable purchases only, and read the registers each time
Read the source-level variable names shown in the decompiler
Place a breakpoint on the very first instruction of the game
questions.explanation: If the subtraction runs only in the affordable case, you have evidence for the proposed rule. Testing only one side cannot show the guard.

questions.prompt: What counts as success for the safe first debugger session?
options: Pausing and resuming, and knowing what each panel shows
Changing the gold value and seeing the new number on screen
Finding the instruction that spends gold on the first try
Writing a patch that survives a restart of the game
questions.explanation: The first session changes nothing in the game. You attach, pause, look at the CPU view, and resume.

questions.prompt: The hook is at `0x00CCAF8A` and the displaced span is 6 bytes. What is the return address?
options: `0x00CCAF90`, because 138 + 6 = 144, which is `0x90`
